cards.front:
Choose the correct adverb: 'She speaks ___ during meetings.'

(A) Confident, the adjective form
(B) Confidently, the adverb form
(C) Confidence, the noun form
(D) Confiding, the verb-ing form
cards.back:
(B) Confidently, the adverb form

Grammar — Parts of Speech — Adverbs modify VERBS. 'Speaks (verb) confidently (adverb).' Most adverbs of MANNER end in '-LY' (loud → loudly, quick → quickly). Some don't change: fast (adj+adv), hard, well (good → well). Distractor 1 = adjective ('a confident speaker'). Distractor 3 = noun ('she has confidence').

Some don't change: fast (adj+adv), hard, well (good → well). Distractor 1 = adjective ('a confident speaker'). Distractor 3 = noun ('she has confidence').

cards.front:
Choose the correct: 'He runs ___ in his class.'

(A) Most fast (incorrect form here)
(B) Fastest, the superlative adv form
(C) More faster, redundant double form
(D) Most fastest, very wrong form
cards.back:
(B) Fastest, the superlative adv form

Grammar — Parts of Speech — FAST = same form for adjective + adverb. Comparative: faster; Superlative: fastest. 'In his class' = 3+ runners → SUPERLATIVE = fastest. Common error: double comparison ('more faster' or 'most fastest') — never combine the two.

cards.front:
Identify the ADVERB OF FREQUENCY: 'I ___ go to the gym.'

(A) Quickly, an adv of manner
(B) Often (frequency adverb)
(C) There, an adv of place
(D) Yesterday, an adv of time
cards.back:
(B) Often (frequency adverb)

Grammar — Parts of Speech — Adverbs of FREQUENCY: always, usually, often, frequently, sometimes, occasionally, rarely, seldom, never, hardly ever. Position: usually BEFORE main verb but AFTER 'be' verb. 'I OFTEN go' / 'She is OFTEN late'. Distractor 1 = manner. Distractor 3 = place. Distractor 4 = time (when something happened).

'I OFTEN go' / 'She is OFTEN late'. Distractor 1 = manner. Distractor 3 = place. Distractor 4 = time (when something happened).

cards.front:
Choose: 'The food was ___ delicious.'

(A) Very, an adv of degree
(B) Very much, redundant intensifier
(C) Most very, wrong combination
(D) Many, used for countable plurals
cards.back:
(A) Very, an adv of degree

Grammar — Parts of Speech — VERY + adjective/adverb (in present/future/positive sense). 'Very delicious', 'very fast', 'very much'. Use 'VERY MUCH' with verbs (I like it very much) or 'much' alone with comparative (much better). Distractor 4 = quantifier for countable nouns ('many books').

cards.front:
Identify the adverb in: 'The boy ran very quickly.'

(A) Boy, the doer of the action only
(B) Quickly, modifying ran (a verb)
(C) Ran, the main verb of the line
(D) Very, modifying quickly here
cards.back:
(B) Quickly, modifying ran (a verb)

Grammar — Parts of Speech — QUICKLY = adverb modifying RAN (verb). VERY also = adverb (degree) modifying 'quickly'. 'Very quickly' = adv phrase. The QUESTION asks for adverb of MANNER (= QUICKLY). 'Very' is also an adverb but modifies an adverb. Multiple adverbs in one sentence = common.
cards.option1: Boy, the doer of the action only
cards.option2: Ran, the main verb of the line

cards.front:
Common error: 'She speaks ___ better English than her brother.' (much/many/very)

(A) Many, used for countables
(B) Much, used with comparatives
(C) Very, an adv of degree only
(D) Much many, redundant pair
cards.back:
(B) Much, used with comparatives

Grammar — Parts of Speech — MUCH + comparative ('much better', 'much faster'). VERY + positive adjective ('very good'). VERY × comparative is generally wrong ('very better' incorrect; use 'much better'). Other comparative intensifiers: far, a lot, lots, considerably, rather, much. 'I am MUCH happier now' / 'It's a LOT bigger'.
cards.option2: Very, an adv of degree only

VERY × comparative is generally wrong ('very better' incorrect; use 'much better'). Other comparative intensifiers: far, a lot, lots, considerably, rather, much. 'I am MUCH happier now' / 'It's a LOT bigger'.

cards.front:
Choose: 'She arrived ___ after the meeting started.'

(A) Slow, the adjective form
(B) Late, an adv of time
(C) Lately, meaning recently in time
(D) Latest, the superlative form
cards.back:
(B) Late, an adv of time

Grammar — Parts of Speech — LATE = late in time (after expected time). 'She arrived LATE'. LATELY = recently / in recent times ('I haven't seen him lately'). Don't confuse: HARD (with effort) vs HARDLY (almost not); NEAR (close) vs NEARLY (almost); HIGH (in elevation) vs HIGHLY (extremely / much). These '-ly' forms have different meanings, not just adverb-of-adjective.

cards.front:
Choose the correct article: ____ Ganges is considered sacred in Hinduism.

(A) A
(B) The
(C) An
(D) No article
cards.back:
(B) The

(B) An
(C) The

(A) a
(B) the
(C) an

cards.front:
Choose the correct article: 'She is ___ honest girl.'

(A) an (vowel sound starts 'h')
(B) a (consonant 'h' is silent)
(C) the (specific girl meant)
(D) no article (zero usage here)
cards.back:
(A) an (vowel sound starts 'h')

Grammar — Parts of Speech — ARTICLE RULE: 'A' before words starting with CONSONANT SOUND; 'AN' before words starting with VOWEL SOUND. KEY: it's the SOUND that matters, not the spelling letter. 'HONEST' starts with letter 'h' but the 'h' is SILENT — so it sounds like 'onest' (vowel sound) → 'AN HONEST'. SIMILARLY: (1) 'an HOUR' (h silent, sounds like 'our'). (2) 'an HEIR' (h silent). (3) 'an HONOUR'. CONTRAST WITH 'h' PRONOUNCED: 'a HOUSE', 'a HORSE', 'a HEAVENLY view'. EXAMPLES with VOWEL LETTERS but CONSONANT SOUND: (1) 'a UNIVERSITY' (sounds 'yu' like 'you'). (2) 'a USEFUL tool' (sounds 'yu'). (3) 'a UNICORN' (sounds 'yu'). (4) 'a ONE-EYED giant' (sounds 'wun' like 'wun'). (5) 'a EUROPEAN'. CONTRAST: 'an UMBRELLA' (sounds 'um'); 'an UNCLE'; 'an HOUR' (h silent → vowel sound 'our'). EXAM TRAP: students mechanically apply 'A before consonant LETTER, AN before vowel LETTER' — wrong; it's about SOUND, not spelling. PYQ FREQUENCY: article rules are SSC CGL, IBPS PO English staples — 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
Pick the correct article: 'I bought ___ apple from the market.'

(A) an (vowel sound 'a')
(B) a (a consonant rule)
(C) the (specific apple needed)
(D) no article needed (zero use)
cards.back:
(A) an (vowel sound 'a')

Grammar — Parts of Speech — 'APPLE' starts with VOWEL SOUND ('a' in 'app'). So article is 'AN'. KEY: 'an' before all 5 vowel sounds — A, E, I, O, U (when pronounced as vowel). VOWEL-START WORDS taking 'AN': an apple, an egg, an inch, an orange, an umbrella, an idea, an island, an enemy, an opera. CONSONANT-START WORDS taking 'A': a book, a car, a dog, a school, a tree, a window. INDEFINITE ARTICLE 'A/AN' USAGE: (1) Refers to ANY ONE of a class — 'I want an apple' (any apple). (2) Introduces a NEW item not previously mentioned. (3) Used with COUNTABLE NOUNS in singular. DEFINITE ARTICLE 'THE' USAGE: (1) Refers to a SPECIFIC item known to speaker + listener. 'The apple I bought yesterday'. (2) Used with UNIQUE entities — the sun, the moon, the President of India. (3) Used with SUPERLATIVES — the best, the tallest. (4) Used with PROPER NOUNS like rivers, oceans, mountains (the Ganga, the Pacific, the Himalayas). EXAMPLES: 'I read A book yesterday' (some book) vs 'I read THE book' (specific). PYQ FREQUENCY: a/an/the usage in SSC CGL, IBPS PO 2-3× per paper. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests article-rule discipline.

cards.front:
Choose the correct: 'He is ___ M.B.B.S. doctor.'

(A) an (M sounds like 'em')
(B) a (M starts a consonant)
(C) the (specific doctor named)
(D) no article needed (zero usage)
cards.back:
(A) an (M sounds like 'em')

Grammar — Parts of Speech — 'M.B.B.S.' is pronounced letter-by-letter: 'EM-BEE-BEE-ESS'. The first sound is 'EM' — a VOWEL SOUND. So article is 'AN'. KEY RULE: for ABBREVIATIONS / INITIALISMS, decide article by FIRST SOUND when read aloud: (1) 'an MBA' (em-bee-ay — vowel 'em'). (2) 'an MA' (em). (3) 'an LLB' (el). (4) 'an FRCS' (ef). (5) 'an SOS' (es). (6) 'an X-ray' (eks). (7) 'an MBBS doctor'. (8) 'a NATO meeting' (NATO read as 'NAY-toe' — consonant). (9) 'a UNICEF program' (yoo). LETTERS BY SOUND: A (ay/eh), E (ee), F (ef), H (aitch), I (eye), L (el), M (em), N (en), O (oh), R (are), S (es), X (eks). All these have VOWEL onset → take 'an'. B (bee), C (see), D (dee), G (jee), J (jay), K (kay), P (pee), Q (kyoo), T (tee), U (yoo), V (vee), W (double-yoo), Y (why), Z (zee/zed) — start with consonant SOUND → take 'a'. SAMPLE: 'a B.A. degree' (bee = consonant); 'an L.L.B. degree' (el = vowel). PYQ FREQUENCY: article-with-acronyms in SSC CGL, IBPS PO, RBI Grade B 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Choose: '___ Ganges is a sacred river of India.'

(A) The (definite, river name)
(B) A (an indefinite article)
(C) An (a vowel-sound start)
(D) No article (zero used here)
cards.back:
(A) The (definite, river name)

Grammar — Parts of Speech — 'THE' is used with NAMES OF RIVERS, OCEANS, SEAS, MOUNTAIN RANGES. 'THE GANGES' is correct. RIVERS taking 'the': the Ganges, the Yamuna, the Indus, the Brahmaputra, the Nile, the Amazon, the Mississippi, the Thames. OCEANS: the Pacific, the Atlantic, the Indian Ocean, the Arctic. SEAS: the Arabian Sea, the Mediterranean, the Black Sea. MOUNTAIN RANGES: the Himalayas, the Western Ghats, the Alps, the Andes, the Rockies. SINGULAR MOUNTAINS: usually NO article — Mount Everest, Mount Kilimanjaro, Mount Fuji (NO 'the'). EXCEPTION: 'the Matterhorn' (some single mountains take 'the'). DESERTS: the Sahara, the Thar, the Gobi. ISLAND GROUPS: the Andaman Islands, the Maldives, the Bahamas. SINGLE ISLANDS: usually NO article — Sri Lanka, Cuba, Madagascar, Java. CONTINENTS, COUNTRIES (most): NO article — Asia, India, Japan, Australia. EXCEPT: the United Kingdom, the United States, the Netherlands, the Philippines (plural/group names). LANGUAGES: NO article — English, Hindi, French, Mandarin. PYQ FREQUENCY: 'the + proper noun' usage in SSC CGL, IBPS PO, RBI English 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
Pick the article: '___ honesty is the best policy.'

(A) No article (abstract noun general)
(B) The (specific honesty meant)
(C) A (indefinite singular ref)
(D) An (vowel-sound start one)
cards.back:
(A) No article (abstract noun general)

Grammar — Parts of Speech — ABSTRACT NOUNS used in GENERAL SENSE take NO ARTICLE (zero article). 'Honesty is the best policy' = honesty as a general concept; no specific instance. Other abstract nouns in general use: love, beauty, courage, wisdom, knowledge, faith, kindness — usually no article when speaking generally. EXCEPTIONS — 'THE' is used WHEN: (1) Followed by a SPECIFYING phrase: 'THE honesty of his answer impressed me'. (2) Talking about a SPECIFIC instance: 'THE wisdom he showed was admirable'. ABSTRACT NOUNS USED WITH SPECIFIC ARTICLES: 'a kindness' (a specific kind act), 'an honesty I rarely see' (a particular instance). UNCOUNTABLE NOUNS — material/abstract: usually NO article when general. 'Water is essential' (general); 'THE water in this glass' (specific). MASS NOUNS without article: water, milk, sugar, rice, music, advice, information, news, furniture, luggage. WHEN used in COUNTING context, they take articles or quantifiers: 'a glass of water', 'two pieces of advice' (advice itself is uncountable; 'pieces of advice' is countable). KEY: 'NEWS' is uncountable — 'The news IS good' (NOT 'are'); 'INFORMATION' is uncountable. PYQ FREQUENCY: zero-article + abstract nouns in SSC CGL Tier 2, IBPS PO Mains 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Choose: 'The ___ rich are not always happy.'

(A) no extra article needed (the+adjective)
(B) a (rich is just one person here)
(C) an (vowel sound start 'r')
(D) the (already added there)
cards.back:
(A) no extra article needed (the+adjective)

Grammar — Parts of Speech — 'THE + ADJECTIVE' = represents a CLASS or GROUP. 'The rich' = rich PEOPLE in general; 'the poor' = poor people; 'the elderly' = elderly people. NO further article needed. SAMPLE: (1) 'THE BRAVE deserves the fair' = brave people. (2) 'THE INJURED were taken to hospital' = injured people. (3) 'THE DEAD have been honoured'. (4) 'THE BLIND can read with Braille'. cards.front:

COMMON LIST: criterion → criteria, phenomenon → phenomena, datum → data, medium → media, bacterium → bacteria, syllabus → syllabi/syllabuses. USAGE TIP: 'data is' vs 'data are' is now a stylistic choice — formal scientific writing uses 'data are' (treating data as plural of datum); colloquial usage treats 'data' as singular mass-noun. EXAMINER MINDSET: testing whether you've memorized the Greek/Latin plural list — a standard editor-level skill in journalism, academia, civil services drafting.

(A) Mice is the correct plural
(B) Mouses alone alone alone
(C) Mices alone alone alone alone
(D) Mouse alone alone alone alone
cards.back:
(A) Mice is the correct plural

Grammar — Parts of Speech — VOWEL-CHANGE PLURAL (Old English umlaut pattern): mouse → mice; goose → geese; foot → feet; tooth → teeth; man → men; woman → women. INTERESTING TWIST: 'computer mouse' (the device) is plural as 'mouses' OR 'mice' depending on style guide — Oxford prefers 'mice', Microsoft style guide allows 'mouses'. ETYMOLOGY: this i-mutation reflects Proto-Germanic vowel-fronting before plural suffix; the suffix later disappeared but the vowel change stayed. EXAM TRAP: 'mooses' for moose — moose's plural is 'moose' (no change), not 'mooses' or 'meese'. RELATED IRREGULARS: child → children (-en plural), ox → oxen, brother → brethren (archaic). PYQ FREQUENCY: 1-2 such irregular-plural Qs every SSC CGL Tier 1 paper.

(B) Leafs alone alone alone alone
(C) Leaffes alone alone alone

cards.back:
(A) Leaves is the correct plural

Grammar — Parts of Speech — F → V change rule: nouns ending in -f or -fe often change to -ves in plural. EXCEPTIONS (just add -s): chief → chiefs; roof → roofs; cliff → cliffs; belief → beliefs; proof → proofs. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests pattern-recognition + memorization of exceptions — a classic 'rule + irregular' English structure.

cards.front:
What is the plural of the foreign-origin noun 'cactus'?

(A) Cacti is the standard plural
(B) Cactuses alone alone alone
(C) Cactuss alone alone alone
(D) Cactusi alone alone alone alone
cards.back:
(A) Cacti is the standard plural

Grammar — Parts of Speech — Latin -us nouns typically pluralize with -i: cactus → cacti; nucleus → nuclei; alumnus → alumni; radius → radii; fungus → fungi; stimulus → stimuli; locus → loci; syllabus → syllabi (or syllabuses). NOTE: 'cactuses' IS accepted by Oxford and Webster as an alternative plural — but for SSC/IBPS exams, 'cacti' is the safer pick. EXCEPTIONS to -us → -i: 'genus' → 'genera' (Greek-style), 'corpus' → 'corpora'. EXAM TIP: when you see -us, ask 'is it Latin?' — if yes, default to -i; if uncertain, regular -es works in most modern contexts. INTERESTING: 'octopus' is GREEK origin, not Latin, so technically 'octopi' is hypercorrect — Greek would give 'octopodes'; modern usage allows 'octopuses' (most natural) or 'octopi' (semi-popular). PYQ ANGLE: 'cacti', 'fungi', 'alumni' all appear in SSC CGL across years.

cards.front:
Which sentence uses noun-number CORRECTLY? 'The news ___ coming in fast.'

(A) is — news takes singular verb
(B) are — news is plural alone
(C) were — news is plural alone
(D) have alone alone alone alone
cards.back:
(A) is — news takes singular verb

Grammar — Parts of Speech — Despite ending in -s, NEWS is grammatically SINGULAR (an uncountable mass noun): 'the news IS encouraging'; 'no news IS good news'. Same pattern: mathematics, physics, economics, politics, statistics, civics, ethics, athletics, gymnastics — all -ics nouns are singular when referring to the SUBJECT/FIELD. BUT they can be plural when referring to ACTIVITIES/QUALITIES: 'his statistics ARE impressive' (= his data/numbers); 'her politics ARE radical' (= her political views). MEMORY TRICK — singular -s nouns: NEWS, SCIENCE-NAMES (-ics), MEASLES, MUMPS, BILLIARDS, DOMINOES. EXAM TRAP: 'the data are/is' — both accepted; formal science prefers 'data are', everyday English often uses 'data is'. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests whether you recognize that morphology (the -s) doesn't always equal plural number — mass-noun grammar is a higher-order English skill.

cards.front:

(A) for (duration of time)
(B) since (a starting point)
(C) from (similar to since)

Grammar — Parts of Speech — FOR + DURATION (length of time); SINCE + STARTING POINT (specific time/date). 'Waiting FOR 2 hours' = duration. 'Waiting SINCE 9 AM' = starting point. EXAMPLES: (1) 'I have lived here for 5 years.' (2) 'I have lived here since 2020.' (3) 'I haven't seen her for 3 months.' (4) 'I haven't seen her since June.' KEY USAGE: FOR — duration: 'for an hour, for 2 days, for years'. SINCE — point in time: 'since Monday, since 1990, since I was a child, since lunch'. SAMPLE COMBINATIONS — 'I've been studying for 3 hours since 8 PM' (both used together). FROM — similar to 'since' for STARTING POINT but typically used with END point: 'from Monday TO Friday', 'from morning till night', 'from 9 to 5'. WHEN to use FROM vs SINCE: SINCE is for present-perfect tense + still ongoing; FROM is for an ENDED PERIOD. e.g., 'I worked there FROM 2018 TO 2022' (no longer there) vs 'I have worked there SINCE 2018' (still working). IN: typically with a complete period — 'in 2020, in March, in the morning'. AT: with specific times — 'at 5 PM, at midnight'. PYQ FREQUENCY: for/since distinction in SSC CGL, IBPS PO English 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
Choose: 'She is angry ___ him ___ his behaviour.'

(A) with, for / about (with-person, for-reason)
(B) at, on (at-person, on-reason) (option here)
(C) from, of (from-person, of-reason)
(D) to, in (wrong combinations) (option here)
cards.back:
(A) with, for / about (with-person, for-reason)

Grammar — Parts of Speech — EMOTION + PERSON + REASON construction: 'angry WITH (a person) FOR/ABOUT (a reason/thing)'. So 'angry WITH him FOR/ABOUT his behaviour'. Both 'for' and 'about' work; 'for' more common with concrete reasons. KEY EMOTION-PREPOSITION PAIRS (memorize): (1) ANGRY: with someone, at/about something. (2) AFRAID OF something/someone. (3) PROUD OF something/someone. (4) ASHAMED OF. (5) JEALOUS OF. (6) FOND OF. (7) SUSPICIOUS OF. (8) AWARE OF. (9) CAPABLE OF. (10) FAMOUS FOR. (11) RESPONSIBLE FOR. (12) GRATEFUL FOR. (13) SORRY FOR/ABOUT. (14) GOOD AT (skill). (15) INTERESTED IN. (16) CONFIDENT OF/IN. (17) WORRIED ABOUT. (18) ENTHUSIASTIC ABOUT. (19) TIRED OF. (20) BORED OF/WITH. ADJECTIVE-DEPENDENT PREPOSITION: many emotion-adjectives have FIXED prepositions; learn pairs by heart. EXAM TIP: when stuck, try inserting each preposition; the 'natural' choice is typically correct. SAMPLE: 'He is GOOD AT mathematics' (NOT 'in'). 'She is INTERESTED IN history' (NOT 'on'). 'The dog is AFRAID OF thunder' (NOT 'from'). PYQ FREQUENCY: adjective-preposition combinations in SSC CGL, IBPS PO 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
Pick the correct: 'The book is divided ___ ten chapters.'

(A) into (entry/separation)
(B) in (states a location)
(C) to (movement preposition)
(D) at (a specific point)
cards.back:
(A) into (entry/separation)

Grammar — Parts of Speech — 'DIVIDED INTO' is the standard collocation for SEPARATING something into PARTS/SECTIONS. 'Into' = movement INTO + becoming part of = SEPARATION result. KEY DISTINCTION: IN vs INTO: (1) IN — describes a STATIC LOCATION (where something IS): 'The book is IN the bag.' (2) INTO — describes ENTRY or TRANSFORMATION: 'He went INTO the room.' 'The water turned INTO ice.' PRACTICE: (1) 'The lecture was divided INTO three parts' (NOT 'in'). (2) 'Pour the water INTO the glass' (movement). (3) 'She broke the chocolate INTO 10 pieces.' (4) 'Translate this INTO Hindi' (transformation). VS IN — STATIC: 'I am IN the room.' 'The pen is IN my hand.' COMMON DIVIDED-INTO contexts: (a) Books/chapters: 'divided into chapters'. (b) Numbers: 'divide 100 INTO 4 equal groups = 25 each'. (c) Time periods: 'divided into seasons'. (d) Geographic regions: 'India is divided into 28 states'. EXAM TRAP: 'in' or 'into'? — if there's MOTION, BREAKING UP, or TRANSFORMATION: use 'into'. If static location: use 'in'. PYQ FREQUENCY: in/into distinction in SSC CGL, IBPS PO 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Choose: 'I differ ___ you on this point.'

(A) from / with (both correct)
(B) to (wrong preposition)
(C) in (wrong here)
(D) of (a wrong choice)
cards.back:
(A) from / with (both correct)

Grammar — Parts of Speech — BOTH 'differ FROM' AND 'differ WITH' are CORRECT but with DIFFERENT NUANCES: (1) DIFFER FROM = TO BE DIFFERENT (in nature, type, kind). 'Apples differ FROM oranges in taste.' (2) DIFFER WITH = TO DISAGREE (in opinion). 'I differ WITH you on this point' = I disagree with you. SAMPLE: 'My view differs WITH the popular opinion' (disagreement); 'Indian English differs FROM American English' (difference in form). VERB-PREPOSITION PAIRS to memorize: (1) DIFFER FROM/WITH (above). (2) AGREE WITH (a person) / TO (a proposal): 'I agree with you / I agree to your plan'. (3) ARGUE WITH (a person) / ABOUT (a topic). (4) APOLOGIZE TO (a person) / FOR (an act). (5) BORROW FROM (a person/place). (6) COMPARE TO/WITH: 'compare TO' (find similarities) / 'compare WITH' (find differences). (7) CONSIST OF (be made up of). (8) CONGRATULATE ON (an achievement). (9) DEPEND ON. (10) PREFER X TO Y. (11) REMIND OF / ABOUT. (12) REPLY TO. (13) SEARCH FOR. (14) THANK FOR. (15) WRITE TO (a person) / IN (a language). EXAM TIP: certain verbs have fixed prepositions; learn through usage. PYQ FREQUENCY: verb-preposition pairs in SSC CGL Tier 2, IBPS PO English 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Identify the correct: 'The cat jumped ___ the table.'

(A) onto (movement to top of)
(B) on (static location)
(C) in (inside the table)
(D) at (a specific spot)
cards.back:
(A) onto (movement to top of)

Grammar — Parts of Speech — 'ONTO' = movement to a SURFACE; SETTLES on top of. 'The cat jumped ONTO the table' = jumped + ended up on top. KEY DISTINCTION: ON vs ONTO: (1) ON — STATIC location on a surface. 'The book is ON the table.' (2) ONTO — MOTION leading TO the surface. 'He climbed ONTO the roof.' SIMILAR DIRECTIONAL PREPOSITIONS: (a) IN/INTO — 'water IN the glass' (static) vs 'pour water INTO glass' (motion). (b) OFF/OFF OF (US) — 'jumped OFF the chair'. (c) UP/UP TO — 'walk UP to me'. (d) DOWN/DOWN INTO — 'fell down into the well'. (e) ACROSS/THROUGH — 'walked across the bridge' vs 'walked through the tunnel'. (f) OVER/UNDER — 'jumped over the fence' vs 'crawled under the fence'. (g) AROUND — 'walked around the house'. STILL/MOVEMENT pattern: STATIC = simple preposition; MOTION = compound (often + 'to'). NUANCE: 'into', 'onto', 'upon' are all motion-emphasizing variants. UPON (formal/literary): 'climbed upon a hill'. INFORMAL: often just 'on'. EXAM-FAVOURITE TRAP: a motion verb (jump, run, climb, walk, crawl) typically pairs with motion preposition (into, onto, up to). PYQ FREQUENCY: motion vs static prepositions in SSC CGL, IBPS PO 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Pick the correct: 'I have known him ___ a long time.'

(A) for (duration of friendship)
(B) since (a starting point)
(C) from (a starting point)
(D) by (a deadline preposition)
cards.back:
(A) for (duration of friendship)

Grammar — Parts of Speech — 'FOR a long time' — duration of relationship. Use FOR with TIME PERIODS (an hour, a day, a year, a long time, ages, a moment, a while, a fortnight). Use SINCE with STARTING POINTS (Monday, 1990, I was 5 years old, lunch). KEY: 'a long time' is a DURATION phrase, not a specific starting point — 'for' is correct. EXAMPLES: (1) 'He has been working here FOR 10 years.' (2) 'They've been married SINCE 2010.' (3) 'I haven't seen her FOR ages.' (4) 'I haven't seen her SINCE my last visit.' COMMON 'FOR' + DURATION expressions: for an hour, for ages, for a moment, for a while, for some time, for many years, for a fortnight, for the past month. COMMON 'SINCE' + STARTING POINT: since Monday, since 5 PM, since this morning, since last week, since 2020, since I started college, since lunch, since the meeting. ALSO USED: PRESENT PERFECT TENSE typically requires for/since: 'I HAVE LIVED here for 5 years' (still living) / 'I HAVE BEEN WAITING since 9' (still waiting). PAST SIMPLE doesn't typically use for/since for completed periods (use 'from-to'): 'I lived there FROM 2010 TO 2015.' PYQ FREQUENCY: for/since with present perfect in SSC CGL, IBPS PO 1× per paper.

(B) She bore with a son last year.
(C) The bridge cannot bear with the weight.
(D) He bore with the trophy proudly.
cards.back:
(A) Please bear with me while I set up the projector.

Grammar — Parts of Speech — 'Bear with (someone)' = be patient with someone. 'Bear a child' uses plain bear. 'Bear the weight' = support the weight (no 'with'). 'Bear the trophy' — the trophy is just carried; no 'with'.

cards.option2: The bridge cannot bear with the weight.
cards.option3: He bore with the trophy proudly.

cards.front:
Choose: 'The book is ___.' (mine / my)

(A) Mine (possessive pronoun)
(B) My (possessive adjective only)
(C) Me (object pronoun)
(D) I (subject pronoun)
cards.back:
(A) Mine (possessive pronoun)

Grammar — Parts of Speech — POSSESSIVE PRONOUN (stand-alone, no noun follows): MINE, YOURS, HIS, HERS, ITS, OURS, THEIRS. Used after BE-verb or alone: 'The book is MINE'. POSSESSIVE ADJECTIVE (modifies a following noun): MY, YOUR, HIS, HER, ITS, OUR, THEIR. Used before noun: 'My book' / 'her car'. INSIGHT — many languages don't distinguish possessive pronoun + adjective; English does. Common error: 'The book is MY' (wrong; 'my' needs a noun after it). Pronoun classification: PERSONAL (I, you, he); POSSESSIVE (mine; my); REFLEXIVE (myself); DEMONSTRATIVE (this, that); RELATIVE (who, which); INTERROGATIVE (who?); INDEFINITE (someone, anything).

cards.front:
Choose: 'Between you and ___, the secret is safe.' (I / me)

(A) Me (object of preposition)
(B) I (subject pronoun, wrong)
(C) Myself (reflexive, wrong here)
(D) Mine (possessive, wrong here)
cards.back:
(A) Me (object of preposition)

Grammar — Parts of Speech — After PREPOSITIONS (between, for, to, with, etc.) → use OBJECT PRONOUN: ME, you, HIM, HER, IT, US, THEM. 'Between you and ME' (correct). Common HYPER-correction: people say 'between you and I' thinking 'I' sounds polite — actually WRONG. SUBJECT pronouns (I, he, she, we, they) used as SUBJECTS of clauses ('I am tired'). 'Between you + me' is on every grammar test. Other tricky cases: 'just for you and me' (NOT 'and I'); 'gave it to him and me' (NOT 'he and I'). Test: drop the other person → 'between me' (sounds right) vs 'between I' (sounds wrong).

cards.front:
Choose: 'The man ___ called yesterday is my uncle.' (who / whom)

(A) Who (subject of called)
(B) Whom (object form, wrong here)
(C) Whose (possessive form, wrong)
(D) Which (for things, not people)
cards.back:
(A) Who (subject of called)

Grammar — Parts of Speech — WHO vs WHOM rule: WHO = subject (does the action); WHOM = object (receives action). 'WHO called' (he is the doer of calling). Compare: 'The man WHOM I called' = I called him; he is the OBJECT. SHORTCUT TEST: replace with HE/SHE (subject) or HIM/HER (object). 'HE called' fits → 'who'. 'I called HIM' fits → 'whom'. Modern usage: 'whom' is fading in conversational English; 'who' often replaces it. But formal writing + grammar tests still distinguish. WHOSE = possessive for both people + things ('the man whose car...'). WHICH = things only ('the car which...').

cards.front:
Choose: 'She did the work all by ___.'

(A) Herself (reflexive pronoun)
(B) Her (object pronoun)
(C) Hers (possessive pronoun)
(D) Sheself (incorrect form)
cards.back:
(A) Herself (reflexive pronoun)

Grammar — Parts of Speech — REFLEXIVE pronoun used when subject + object are SAME person, OR for emphasis. 'BY HERSELF' = alone, without help. List of reflexives: myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves. NOTE: ONESELF (not 'oneself's). Don't say: 'hisself' (wrong; correct = himself); 'theirselves' (wrong; correct = themselves). EMPHATIC use: 'I myself saw it' = I personally saw it (intensifier). REFLEXIVE: 'I cut myself' = I cut me (subject = object). Common use: 'enjoy yourself' (have fun), 'help yourself' (serve yourself food).

cards.front:
Choose: 'Neither John nor his brothers ___ available.' (is / are)

(A) Are (verb agrees with closer subject)
(B) Is (singular, wrong here) too
(C) Was (singular past, wrong) too
(D) Were (plural past, wrong tense)
cards.back:
(A) Are (verb agrees with closer subject)

Grammar — Parts of Speech — NEITHER ... NOR / EITHER ... OR — verb agrees with NEAREST subject (proximity rule). 'Brothers' (plural) is closest → 'ARE'. If reversed: 'Neither his brothers nor John IS available' (singular John closer). KEY RULES related to subject-verb agreement: (1) Singular subjects joined by 'AND' = plural verb ('John and Mary are'). (2) Joined by 'OR/NOR' = nearer subject's number. (5) Collective nouns (team, government) = singular if as a whole, plural if members ('The team is winning' / 'The team have their problems').

cards.front:
Identify the type: 'If you heat ice, it melts.'

(A) Zero conditional (general truth)
(B) First conditional (real future)
(C) Second conditional (unreal now)
(D) Third conditional (unreal past)
cards.back:
(A) Zero conditional (general truth)

Verb Forms & Tenses — ZERO CONDITIONAL: 'If + present simple, present simple.' Used for SCIENTIFIC FACTS, GENERAL TRUTHS, automatic consequences. Example: 'If you heat ice, it melts.' EVERY time you heat ice, it melts — universal truth. STRUCTURE: IF + V1 (present simple), V1 (present simple). 'When' can replace 'if' in zero conditional with the same meaning ('When you heat ice, it melts'). FOUR MAIN CONDITIONALS: (0) ZERO — facts: If + present, present. 'If you mix red and blue, you get purple.' (1) FIRST — real future: If + present, will + V1. 'If it rains, I will stay home.' (2) SECOND — unreal/hypothetical present/future: If + past, would + V1. 'If I were rich, I would travel.' (3) THIRD — unreal past: If + past perfect, would have + V3. 'If I had studied, I would have passed.' MIXED — combinations of past unreal cause + present unreal effect: 'If I had studied harder, I would be a doctor now.' KEY EXAM TRAP: 'will' NEVER goes in the IF-CLAUSE in standard conditionals. PYQ FREQUENCY: conditionals appear in SSC CGL, IBPS PO English 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
Choose the correct form: 'If it ___ tomorrow, we will cancel the picnic.'

(A) rains (first-conditional, present)
(B) will rain (no will in if-clause)
(C) rained (this is past form here)
(D) would rain (a 2nd-cond marker)
cards.back:
(A) rains (first-conditional, present)

Verb Forms & Tenses — FIRST CONDITIONAL: refers to REAL/POSSIBLE FUTURE situations. STRUCTURE: 'If + PRESENT SIMPLE, WILL + base verb'. So 'If it RAINS tomorrow, we WILL cancel the picnic.' KEY ERROR (very common): students write 'If it WILL RAIN' — INCORRECT. The IF-CLAUSE uses present tense even though it refers to the future. Reason: English uses present-tense in the if-clause to describe the FUTURE CONDITION; 'will' is reserved for the result-clause. EXCEPTIONS — 'will' CAN appear in if-clause when: (a) Polite request: 'If you WILL wait here, I'll get the manager.' (b) Stress on willingness: 'If you WILL NOT cooperate, we'll have to fire you.' But these are special, NOT standard conditional. ALSO ACCEPTABLE: 'might', 'may', 'can', 'should', 'shall' in result-clause: 'If it rains, I MIGHT stay home' (less certain than 'will stay home'). FIRST CONDITIONAL is for FUTURE possibilities you consider REAL. SECOND CONDITIONAL ('If I were you, I would not go') is for HYPOTHETICAL/UNREAL situations. PYQ FREQUENCY: first vs second conditional confusion is a top SSC CGL, IBPS PO English MCQ — 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
Choose the correct form: 'If I ___ a millionaire, I would travel the world.'

(A) were (subjunctive for hypothetical)
(B) was (regular past tense form)
(C) am (the present-tense form)
(D) had been (a past perfect tense)
cards.back:
(A) were (subjunctive for hypothetical)

Verb Forms & Tenses — SECOND CONDITIONAL: hypothetical/unreal PRESENT or FUTURE. STRUCTURE: 'If + past simple, would + base verb'. Special case: SUBJUNCTIVE — 'were' is used (instead of 'was') for ALL persons in formal English with the verb 'BE'. So 'If I WERE a millionaire' (NOT 'If I WAS a millionaire' in formal usage). 'If he WERE here, he would help.' PURPOSE OF SUBJUNCTIVE: emphasizes that the situation is HYPOTHETICAL — opposite of reality. INFORMAL ENGLISH allows 'was': 'If I was rich, I'd buy a house' — acceptable in casual speech but marked DOWN in formal exams. KEY EXAM PATTERN: 'If I were' = correct in SSC CGL, IBPS PO English-section. EXTENSION TO PHRASES: 'If I were you, I would...' (advice-giving formula); 'I wish I were taller' (regret/desire); 'It's time you were leaving' (suggestion). MIXED CONDITIONAL: 'If I had studied harder (past), I would be successful now (present)' — combines third-conditional cause + second-conditional effect. PYQ FREQUENCY: 'were' vs 'was' in conditionals is a top SSC, IBPS English MCQ — 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Pick the correct form: 'If I had known earlier, I ___ helped you.'

(A) would have (third conditional)
(B) will have (wrong tense form)
(C) would (incomplete conditional)
(D) had (a wrong auxiliary mix)
cards.back:
(A) would have (third conditional)

Verb Forms & Tenses — THIRD CONDITIONAL: UNREAL PAST — situations that DIDN'T happen. STRUCTURE: 'If + past perfect (had + V3), would have + V3'. So 'If I HAD KNOWN, I WOULD HAVE HELPED you' = I didn't know, so I didn't help. The past is fixed; this clause expresses REGRET or COUNTERFACTUAL musing. KEY VERB FORMS: PAST PERFECT (had + V3) in if-clause; MODAL PERFECT (would/could/might + have + V3) in result-clause. EXAMPLES: (1) 'If she had studied, she would have passed' (regret about exam failure). (2) 'If I had taken the umbrella, I wouldn't have got wet' (mixed positive in if + negative in result). (3) 'If they had left earlier, they could have caught the train' (could expresses missed possibility). USE: expressing REGRET, CRITICISM, COUNTERFACTUAL ANALYSIS — common in personal reflection, journalism, political analysis. EXAM TRAP: students miss the 'have' in the result-clause: 'I would helped' — INCORRECT; needs 'I would HAVE helped'. PYQ FREQUENCY: third conditional structure in SSC CGL, IBPS PO English — 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Choose the right form: 'UNLESS you study hard, you ___ pass.'

(A) will not (negative result)
(B) would not (a 2nd-cond modal)
(C) do not (a present-tense form)
(D) did not (a past-tense form)
cards.back:
(A) will not (negative result)

Verb Forms & Tenses — 'UNLESS' = 'IF NOT'. So 'Unless you study hard' = 'If you don't study hard'. The structure follows FIRST CONDITIONAL: 'If you don't study hard, you WILL NOT pass' → 'Unless you study hard, you WILL NOT pass'. Same logic: present in unless-clause, will in result-clause. KEY: unless ALREADY contains the negative meaning, so DON'T add another negative in the unless-clause. WRONG: 'Unless you don't study hard, you will pass' — DOUBLE NEGATIVE, incorrect. CORRECT: 'Unless you study hard, you will fail.' EQUIVALENTS: 'unless' ≈ 'if...not' or 'except if'. 'I won't go unless you come' = 'I won't go if you don't come' = 'I will go ONLY IF you come'. RELATED CONDITIONALS: (1) 'PROVIDED THAT' / 'AS LONG AS' = 'IF', with emphasis on condition: 'You can stay provided that you pay rent'. (2) 'IN CASE' = for precaution: 'Take an umbrella in case it rains' (= because it might rain). (3) 'OTHERWISE' = 'or else': 'Hurry up, otherwise we'll be late'. PYQ FREQUENCY: 'unless' usage is a top SSC CGL Tier 2, IBPS PO MCQ — 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Identify the conditional: 'If I had studied medicine, I would be a doctor today.'

(A) Mixed conditional (past cause, present effect)
(B) Pure third conditional (only past)
(C) Pure second conditional (just present)
(D) First conditional with future result
cards.back:
(A) Mixed conditional (past cause, present effect)

Verb Forms & Tenses — MIXED CONDITIONAL — combines TWO types in one sentence. STRUCTURE: 'If + past perfect (3rd conditional cause), would + V1 (2nd conditional effect)'. EXAMPLE breakdown: 'If I HAD STUDIED medicine [past unreal, didn't happen], I WOULD BE a doctor today [present unreal effect]'. The PAST didn't happen, hence the PRESENT consequence is also unreal. PURE 3RD CONDITIONAL would have been: 'If I had studied medicine, I would have been a doctor' (entirely past — sounds odd because being a doctor is a present-state implication). PURE 2ND CONDITIONAL: 'If I studied medicine, I would be a doctor' (hypothetical present-future, ignoring real past). MIXED IS GOOD when CAUSE is past + EFFECT is present. ANOTHER VARIANT: 'If she WERE more careful (present unreal), she WOULD HAVE PASSED the exam (past hypothetical)' — present-cause + past-effect mix. USAGE: mixed conditionals are common in REGRET expressions and counterfactual analysis: 'If you'd called me yesterday, I wouldn't be in this mess now.' PYQ FREQUENCY: mixed conditionals are advanced English — 1 per CAT, 1 per IBPS PO Mains, occasional SSC CGL Tier 2.

cards.front:
Pick the correct form: 'I wish I ___ taller. (expressing regret)'

(A) were (subjunctive for unreal)
(B) was (an informal usage form)
(C) am (a present-tense form)
(D) have been (pres-perfect form)
cards.back:
(A) were (subjunctive for unreal)

Verb Forms & Tenses — WISHES — closely related to second conditional structurally. PATTERN: 'I wish + past simple' for PRESENT REGRET/UNREAL DESIRE: 'I wish I WERE taller' (I'm not, but I want to be). 'I wish I HAD a car' (don't have one). 'I wish I COULD speak French' (can't). FOR PAST REGRETS: 'I wish + past perfect' (i.e., 'had + V3'): 'I wish I HAD STUDIED harder' (didn't, regret it now). FOR ANNOYING SITUATIONS: 'I wish + would + V1': 'I wish you would stop interrupting' (criticism). 'IF ONLY' is a stronger form: 'If only I were rich!' (more emphatic than 'I wish'). KEY: 'WERE' is used for ALL persons (I, you, he, she, it, we, they) in formal English with 'wish' or '2nd conditional' — this is the SUBJUNCTIVE MOOD. Informal English allows 'was' but exams prefer 'were'. WHY THIS RULE: signals that the statement is COUNTERFACTUAL, not historical. cards.front:
Choose the correct modal: 'You ___ wear a helmet while riding a bike.' (strong obligation, legal requirement)

(A) must (a rule of law)
(B) might (low certainty here)
(C) could (ability sense it)
(D) would (conditional sense)
cards.back:
(A) must (a rule of law)

Verb Forms & Tenses — MUST = STRONG OBLIGATION; usually rules, laws, or critical requirements. 'You MUST wear a helmet' = legally required. CONTRAST: SHOULD = recommendation/advice ('you should sleep more') — softer than must. WOULD = conditional or polite past ('I would help if I could'); not for present obligation. MIGHT = low possibility ('it might rain'); does not express obligation. COULD = past ability ('I could swim at age 5') or polite request ('could you help?'); not obligation. SUMMARY OF MODAL FUNCTIONS: (1) Permission: may, can, could (polite). (2) Possibility: may, might, could. (3) Ability: can, could. (4) Obligation: must, should, ought to, have to. (5) Future: will, shall. (6) Past habit: used to, would. KEY EXAM TRAP: 'must' vs 'have to' — both express obligation but 'must' is more PERSONAL/INTERNAL ('I must finish this'); 'have to' is EXTERNAL ('I have to attend the meeting'). PYQ FREQUENCY: modal-fill-blanks appear in CGL, IBPS Clerk, RRB English 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
Identify the correct modal: 'When I was a child, I ___ run very fast.'

(A) could (past tense of can)
(B) can (the present-tense form)
(C) may (a possibility marker)
(D) should (suggesting advice now)
cards.back:
(A) could (past tense of can)

Verb Forms & Tenses — COULD is the PAST TENSE of CAN (ability). 'When I was a child' indicates PAST time, so 'could' is correct. The sentence describes a past ability. PAST ABILITY EXAMPLES: 'She could swim at age 4', 'He could read fluently by 5'. CAN — present ability: 'I can swim'. WAS/WERE ABLE TO is also used, especially for SPECIFIC past achievements: 'I WAS ABLE TO solve the puzzle' (specific success); but 'I could solve puzzles' (general past ability). SHOULD = advice/recommendation in present/future, NOT past ability. POLITE-REQUEST USE: 'Could you pass the salt?' is more polite than 'Can you pass the salt?'. CONDITIONAL USE: 'If I had time, I could help' (hypothetical present). EXAM TRAP: 'could' vs 'managed to' — when describing ONE specific past success against difficulty, 'managed to' is preferred ('he managed to climb Everest', NOT 'he could climb Everest' — sounds like ability not achievement). PYQ FREQUENCY: 1-2 modal Qs per SSC CGL.

cards.front:
Choose the correct modal: '___ I borrow your pen for a moment?' (polite request)

(A) May (formal polite ask)
(B) Will (a future-tense modal)
(C) Should (suggesting advice now)
(D) Must (strong obligation tense)
cards.back:
(A) May (formal polite ask)

Verb Forms & Tenses — MAY is the most FORMAL/POLITE modal for asking permission: 'May I borrow your pen?' CAN and COULD are also acceptable but more INFORMAL: 'Can I borrow your pen?' (casual), 'Could I borrow your pen?' (slightly more polite than can). FORMALITY HIERARCHY for permission requests: MAY (most formal) > COULD > CAN (most casual). WILL is for FUTURE tense or REQUESTS (not permission): 'Will you help me?' SHOULD is for ADVICE: 'Should I take an umbrella?' MUST is OBLIGATION: 'I must leave now'. EXAM-FAVOURITE TRAP: 'Can I X?' vs 'May I X?' — strict grammarians say MAY is for permission, CAN is for ability ('I CAN run' = I'm able to). In modern usage CAN is widely accepted for permission, but MAY is preferred in FORMAL writing/exams. INDIA EXAMS: SSC CGL, IBPS, RBI Grade B all prefer MAY for permission in formal contexts. PYQ FREQUENCY: 1-2 polite-request Qs per SSC, IBPS English. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests politeness-formality awareness.

cards.front:
Pick the correct modal: 'It ___ rain tomorrow — the sky looks cloudy.' (showing possibility)

(A) might (uncertain possibility)
(B) must (a high certainty modal)
(C) shall (a strong intention modal)
(D) would (a conditional modal here)
cards.back:
(A) might (uncertain possibility)

Verb Forms & Tenses — MIGHT expresses LOW-TO-MODERATE possibility (~40-60% certainty). 'It might rain' = possible but not certain. POSSIBILITY HIERARCHY (low to high): MIGHT (~30-50%) → MAY (~50-60%) → COULD (~50-60%) → SHOULD (~70-80%, expectation) → WILL (~95%+, certainty). MUST in possibility sense = HIGH CERTAINTY based on evidence: 'He must be home — his car is here' (deduction from observation). It does NOT express raw possibility — must is for confident inference. SHALL = strong intention/commitment ('I shall return'), older usage for future with first person. WOULD = conditional/hypothetical ('it would rain if there's enough humidity'). EXAM-FAVOURITE distinction: MAY vs MIGHT — 'may' is slightly stronger possibility; 'might' is more tentative. In conditional or past contexts, 'might' is preferred: 'If you had asked, I might have helped'. PYQ FREQUENCY: possibility-modal Qs in CGL, IBPS, RRB English 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
Identify the correct modal: 'Students ___ submit their assignments by Friday.' (advice/recommendation)

(A) should (a softer advice modal)
(B) could (an ability marker)
(C) would (conditional sense modal)
(D) might (a low possibility)
cards.back:
(A) should (a softer advice modal)

Verb Forms & Tenses — SHOULD = advice, recommendation, expectation. 'Students should submit by Friday' = recommended deadline. SHOULD vs MUST: 'should' is SOFTER, suggests it's a good idea but not strictly enforced; 'must' is MANDATORY, no exceptions. SHOULD also expresses: (1) Expectation: 'The bus should arrive at 9' (expected time). (2) Probability: 'Sleep should help your headache'. (3) Hypothetical past: 'You should have called me' (criticism for not doing). OUGHT TO = synonym of should but more FORMAL. 'Students ought to submit by Friday' — same meaning, more polished. NEAR-EQUIVALENTS to 'should': 'had better' (slightly stronger warning); 'are advised to' (more formal). KEY EXAM TIP: when the sentence implies ADVICE, SUGGESTION, or MILD OBLIGATION, choose SHOULD. When it implies STRICT OBLIGATION, choose MUST. PYQ FREQUENCY: should/must distinction is a SSC CGL, IBPS Clerk top-3 grammar MCQ — 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Choose the modal: 'You ___ have told me earlier — now it is too late.' (regret about past)

(A) should (regret + perfect tense)
(B) must (a present obligation)
(C) will (the future tense modal)
(D) can (the ability marker now)
cards.back:
(A) should (regret + perfect tense)

Verb Forms & Tenses — 'SHOULD HAVE + past participle' — expresses REGRET or CRITICISM about a past action that DIDN'T happen. 'You should have told me earlier' = you didn't tell me, and that was wrong. STRUCTURE: SUBJECT + SHOULD + HAVE + V3 (past participle). PARALLEL FORMS: (1) 'COULD HAVE + V3' = past possibility/missed opportunity ('I could have studied harder'). (2) 'WOULD HAVE + V3' = past hypothetical ('I would have helped if I'd known'). (3) 'MIGHT HAVE + V3' = past low-possibility ('she might have left already'). (4) 'MUST HAVE + V3' = past deduction with high confidence ('he must have forgotten'). KEY ERROR: students often write 'You should told me' (missing 'have') — incorrect; modal-perfect REQUIRES auxiliary 'have'. NEGATIVE: 'shouldn't have' = criticizing what someone DID do ('you shouldn't have spent so much'). PYQ FREQUENCY: modal-perfect (modal + have + V3) is a top SSC CGL Tier 2, IBPS PO Mains MCQ — 1-2× per paper.

cards.front:
Pick the correct modal: 'I ___ rather have tea than coffee.' (preference)

(A) would (used in 'would rather')
(B) should (advice or expectation)
(C) could (an ability sense modal)
(D) might (a low possibility one)
cards.back:
(A) would (used in 'would rather')

Verb Forms & Tenses — 'WOULD RATHER' = expression of PREFERENCE, equivalent to 'prefer'. 'I would rather have tea than coffee' = 'I prefer tea to coffee'. STRUCTURE: SUBJECT + WOULD RATHER + BASE VERB. CONTRACTED FORM: I'd rather, you'd rather, etc. CHOICE-COMPARISON: 'I would rather X than Y' (X is preferred). PARALLEL EXPRESSIONS: (1) 'I prefer X to Y' (formal). (2) 'I'd prefer X' (slightly less direct than 'would rather'). (3) 'I'd sooner X' (synonym of 'would rather', slightly informal). DOUBLE-SUBJECT FORM: when expressing what you wish OTHER people would do, use PAST TENSE: 'I would rather YOU CAME on time' (you tend to be late, and I wish you'd change). KEY ERROR: students sometimes write 'I would rather to have tea' — INCORRECT (no 'to'); should be 'I would rather HAVE tea'. PYQ FREQUENCY: 'would rather' constructions appear in SSC CGL, IBPS PO English — 1× per cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests idiomatic-modal mastery.

Choose the correct indirect form of: "Hurrah! We have won the match," he said.

(B) He exclaimed with joy that they had won the match.
(C) He told that we have won the match.
(D) He shouted that they win the match.

cards.front:
Choose the correct indirect form of: The teacher said, "The earth revolves around the sun."

(A) The teacher said that the earth revolved around the sun.
(B) The teacher said that the earth revolves around the sun.
(C) The teacher said that the earth had revolved around the sun.
(D) The teacher told that the earth was revolving around the sun.
cards.back:
(B) The teacher said that the earth revolves around the sun.

Verb Forms & Tenses — Important EXCEPTION to the tense-backshift rule: when the reported sentence is a UNIVERSAL TRUTH, scientific fact, geographical fact, habitual action that remains true, or a proverb — the present tense in the reported speech is RETAINED even if the reporting verb is in the past. Examples: 'He said that honesty IS the best policy' (proverb); 'She said that water BOILS at 100°C' (scientific fact); 'They said that the sun RISES in the east' (geographical fact). Tense backshift would suggest the fact stopped being true — which it didn't.

cards.option2: The teacher said that the earth had revolved around the sun.
cards.option3: The teacher told that the earth was revolving around the sun.

cards.front:
Choose the correct indirect form of: She said to me, "Did you finish your homework?"

(A) She asked me did I finish my homework.
(B) She asked me if I had finished my homework.
(C) She told me that I finished my homework.
(D) She asked me whether did I finish my homework.
cards.back:
(B) She asked me if I had finished my homework.

Verb Forms & Tenses — YES/NO questions in reported speech: (1) reporting verb 'said' → 'asked' / 'enquired'; (2) connector 'if' OR 'whether' (NOT 'that'); (3) drop 'do/does/did' inversion → straight subject-verb order; (4) tense backshifts: simple-past 'did finish' → past-perfect 'had finished'. Pronouns: 'you' (the listener = me, the reporter) → 'I'; 'your' → 'my'. WRONG patterns: 'asked DID I finish' (kept inversion); 'asked WHETHER DID I finish' (kept 'did' AND used 'whether'); 'told' (told requires statements, not questions).

cards.option3: She asked me whether did I finish my homework.

cards.front:
In 'the BARKING dog scared the child', the word BARKING is a:

(A) Present participle (acts as adjective)
(B) Gerund (a noun-form verb)
(C) Infinitive (with 'to' before V1)
(D) Continuous tense (verb form)
cards.back:
(A) Present participle (acts as adjective)

Verb Forms & Tenses — PRESENT PARTICIPLE — verb form ending in -ING used as an ADJECTIVE describing a noun. 'Barking' modifies 'dog'. KEY DISTINCTION (the trickiest part): -ING words can be (1) GERUND — verb used as NOUN: 'BARKING is loud' (subject); 'I love BARKING dogs' (the gerund 'barking' acts as adjective here, but consider 'BARKING is annoying' = gerund as subject). (2) PRESENT PARTICIPLE — verb-derived adjective: 'the BARKING dog' (modifies dog). (3) CONTINUOUS TENSE auxiliary: 'the dog IS BARKING' (with 'to be'). PAST PARTICIPLE: -ED form (or V3) — 'a BROKEN window', 'the EXCITED child'. Indicates COMPLETED action or PASSIVE state. PERFECT PARTICIPLE: 'HAVING + V3' — 'HAVING FINISHED the work, she went home' (action completed before main verb). PARTICIPIAL PHRASES are more concise alternatives to 'WHO/WHICH/THAT' clauses: 'The man WHO IS RUNNING toward us' ≈ 'The man RUNNING toward us'. EXAM TRAP: 'dangling participle' — when participle's subject is unclear or wrong: 'Walking down the street, the building looked huge' (incorrect: building isn't walking). PYQ FREQUENCY: SSC CGL Tier 2, IBPS PO English — 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Choose the correct form: 'The ___ window was repaired.' (something already broken)

(A) broken (past participle as adj)
(B) breaking (present participle)
(C) broke (a past simple verb)
(D) to break (an infinitive form)
cards.back:
(A) broken (past participle as adj)

Verb Forms & Tenses — PAST PARTICIPLE = V3 — used as an adjective for COMPLETED actions or PASSIVE states. 'Broken window' = a window that has been broken. PARTICIPLE FORMS — three principal verb forms: (1) BASE (V1): break. (2) PAST SIMPLE (V2): broke. (3) PAST PARTICIPLE (V3): broken. REGULAR verbs: V2 = V3 (both add -ed): play/played/played, work/worked/worked. IRREGULAR verbs: V2 ≠ V3: break/broke/broken, see/saw/seen, run/ran/run, do/did/done, write/wrote/written. ADJECTIVE USAGE: -ED participle indicates SOMETHING THAT HAS HAD AN ACTION DONE TO IT (passive/completed). 'a frozen lake' (was frozen), 'an excited child' (became excited), 'a written agreement' (has been written). VS -ING (PRESENT PARTICIPLE) — active/ongoing: 'a freezing lake' (currently freezing), 'an exciting movie' (causing excitement), 'a writing pad'. KEY DISTINCTION trap: '-ed adjective describes what RECEIVES the action; -ing adjective describes what CAUSES the action.' 'Bored vs Boring' — 'I am bored' (someone made me bored); 'the lecture is boring' (it causes boredom). PYQ FREQUENCY: -ed/-ing distinction in SSC CGL, IBPS PO, RBI 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
Choose the correct: 'The lecture was BORED / BORING.' (the lecture caused tedium)

(A) Boring (active causing emotion)
(B) Bored (passive feeling instead)
(C) Bores (present-tense form here)
(D) To bore (an infinitive form)
cards.back:
(A) Boring (active causing emotion)

Verb Forms & Tenses — BORING (-ing) is used when the SUBJECT CAUSES the emotion: 'the lecture is BORING' (it makes me bored). BORED (-ed) is used when the SUBJECT FEELS the emotion: 'I am BORED' (the lecture made me bored). RULE: -ING describes the CAUSE of the feeling; -ED describes the EXPERIENCER of the feeling. COMMON PAIRS to memorize: (1) BORING/BORED. (2) EXCITING/EXCITED. (3) INTERESTING/INTERESTED. (4) AMUSING/AMUSED. (5) FRIGHTENING/FRIGHTENED. (6) AMAZING/AMAZED. (7) CONFUSING/CONFUSED. (8) DISAPPOINTING/DISAPPOINTED. (9) TIRING/TIRED. (10) FASCINATING/FASCINATED. EXAMPLES: 'The horror movie is FRIGHTENING' (it causes fear) vs 'the kids were FRIGHTENED' (they felt fear). EXAM TRAP: students often write 'I am boring' to mean 'I am feeling bored' — INCORRECT in formal English; 'I am boring' means 'I cause others to be bored'. KEY: subject-feeling sentences need -ED; description of stimuli use -ING. PYQ FREQUENCY: -ing/-ed feeling-adjective MCQs in SSC CGL, IBPS Clerk, RRB English — 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Identify the dangling participle: 'Walking down the street, the building looked huge.'

(A) Subject mismatch — building doesn't walk
(B) It is grammatically correct here
(C) Past tense should be used
(D) Comma should be a semicolon
cards.back:
(A) Subject mismatch — building doesn't walk

Verb Forms & Tenses — DANGLING PARTICIPLE — when the participial phrase doesn't logically connect to the SUBJECT of the main clause. The implied subject of 'walking' is missing or wrong. 'Walking down the street' should describe a PERSON, but the main clause's subject is 'the building' — buildings don't walk! CORRECT VERSIONS: (1) 'Walking down the street, I thought the building looked huge' (clear subject 'I'). (2) 'As I walked down the street, the building looked huge' (rewritten as a clause). (3) 'Walking down the street, I noticed the huge building' (subject and modifier match). MORE EXAMPLES of DANGLING participles: (a) 'Driving home, the moon was beautiful' (moon doesn't drive). (b) 'After studying for hours, the test was easy' (test doesn't study). (c) 'Tired and hungry, the dinner tasted great' (dinner isn't tired). RULE: the participial modifier MUST refer to the SUBJECT of the main clause. EXAM-FAVORITE: spotting dangling participles in SSC CGL Tier 2 error-spotting, IBPS PO Mains, CAT — 1-2× per paper. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests grammatical-logical alignment.

cards.front:
Choose the correct form: '___ his keys, he searched the entire house.'

(A) Having lost (perfect participle)
(B) Lost (past tense isolated)
(C) Losing (present participle)
(D) He lost (a separate sentence)
cards.back:
(A) Having lost (perfect participle)

Verb Forms & Tenses — PERFECT PARTICIPLE — formed with HAVING + V3. Used to indicate that the action of the participle was COMPLETED BEFORE the action of the main verb. 'Having lost his keys, he searched' = HE LOST KEYS FIRST, THEN SEARCHED. STRUCTURE: HAVING + V3 (past participle). EXAMPLES: (1) 'Having finished her work, she relaxed' (work done first). (2) 'Having read the report, the manager called a meeting'. (3) 'Having seen the movie before, I didn't want to watch it again'. CONTRAST: present participle 'LOSING his keys, he searched...' would imply CONCURRENT actions (he was losing AND searching at the same time — illogical here). PERFECT PARTICIPLE PASSIVE: 'HAVING BEEN + V3': 'Having been informed of the change, she adjusted her plans.' USE CASES: (1) Cause-effect: 'Having missed the bus, he was late'. (2) Time sequence: 'Having graduated, she joined a tech firm'. (3) Reason/justification: 'Having seen evidence, the jury convicted'. PYQ FREQUENCY: perfect participle in advanced English MCQs — CAT, IBPS PO Mains, RBI Grade B — 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Identify the participle in: 'The water FLOWING from the tap was contaminated.'

(A) FLOWING (present participle)
(B) TAP (a regular noun)
(C) WATER (the subject noun)
(D) CONTAMINATED is gerund here
cards.back:
(A) FLOWING (present participle)

Verb Forms & Tenses — FLOWING is a PRESENT PARTICIPLE acting as an ADJECTIVE — modifies 'water'. The full noun phrase 'the water flowing from the tap' = 'the water THAT IS flowing from the tap' (relative clause shortened). PARTICIPIAL PHRASES are concise alternatives to relative clauses: 'the man WHO IS RUNNING' = 'the man RUNNING'. STRUCTURE: noun + participle phrase. EXAMPLES: (1) 'the boy SITTING on the bench' = 'the boy who is sitting'. (2) 'the dog BARKING loudly' = 'the dog that is barking loudly'. (3) 'the team WINNING the match' = 'the team that is winning'. NOTE: 'CONTAMINATED' in this sentence is a PAST PARTICIPLE used as a PREDICATE ADJECTIVE — describes the state of water. SO the sentence has TWO participles: 'flowing' (present participle modifying water) and 'contaminated' (past participle as predicate adjective). PARTICIPIAL PHRASES SAVE WORDS — make writing more concise. EXAM TIP: identify participles by looking for -ING or -ED/V3 forms acting as adjectives. PYQ FREQUENCY: participle identification in SSC CGL, IBPS PO 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Pick the correct form: 'The students ___ in the library are preparing for exams.'

(A) studying (present participle)
(B) studied (past participle)
(C) study (a base verb form)
(D) studies (a wrong verb form)
cards.back:
(A) studying (present participle)

Verb Forms & Tenses — PRESENT PARTICIPLE 'STUDYING' — modifies 'students' (those who are currently studying). The phrase 'studying in the library' describes WHICH students. FULL EXPANSION: 'The students who are studying in the library are preparing for exams.' This is a PARTICIPIAL PHRASE replacing a 'who is/are + V-ing' relative clause. WHY NOT 'STUDIED'? Past participle implies COMPLETED action — but the sentence wants to describe ONGOING activity (students currently studying). 'Studied' would be passive: 'students studied in the library' = 'students who have been studied' (illogical). WHY NOT 'STUDY'? Base form requires auxiliary; 'who study' (relative clause) is grammatical but not a participial phrase. WHY NOT 'STUDIES'? That's the third-person-singular present (he/she studies); doesn't agree with plural 'students'. KEY METHOD: when describing an ONGOING ACTION done BY the noun, use PRESENT PARTICIPLE (-ing). When describing a COMPLETED ACTION done TO the noun, use PAST PARTICIPLE (-ed/V3). PYQ FREQUENCY: participial-phrase MCQs in SSC CGL, IBPS PO English 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
Convert to passive: 'They will complete the project tomorrow.'

(A) The project will be completed tomorrow
(B) Project will completed by them now
(C) The project completes by them tomorrow
(D) Project shall complete tomorrow itself
cards.back:
(A) The project will be completed tomorrow

Verb Forms & Tenses — FUTURE SIMPLE PASSIVE: Subject + WILL/SHALL + BE + V3 (past participle) (+ by + agent). 'They will COMPLETE the project tomorrow' (active) → 'The project WILL BE COMPLETED tomorrow (by them)' (passive). 'By them' often dropped if agent is generic ('they'). PASSIVE VOICE FORMULAS for major tenses: (1) PRESENT SIMPLE: am/is/are + V3. 'She writes a letter' → 'A letter is written by her'. (2) PRESENT CONTINUOUS: am/is/are + being + V3. 'She is writing' → 'A letter is being written'. (3) PRESENT PERFECT: have/has + been + V3. 'She has written' → 'A letter has been written'. (4) PAST SIMPLE: was/were + V3. 'She wrote' → 'A letter was written'. (5) PAST CONTINUOUS: was/were + being + V3. (6) PAST PERFECT: had + been + V3. (7) FUTURE SIMPLE: will + be + V3. (8) FUTURE PERFECT: will + have + been + V3. KEY ELEMENTS: object of active becomes SUBJECT of passive; main verb becomes V3; appropriate FORM of 'BE' is added; original subject becomes 'by + agent' (often optional). PYQ FREQUENCY: passive voice tense conversions in SSC CGL, IBPS PO English — 1-2× per cycle.

cards.option2: The project completes by them tomorrow

cards.front:
Choose the correct passive: 'Someone has stolen my bicycle.'

(A) My bicycle has been stolen
(B) My bicycle was stolen here also
(C) My bicycle is stolen by someone
(D) My bicycle stolen by someone there
cards.back:
(A) My bicycle has been stolen

Verb Forms & Tenses — PRESENT PERFECT PASSIVE: HAS/HAVE + BEEN + V3. Active: 'Someone has STOLEN my bicycle' → Passive: 'My bicycle HAS BEEN STOLEN' (by someone — often dropped because 'someone' is unspecific). Tense PRESERVED: active is present perfect; passive must also be present perfect. KEY POINT: don't change the TENSE when converting voice. Each tense has its own passive structure. INDEFINITE AGENTS — 'BY' clause often DROPPED: when active subject is 'someone', 'people', 'they' (general) — passive often omits 'by ___' since it adds no info. EXAMPLES: (1) 'They speak English in Australia' → 'English is spoken in Australia' (drop 'by them'). (2) 'People built this temple in 1500 CE' → 'This temple was built in 1500 CE'. (3) 'Someone is knocking at the door' → 'The door is being knocked at'. PASSIVE WITHOUT AGENT is sometimes preferred when: (a) Agent is unknown. (b) Agent is obvious/unimportant. (c) Writer wants to FOCUS on the action/result, not the doer (common in scientific writing, news, official statements). PYQ FREQUENCY: voice transformations with present perfect in SSC CGL, IBPS PO 1× per paper.

cards.front:
Choose the correct passive: 'The teacher must answer this question.'

(A) This question must be answered
(B) This question must answer here
(C) This question must be answer there
(D) Question must answered by teacher
cards.back:
(A) This question must be answered

Verb Forms & Tenses — MODAL PASSIVE: MODAL + BE + V3. 'must answer' (active modal+verb) → 'must be answered' (passive). Common modals in passive constructions: CAN, COULD, MAY, MIGHT, MUST, SHOULD, OUGHT, WILL, WOULD. STRUCTURE: SUBJECT + MODAL + BE + V3 (+ by + agent). EXAMPLES: (1) 'You must complete the form' → 'The form must be completed.' (2) 'They can solve this problem' → 'This problem can be solved.' (3) 'You should clean the room' → 'The room should be cleaned.' (4) 'She might write the report' → 'The report might be written.' MODAL PASSIVE MISTAKES: (a) Forgetting 'BE': 'must answered' (WRONG); needs 'must be answered'. (b) Wrong V3: 'must be answer' (WRONG); needs the past participle 'answered'. PRACTICE: convert these to passive — 'Workers should repair the road' → 'The road should be repaired.' 'They might cancel the match' → 'The match might be cancelled.' 'You can use this pen' → 'This pen can be used.' EXAM-FAVORITE: SSC CGL Tier 2, IBPS PO English error-spotting includes modal passive mistakes. PYQ FREQUENCY: 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Convert to passive: 'They gave me a gift.'

(A) I was given a gift (by them)
(B) A gift was given me by them
(C) Me was given by them a gift
(D) By them I given a gift
cards.back:
(A) I was given a gift (by them)

Verb Forms & Tenses — TWO-OBJECT VERBS (give, send, offer, lend, owe, pay, show, teach, tell, write) — when converted to passive, EITHER OBJECT can become the subject. Active: 'They gave ME a gift' (me = INDIRECT object; gift = DIRECT object). Passive Option 1 (preferred): 'I WAS GIVEN a gift (by them)' — indirect object becomes subject. Passive Option 2 (less common): 'A gift WAS GIVEN to me (by them)' — direct object as subject; note 'TO' before 'me' to maintain meaning. KEY DETAIL: in option 1, 'a gift' remains; in option 2, 'me' becomes 'to me' (preposition added). EXAM-FAVORITE: option 1 form (person becomes subject) is MORE COMMON in modern English. PRACTICE: (1) 'She told us a story' → 'We were told a story' OR 'A story was told to us'. (2) 'He sent her flowers' → 'She was sent flowers' OR 'Flowers were sent to her'. (3) 'They paid him 5000 rupees' → 'He was paid 5000 rupees' OR '5000 rupees were paid to him'. ANALOGY: 'GIVE' has 2 objects; 'me' is the recipient (indirect), 'gift' is the thing given (direct). Indirect-object-as-subject is preferred in passive. PYQ FREQUENCY: dative-object passives in SSC CGL Tier 2, IBPS PO English 1× per paper.

cards.front:
Choose the correct passive: 'Open the door!' (imperative)

(A) Let the door be opened
(B) The door must open you here
(C) Door is opened by someone there
(D) Open the door is required now
cards.back:
(A) Let the door be opened

Verb Forms & Tenses — IMPERATIVE PASSIVE: typically uses 'LET + OBJECT + BE + V3'. Active: 'Open the door!' → Passive: 'LET THE DOOR BE OPENED.' Or alternatively: 'You are requested to open the door' (longer formal version). STRUCTURE: 'LET + OBJECT-AS-SUBJECT-OF-PASSIVE-CLAUSE + BE + V3'. EXAMPLES: (1) 'Close the window' → 'Let the window be closed'. (2) 'Solve this problem' → 'Let this problem be solved'. (3) 'Bring water' → 'Let water be brought'. (4) 'Don't disturb me' → 'Let me not be disturbed' OR 'I should not be disturbed'. NEGATIVE IMPERATIVES: 'Don't write on the wall' → 'Let the wall not be written on' OR 'You are not to write on the wall'. KEY ALTERNATIVES depending on tone: (a) 'You are advised/requested/ordered to + V1': formal. (b) 'Let + object + be + V3': standard imperative passive. (c) 'It is to be + V3': very formal. EXAM TIP: 'LET' construction is the EXAM-favorite for imperative passive — appears in SSC CGL, IBPS PO, RBI English sections. INDIA exam contexts heavily test this construction. PYQ FREQUENCY: imperative-passive in SSC CGL Tier 2 voice-conversion section 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Convert to passive: 'Did the dog bite him?' (interrogative)

(A) Was he bitten by the dog?
(B) Was the dog bitten by him?
(C) Did him be bitten by the dog?
(D) Bites him by the dog?
cards.back:
(A) Was he bitten by the dog?

Verb Forms & Tenses — INTERROGATIVE (question) PASSIVE: maintain the same TENSE; rearrange so the OBJECT becomes SUBJECT, and the helping verb (auxiliary) precedes the new subject. Active: 'DID the dog BITE him?' (past simple interrogative). Passive: 'WAS he BITTEN by the dog?' (past simple passive interrogative). KEY METHOD: (1) Identify the active subject ('the dog'), object ('him'), main verb ('bite'). (2) Make the object the new subject ('he' subject form). (3) Use the appropriate passive structure for the same tense (past simple → was/were + V3). (4) For questions, AUXILIARY comes before SUBJECT. EXAMPLES: (a) 'Is she writing a letter?' → 'Is a letter being written by her?' (present continuous passive). (b) 'Have you finished the task?' → 'Has the task been finished by you?' (present perfect). (c) 'Will they invite us?' → 'Will we be invited by them?' (future simple). (d) 'Can you solve this?' → 'Can this be solved by you?' (modal). EXAM TRAP: students forget to convert pronouns: 'him' → 'he' (subject case); 'her' → 'she'; 'us' → 'we'; 'them' → 'they'. PYQ FREQUENCY: interrogative passives in SSC CGL Tier 2, IBPS PO English — 1× per cycle.

cards.option2: Did him be bitten by the dog?

cards.front:
Convert to passive: 'I remember meeting him.' (gerund)

(A) I remember being met by him
(B) He remembers meeting by me
(C) I remember to be met by him
(D) He is remembered by my meeting
cards.back:
(A) I remember being met by him

Verb Forms & Tenses — GERUND PASSIVE: convert 'meeting + object' (gerund as a -ing noun-form verb) to 'being + V3' (passive gerund). Active: 'I remember MEETING him' (gerund 'meeting' is the noun-form verb). Passive: 'I remember BEING MET by him.' Note: the SUBJECT 'I' stays SAME; only the gerund verb structure changes. STRUCTURE: passive gerund = 'being + V3' (also 'having been + V3' for perfect-passive gerund). EXAMPLES: (1) 'I love being praised' (passive gerund — 'someone praises me, and I love that'). (2) 'He hates being interrupted'. (3) 'She fears being noticed'. (4) 'Being told the truth was painful' (gerund as subject in passive form). PERFECT PASSIVE GERUND: 'having been + V3' = past completed action. 'Having been informed of the issue, she acted promptly'. KEY: gerunds are -ING verbs functioning as NOUNS. Passive gerunds describe the noun receiving an action. CONTRAST WITH INFINITIVE PASSIVE: 'to be + V3' — 'I want to be praised'. EXAM TRAP: don't confuse gerund passive 'being + V3' with present participle in continuous tense 'is being + V3'. PYQ FREQUENCY: gerund-passive constructions in CAT, IBPS PO Mains, RBI English — 1× per cycle.

cards.option3: He is remembered by my meeting

cards.front:
Convert: Ravi said, 'I am writing a letter.' to indirect speech:

(B) Ravi said that he was writing a letter.
(C) Ravi said he is writing a letter then.
(D) Ravi told that he wrote a letter then.
cards.back:

Verb Forms & Tenses — Rules: (1) Pronoun shift — I → he (since Ravi is male, third-person). (2) Tense backshift — Present continuous (am writing) → Past continuous (was writing). (3) Reporting verb 'said' (no object) followed by 'that' clause. Distractor 1 — pronoun + tense not changed. Distractor 3 — tense not changed. Distractor 4 — wrong tense + 'told' needs an object.

cards.front:
Convert: She said, 'I will go to Delhi tomorrow.' to indirect speech:

(A) She said she will go to Delhi tomorrow.
(B) She said she would go to Delhi the next day.
(C) She said that she would go Delhi tomorrow.
(D) She said that she goes to Delhi next day.

Verb Forms & Tenses — Two key shifts: (1) MODAL — 'will' → 'would' (backshift). (2) TIME — 'tomorrow' → 'the next day'. Standard time shifts: today → that day; tonight → that night; yesterday → the previous day; tomorrow → the next day; last week → the previous week; ago → before. Distractor 1 — no shifts. Distractor 3 — kept 'tomorrow'. Distractor 4 — wrong tense.

(D) Was using (past continuous form)

Verb Forms & Tenses — USED TO + base verb = PAST HABIT (something done regularly in past, not anymore). 'I used to play cricket' = I played cricket regularly back then. NEGATIVE: 'didn't use to' (no 'd' on use). NOT same as 'I am used to / get used to' (= 'accustomed to' + noun/gerund). 'I am used to spicy food' = accustomed; 'I used to eat spicy food' = past habit. WOULD also expresses past habits with action verbs only ('When I was 10, I would play cricket'). NOT WOULD with state verbs ('I would be tall' is wrong; use 'I used to be tall'). cards.front:
Identify the correct comparative form: 'My house is ___ than yours.'

(A) bigger (regular comparative)
(B) more big (a wrong form)
(C) biggest (a superlative form)
(D) most big (a wrong form)
cards.back:
(A) bigger (regular comparative)

Sentence & Error Correction — DEGREES OF COMPARISON — three forms: (1) POSITIVE: BIG (just describes). (2) COMPARATIVE: BIGGER (compares two things; uses '-er' or 'more'). (3) SUPERLATIVE: BIGGEST (compares three+ things; uses '-est' or 'most'). RULES for adding -er/-est vs more/most: (a) ONE-SYLLABLE adjectives: usually -er/-est (big→bigger; tall→taller; small→smaller). (b) TWO-SYLLABLE adjectives ending in -y: change y→i, add -er/-est (happy→happier→happiest; busy→busier→busiest). (c) TWO+ SYLLABLE adjectives: usually 'more'/'most' (beautiful→more beautiful→most beautiful; difficult→more difficult). (d) Some 2-syllable can take EITHER (clever→cleverer/more clever; both correct). DOUBLE COMPARISON ERRORS: 'more bigger' or 'most biggest' — INCORRECT. Use either '-er' OR 'more', not both. SAMPLE GOOD: 'My house is bigger than yours' (compares 2). 'This is the biggest house on the street' (compares 3+). PYQ FREQUENCY: degrees-of-comparison in SSC CGL Tier 1, IBPS Clerk Pre, RRB English 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:

(A) the most intelligent (superlative)
(B) more intelligent (comparative)
(C) intelligent (just positive)
(D) most intelligent (without 'the')

The phrase identifies a UNIQUE entity in a group, so DEFINITE ARTICLE 'the' is needed. PRACTICE: (1) 'Mt Everest is THE TALLEST mountain in the world.' (2) 'Honesty is THE BEST policy.' (3) 'This is THE OLDEST temple in India.' WHY 'THE': because the SUPERLATIVE PICKS OUT a SPECIFIC item (the unique 'best/tallest/longest one'). EXCEPTIONS — superlative WITHOUT 'the' (more rare): (a) When superlative is used as ADVERB: 'She works hardest of all the team.' (b) Predicative use sometimes: 'She is best when relaxed.' PRACTICE — IRREGULAR forms (memorize): (1) good → better → best. (2) bad → worse → worst. (3) much/many → more → most. (4) little → less → least. (5) far → farther/further → farthest/furthest. (6) old → older/elder → oldest/eldest. PYQ FREQUENCY: superlative + 'the' in SSC CGL, IBPS English 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Correct sentence: 'No other planet in our solar system is ___ Jupiter.'

(A) as large as (positive comparison)
(B) larger than Jupiter again
(C) as larger as Jupiter (wrong)
(D) the largest as Jupiter only
cards.back:
(A) as large as (positive comparison)

Sentence & Error Correction — POSITIVE-DEGREE COMPARISON uses 'AS + adjective + AS' to indicate equality. 'No other planet is AS LARGE AS Jupiter' = 'no other matches Jupiter's size' — implies Jupiter is the largest. NEGATIVE FORM: 'NOT AS X AS' or 'NOT SO X AS' (older). PRACTICE: (1) 'My brother is as tall as me' (positive equal). (2) 'Diamond is not as soft as graphite' (positive inequality). EQUIVALENT in COMPARATIVE: 'Jupiter is LARGER THAN any other planet' — same meaning, different degree. EQUIVALENT in SUPERLATIVE: 'Jupiter is THE LARGEST planet (in our solar system)'. KEY DEGREE TRANSFORMATIONS — interchanging: (1) POSITIVE: 'No other X in Y is as ADJ as Z' (e.g., 'No other planet is as large as Jupiter'). (2) COMPARATIVE: 'Z is more ADJ than any other X in Y' or 'Z is more ADJ than all other X' (e.g., 'Jupiter is larger than any other planet'). (3) SUPERLATIVE: 'Z is the most ADJ X in Y' (e.g., 'Jupiter is the largest planet'). EXAM-FAVOURITE TASK: convert from one degree to another preserving meaning. PRACTICE: 'Honesty is the best policy' (superlative) → 'No other policy is as good as honesty' (positive). PYQ FREQUENCY: degree-conversion in SSC CGL, IBPS PO, CAT 1× per cycle.

(B) the richest (superlative form)

SPECIAL CASES with 'OF THE TWO/THREE': always uses 'THE' even with comparative when 'of the two': 'the better of the two', 'the elder of two brothers'. POSITIVE: comparative for 2 = 'X is bigger than Y'. INCORRECT 'doubly intensive' forms: 'most fastest' (×), 'more better' (×). EXCEPTION — 'most' as 'very': 'most beautiful sunset' could mean 'very beautiful' OR 'the most beautiful' (context-dependent). PYQ FREQUENCY: 'two vs three+' degree usage in SSC CGL, IBPS PO 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
Choose: 'The price of gold is increasing day by day. It is becoming ___ '

(A) more and more expensive (progressive)
(B) most expensive (a superlative)
(C) expensive and expensive (a wrong form)
(D) very most expensive (a wrong form)
cards.back:
(A) more and more expensive (progressive)

Sentence & Error Correction — 'MORE AND MORE + adjective' = expression of GRADUAL INCREASE / progressive change. 'It is becoming MORE AND MORE expensive' = price is rising continuously. PARALLEL FORMS: (a) 'BIGGER and BIGGER' / 'TALLER and TALLER' (using -er + -er). (b) 'MORE and MORE expensive' (using more + more). (c) 'LESS and LESS' for decreasing. (d) 'WORSE and WORSE' for irregular. PRACTICE: (1) 'The traffic is getting worse and worse every year.' (2) 'She became more and more confident as she practiced.' (3) 'The road grew narrower and narrower.' (4) 'The candidates' speeches were less and less convincing.' RELATED IDIOMATIC EXPRESSION: 'THE + comparative ... THE + comparative' = parallel growth: 'The MORE you study, the BETTER you'll do.' 'The HIGHER you go, the COLDER it gets.' 'The MORE the merrier' (proverbial). RELATED — 'AS + adjective + AS POSSIBLE' = maximum extent: 'as quickly as possible'. EXAM TIP: 'more and more X' is GRAMMATICAL & idiomatic; 'most X' is just superlative. PYQ FREQUENCY: progressive comparatives in IBPS PO Mains, CAT, CGL Tier 2 — 1× per cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests idiomatic comparative usage.

cards.front:
Identify the correct: 'Mathematics is ___ subject for me than Hindi.'

(A) a more difficult (right comparative)
(B) a most difficult (superlative)
(C) the more difficult (the not used)
(D) more difficulter (an error here)
cards.back:
(A) a more difficult (right comparative)

Sentence & Error Correction — 'MORE DIFFICULT' is COMPARATIVE form of 'difficult' (3 syllables — uses 'more'). Sentence compares TWO subjects (Math vs Hindi) → COMPARATIVE. With INDEFINITE article 'A': 'A more difficult subject' (introduces it as ONE OF some difficult subjects, not specific). 'THE more difficult' would be used if it's UNIQUE/specific (e.g., 'the more difficult of the two'). KEY: ONE-SYLLABLE adjectives (-er): big→bigger, fast→faster, tall→taller, smart→smarter. TWO-SYLLABLE -y adjectives: happy→happier, busy→busier, easy→easier (change y→i). TWO-SYLLABLE other: usually 'more' (modern→more modern, careful→more careful). THREE+ SYLLABLE: always 'more' (intelligent→more intelligent, beautiful→more beautiful, ridiculous→more ridiculous). (A) Gold is more malleable than any other metal

cards.front:
Identify the error: 'Of the two girls, Mira is the most intelligent.'

(A) Should be 'more intelligent' (only 2 → comparative)
(B) No error, sentence is correct already
(C) 'Two' should be replaced by 'both' here
(D) 'Mira' should not be mentioned at all
cards.back:

Correct: 'Of the two girls, Mira is the more intelligent'. WHEN EXACTLY 2 are compared, English requires comparative. Other 2-vs-3+ markers: 'between A and B' → comparative ('the better of the two'); 'among A, B, C, ...' → superlative ('the best among the three'). PYQ FAVOURITE error.

cards.back:

cards.front:
Choose the correct: '___ this exam, the previous one was much harder.'

(A) Compared to (compared with also acceptable)
(B) Comparing with (a wrong preposition)
(C) In compare with (a wrong phrase)
(D) Compare to (incomplete phrase form)
cards.back:
(A) Compared to (compared with also acceptable)

Sentence & Error Correction — Standard English: COMPARED TO + thing (showing similarity); COMPARED WITH + thing (showing both similarity + difference). 'COMPARED TO' is more common in everyday usage; 'COMPARED WITH' more formal. EQUIVALENT: 'In comparison with/to'. WRONG: 'compare with' (incomplete; missing -ed); 'comparing to/with' (gerund needs subject). PYQ TRAP — 'compare with' is also acceptable in some contexts (e.g., active comparison: 'I compare him with...'); but 'compared to/with' is the participial phrase form for setting up contrast.

cards.front:
Choose the correct question tag: 'She is a doctor, ___?'

(A) isn't she — flip polarity
(B) is she alone alone alone
(C) doesn't she alone alone
(D) wasn't she alone alone alone
cards.back:
(A) isn't she — flip polarity

Sentence & Error Correction — RULE 1 — POLARITY FLIP: positive statement → negative tag; negative statement → positive tag. 'She IS a doctor' (positive) → tag must be NEGATIVE: 'isn't she'. RULE 2 — SAME AUXILIARY: use the SAME helping verb as in the main clause. Here 'is' → 'isn't'. RULE 3 — PRONOUN AGREEMENT: subject must match — 'she' → 'she'. STRUCTURE: [aux + n't + pronoun]. EXAMPLES: 'You are coming, AREN'T YOU?' 'He has finished, HASN'T HE?' 'They will arrive, WON'T THEY?' 'She doesn't know, DOES SHE?' EXCEPTIONS: (a) 'I am' → 'AREN'T I?' (idiomatic, never 'amn't I'). (b) 'Let's go' → 'SHALL WE?' (c) 'Open the door' (imperative) → 'WILL YOU?' or 'WON'T YOU?' (d) 'Nobody knows' (negative meaning even if no 'not') → 'DO THEY?' (A) shall we — let's pattern
(B) won't we alone alone
(C) do we alone alone alone

Sentence & Error Correction — IMPERATIVE TAG RULE: For commands/requests, the standard tag is 'WILL YOU?' or its variants 'WON'T YOU?', 'CAN YOU?', 'COULD YOU?'.
