'LET'S' is a SUGGESTION, not a true imperative → uses 'shall we'. PYQ ANGLE: imperative-tag is a 1-mark Q in SSC CHSL, IBPS Clerk. EXAMINER MINDSET: testing the imperative-special-case rule.

The rule strictly applies to long 'ee' sounds.

(B) Realist (sees things as they are)
(C) Pragmatist (practical-minded)
(D) Cynic (distrustful sceptic)
cards.back:

Synonyms & Antonyms — OPTIMIST (Latin optimus = best) — sees BEST in everything; positive outlook. ANTONYM = PESSIMIST (Latin pessimus = worst) — sees WORST. REALIST sees things AS THEY ARE — middle ground. CYNIC distrusts motives. PRAGMATIST seeks practical solution. INSIGHT — these aren't fully opposed; psychology shows OPTIMISM benefits health, longevity, social bonds (Martin Seligman's 'Learned Optimism'); but excess optimism = naive (DUNNING-KRUGER, irrational exuberance). PESSIMISM has 'defensive' value — preparing for worst case. BALANCE: REALISTIC OPTIMISM = ideal — hope + plan + adapt. Famous quotes: 'Pessimist sees difficulty in every opportunity; optimist sees opportunity in every difficulty' (Churchill).

cards.front:
AQUARIUM literally means a place for what?

(A) Water (a place for water creatures)
(B) Air (an aviary type place)
(C) Earth (a terrarium-style place)
(D) Fire (which is heated chamber)
cards.back:
(A) Water (a place for water creatures)

Word Roots & Word Formation — AQUARIUM — etymology aqua (water, Latin) + -arium (place for) = 'a place for water'. So an aquarium is a tank or building containing water habitats for aquatic life. WORD FAMILY (root AQUA = water, Latin): (1) AQUATIC — relating to water; aquatic animals. (2) AQUEDUCT — water channel/bridge for transport (e.g., Roman aqueducts). (3) AQUAPLANE — water-skiing board; also vehicle losing road traction on wet roads. (4) AQUAMARINE — blue-green gemstone (color of sea-water). (5) AQUACULTURE — farming of aquatic organisms (like fish, prawns, seaweed). (6) AQUEOUS — water-based (e.g., 'aqueous solution'). (7) AQUARELLE — watercolor painting. RELATED PARALLEL ROOT: HYDRO (Greek for water) — hydroelectric, hydrant, dehydrate, hydrology, hydrogen ('water-former', because burning H₂ produces H₂O). KEY DISTINCTION between Latin AQUA and Greek HYDRO: both mean 'water'; English uses both interchangeably. AQUA more in everyday names; HYDRO in scientific/technical terms. PYQ FREQUENCY: AQUA root vocab in SSC CGL, CAT, IBPS PO English 1-2× per cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: rewards systematic root-knowledge.

cards.front:
AQUEDUCT in ancient Roman engineering refers to a:

(A) Channel/bridge for water transport
(B) Underground tunnel for soldiers
(C) Public bath house structure
(D) Granary for storing food crops
cards.back:
(A) Channel/bridge for water transport

Word Roots & Word Formation — AQUEDUCT — etymology aqua (water) + ducere (to lead, conduct) = 'water-leader'. Used by ROMANS to transport fresh water from distant springs/rivers to cities by gravity-driven channels. KEY EXAMPLES: (1) AQUA APPIA (312 BCE) — first Roman aqueduct, by censor Appius Claudius (also built Appian Way). Brought water to Rome from ~16 km away. (2) AQUA CLAUDIA (52 CE) — Emperor Claudius's; ~70 km long; arched portions still standing. (3) PONT DU GARD (France) — UNESCO World Heritage; 50m tall arched aqueduct. (4) AQUEDUCT OF SEGOVIA (Spain) — still in use after 2000 years! ENGINEERING: aqueducts maintained gentle slope (~1:200) over long distances, using arches to maintain elevation. INDIA — TRADITIONAL water-conduction systems: STEPWELLS (baolis, vavs) — Adalaj (Gujarat), Rani-ki-Vav (Patan, UNESCO 2014), Chand Baori (Rajasthan). KARNATAKA HOYSALA tanks. MUGHAL water gardens (Char Bagh) used canals. SIMILAR ROOTS — ducere ('lead'): conduct, deduce, induce, produce, reduce, abduct, viaduct. VIADUCT vs AQUEDUCT: viaduct carries roads/railways; aqueduct carries water. PYQ FREQUENCY: 'aqueduct' in SSC CGL, UPSC History, World History essays.

cards.front:
DEHYDRATE means to remove what from a substance?

(A) Water (de- + hydro- = water removed)
(B) Salt (sodium and chloride here)
(C) Oxygen (the air molecules)
(D) Nutrients (the dietary content)
cards.back:
(A) Water (de- + hydro- = water removed)

Word Roots & Word Formation — DEHYDRATE — etymology de (away, removal) + hydro (water) = 'remove water from'. Common usages: (1) FOOD PRESERVATION: dehydrating fruits/vegetables (raisins, banana chips, dried apricots) — removes water → inhibits microbial growth. (2) MEDICAL: a dehydrated patient has lost too much body water (causes weakness, dizziness, confusion). (3) CHEMICAL: anhydrous reagents are 'water-free' for sensitive reactions. WORD FAMILY (Greek HYDRO = water): (1) HYDRATE — to add water; or a chemical compound containing water (e.g., hydrated copper sulfate CuSO₄·5H₂O is blue; anhydrous is white). (2) HYDROGEN — 'water-former' (H + O makes water). (3) HYDRANT — public water tap (firefighters). (4) HYDROELECTRIC — using water flow to generate electricity. (5) HYDROLOGY — study of water cycles, rivers, groundwater. (6) HYDROPONICS — growing plants in water-based nutrient solution (no soil). (7) HYDROFOIL — boat that lifts above water on submerged 'wings'. (8) HYDROCEPHALUS — 'water on the brain' (medical condition). EVERYDAY HEALTH: average human needs ~2-3 L water/day (more in heat, exercise). DEHYDRATION at >2% body water loss: noticeable thirst, dry mouth; >5% loss: cardio risk. PYQ FREQUENCY: HYDRO words in SSC CGL, NEET 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
ANHYDROUS chemistry means without:

(A) Water (an + hydro = no water)
(B) Air (a vacuum or oxygen-less)
(C) Heat (cool/cold conditions)
(D) Light (kept in the dark only)
cards.back:
(A) Water (an + hydro = no water)

Word Roots & Word Formation — ANHYDROUS — etymology an (without) + hydro (water) + -ous (adjective suffix) = 'without water'. CHEMISTRY: an anhydrous compound is one that lacks water of crystallization (or is water-free). EXAMPLES: (1) ANHYDROUS CuSO₄ (white powder) vs HYDRATED CuSO₄·5H₂O (blue crystals). (2) ANHYDROUS NH₃ (colourless gas) — ammonia in pure form. (3) ANHYDROUS HCl gas vs HCl AQUEOUS (hydrochloric acid). (4) ANHYDROUS NaCl is rare; common table salt absorbs moisture (hygroscopic). (5) ANHYDROUS ETHER, ANHYDROUS ALCOHOL — used in chemistry labs for water-sensitive reactions. WHY ANHYDROUS MATTERS: many reagents react with water (e.g., grignard reagents, sodium metal — react explosively); some catalysts get poisoned by water. ANHYDROUS chemicals stored under DRY ATMOSPHERE (nitrogen, argon) or in DESICCATORS. RELATED CHEMICAL TERMS: (1) HYGROSCOPIC — absorbs water from air (e.g., concentrated H₂SO₄, CaCl₂). (2) DELIQUESCENT — absorbs so much water it dissolves itself (e.g., NaOH pellets in humid air). (3) EFFLORESCENT — loses water of crystallization to air (e.g., washing soda). PYQ FREQUENCY: anhydrous chemistry in NEET, JEE-Main 1× per paper.

cards.front:
HYDROPHOBIA, in pathology, refers to:

(A) Fear of water (rabies symptom)
(B) Love of water swimming activities
(C) Water-borne diseases generally
(D) An infection caused by water itself
cards.back:
(A) Fear of water (rabies symptom)

Word Roots & Word Formation — HYDROPHOBIA — etymology hydro (water) + phobia (fear) = 'fear of water'. CLINICAL CONTEXT: classic LATE-STAGE SYMPTOM of RABIES — patients develop intense fear/aversion to drinking water; even the SIGHT/SOUND of water triggers throat spasms (because rabies virus paralyzes throat muscles). 'HYDROPHOBIA' is sometimes used as a SYNONYM for rabies in older medical literature. RABIES: caused by RABIES VIRUS (Lyssavirus, RNA virus); transmitted by bite of infected animal (dogs in India, bats in Americas). Once symptoms appear, fatality is ~100%. PRE-EXPOSURE PROPHYLAXIS (vaccine) and POST-EXPOSURE PROPHYLAXIS (PEP — vaccine + immunoglobulin) are LIFE-SAVING. INDIA: ~20,000 rabies deaths/year (highest globally); ~99% from dog bites. WORLD RABIES DAY — 28 September. CHEMISTRY USE of 'HYDROPHOBIC': describes substances that REPEL water (oils, fats, waxes, hydrocarbons). HYDROPHILIC = water-loving (sugars, salts, alcohols). Cell membranes have HYDROPHILIC heads (in water) + HYDROPHOBIC tails (away from water) — basis of bilayer structure. PHOBIA suffix: also in CLAUSTROPHOBIA (closed spaces), AGORAPHOBIA (open spaces), ARACHNOPHOBIA (spiders), XENOPHOBIA (foreigners), TRYPOPHOBIA (holes). PYQ FREQUENCY: medical-vocab MCQs in NEET, AIIMS, SSC GA.

cards.front:
HYDROPONICS is a method of growing plants:

(A) In nutrient water without soil
(B) Underwater in marine farms
(C) In greenhouses with extra humidity
(D) By dehydrating roots completely
cards.back:
(A) In nutrient water without soil

Word Roots & Word Formation — HYDROPONICS — etymology hydro (water) + ponos (work, Greek) = 'water-work'. Method of growing plants WITHOUT SOIL, using mineral nutrient solutions in water. INVENTOR: term coined by W.F. Gericke (UC Berkeley, 1937). ADVANTAGES: (1) ~90% less water than traditional farming. (2) Higher YIELD per square meter (vertical stacking possible). (3) No herbicides/pesticides needed. (4) Faster growth (15-50%). (5) Year-round (climate-controlled). (6) Can grow in cities (urban farming). DISADVANTAGES: (1) High initial setup cost. (2) Requires electricity (pumps). (3) Vulnerability to system failure (no soil-buffer). VARIANTS: (a) NFT (Nutrient Film Technique) — thin nutrient stream over roots. (b) DWC (Deep Water Culture) — roots submerged in oxygenated water. (c) AEROPONICS — roots in mist (NASA used for space-experiments). (d) AQUAPONICS — combines fish farming + plant hydroponics; fish waste fertilizes plants. INDIAN COMPANIES — UrbanKisaan, Letcetra, Future Farms. CROPS: lettuce, basil, strawberry, tomato — best-suited; root vegetables (carrots, potatoes) less suited. PYQ FREQUENCY: hydroponics + sustainable-agriculture in UPSC current affairs, NEET environmental.

cards.front:
HYDROLYSIS, a chemistry term, literally means:

(A) Splitting/breaking by water
(B) Combining things using water
(C) Boiling away the water content
(D) Filtering water through media
cards.back:
(A) Splitting/breaking by water

Word Roots & Word Formation — HYDROLYSIS — etymology hydro (water) + lysis (loosening, splitting, Greek) = 'splitting by water'. Chemical reaction where a compound is BROKEN APART by reacting with WATER. EXAMPLES: (1) DIGESTION: starch → glucose (catalyzed by amylase enzyme + water). Proteins → amino acids (peptidase + water). Fats → fatty acids + glycerol (lipase + water). (2) SOAP MAKING: fats + NaOH/KOH + water → soap + glycerol (called SAPONIFICATION, a hydrolysis). (3) METAL OXIDES + water → metal hydroxides (e.g., CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ — slaked lime). (4) HYDROLYSIS OF SALTS: solutions of weak-acid+strong-base salts (e.g., Na₂CO₃) become BASIC; weak-base+strong-acid salts (NH₄Cl) become ACIDIC. CONTRAST WITH RELATED REACTIONS: (a) DEHYDRATION SYNTHESIS — opposite of hydrolysis (joins compounds, releases water). e.g., disaccharide formation: glucose + fructose → sucrose + H₂O. (b) HYDRATION — adds water across a double bond (alkene → alcohol). 'LYSIS' suffix = breakdown: ANALYSIS, ELECTROLYSIS, PARALYSIS, PYROLYSIS, CATALYSIS. PYQ FREQUENCY: hydrolysis in NEET, JEE-Main, CBSE class 12 — 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
INCREDIBLE means:

(A) Extraordinary; hard to believe
(B) Easily believable, ordinary
(C) Boring or commonplace items
(D) Forbidden, taboo, illegal
cards.back:
(A) Extraordinary; hard to believe

Word Roots & Word Formation — INCREDIBLE — etymology IN (not) + CREDIBLE (believable) = 'NOT BELIEVABLE'. COMMON USAGE: extraordinary, amazing, beyond normal expectation; sometimes literally 'unbelievable' (questioning truth). EXAMPLES: (1) 'INCREDIBLE INDIA' — Tourism Ministry's marketing campaign (since 2002, by Ministry of Tourism + Ogilvy & Mather agency); designed to attract foreign tourists by showcasing India's diversity, heritage, culture. (2) 'The view from Mt Everest is incredible' = breathtaking. (3) 'Her story sounds incredible' = hard to believe (literal). (4) 'She has incredible talent' = extraordinary. NUANCE — POSITIVE vs SKEPTICAL: 'incredible' often POSITIVE (amazing), but in context of stories/claims = SKEPTICAL (suspicious of truth). 'I find his alibi incredible' (don't believe). DUAL-USE WORDS like INCREDIBLE: meaning depends on context. SYNONYMS for the POSITIVE sense: amazing, awesome, breathtaking, extraordinary, marvellous, phenomenal, remarkable, spectacular, stupendous, unbelievable. SYNONYMS for SKEPTICAL: implausible, dubious, far-fetched, suspicious. RELATED — INCREDULOUS (different word!) — describes the PERSON who doesn't believe; not the THING. 'She gave me an incredulous look' (her expression was disbelieving). CONFUSION: incredible (about a thing) vs incredulous (about a person's response) — common exam trap! PYQ FREQUENCY: incredible/incredulous distinction in SSC CGL, CAT, IBPS PO 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
FID root means 'trust/faith'. FIDELITY means:

(A) Faithfulness, loyalty (e.g., to spouse)
(B) Wealth and prosperity here
(C) Highest social status only
(D) Boldness in difficult situations
cards.back:
(A) Faithfulness, loyalty (e.g., to spouse)

Word Roots & Word Formation — FIDELITY — etymology Latin 'fidelis' (faithful) + '-ity' = 'state of being faithful'. Means LOYALTY, FAITHFULNESS, especially in marriage or to a cause. WORD FAMILY (root FID = trust, faith): (1) FIDELITY — loyalty. (2) INFIDELITY — unfaithfulness (esp. marital). (3) CONFIDENT — having full trust. (4) CONFIDE — trust someone with secrets. (5) CONFIDENTIAL — secret; trusted. (6) DIFFIDENT — lacking confidence (DI = away). (7) FIDUCIARY — based on trust (financial relationship). (8) PERFIDIOUS — treacherous (PER = through/away, in negative sense). (9) INFIDEL — non-believer (in religious context — historically pejorative; modern usage avoids). (10) BONA FIDE — 'in good faith' (Latin); genuine. (11) AFFIDAVIT — sworn statement (legal). DISTINCT MEANINGS — FIDELITY in different contexts: (a) MARITAL — loyalty to spouse. (b) DOG'S FIDELITY — loyalty to owner (proverbial). (c) AUDIO — high-fidelity (HiFi) sound = TRUE-to-original reproduction. (d) HISTORICAL — fidelity to source documents (no distortion). MOTTO usage: many institutions have 'FIDELITY' or related Latin phrases — US Marines: 'Semper Fidelis' (Always Faithful, since 1883). EDINBURGH ROYAL HIGH SCHOOL: 'Musis Respublica Floret' but variants. UPSC angle: Indian Penal Code Section 497 (adultery — struck down 2018 by SC, Joseph Shine v. Union of India; fidelity is moral/social, not criminal). PYQ FREQUENCY: FID root vocab in SSC CGL, CAT 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
CONFIDE means to:

(A) Trust someone with secrets/feelings
(B) Hide everything carefully here
(C) Combine multiple things together
(D) Confine someone in jail or prison
cards.back:
(A) Trust someone with secrets/feelings

Word Roots & Word Formation — CONFIDE — etymology Latin 'con' (together with) + 'fidere' (to trust) = 'to share trust together'. Means to TRUST SOMEONE with private info, secrets, deep feelings. SAMPLE: 'She confides in her best friend.' 'The patient confided his fears to his doctor.' RELATED WORDS: (1) CONFIDENCE — state of trusting; self-trust. (2) CONFIDENT — having self-trust. (3) CONFIDENTIAL — secret, trusted. (4) CONFIDANT (m) / CONFIDANTE (f) — close friend trusted with secrets. (5) CONFIDENTIALITY — duty of keeping secrets. (6) DIFFIDENT — opposite of confident; lacking confidence. KEY DISTINCTION: (a) CONFIDE IN — share secrets/feelings (intransitive). 'She confides IN him' = she shares with him. (b) CONFIDE TO — entrust formally (less common). 'He confided his savings to the bank.' EXAM TRAP: don't confuse 'CONFIDE' with: (1) CONFINE — restrict (trap, limit, imprison). 'Confine to bed' = bedridden. Different etymology: 'finis' (end, boundary). (2) CONFOUND — confuse, baffle. (3) CONFUTE — disprove. UPSC angle: CONFIDENTIALITY in governance + journalism (RTI exemptions for confidential matters; legal privileges for lawyer-client communication). 'WHISTLEBLOWER' protections (Whistle Blowers Protection Act 2014). PYQ FREQUENCY: CONFIDE/CONFIDENCE-related vocab in SSC CGL, CAT, IBPS PO 1× per cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests careful reading + word-association.

cards.front:
PERFIDIOUS describes someone who is:

(A) Treacherous; deceitful, betraying trust
(B) Highly faithful, trustworthy person
(C) Strong and physically powerful
(D) Wealthy and influential person
cards.back:
(A) Treacherous; deceitful, betraying trust

Word Roots & Word Formation — PERFIDIOUS — etymology Latin 'per' (through, beyond — in negative sense) + 'fid' (trust/faith) = 'breaking through trust' = TREACHEROUS, deceitful, faithless. ANTONYM of FAITHFUL. NOUN: PERFIDY = act of betrayal. SAMPLE: 'A perfidious ally betrayed our plans.' 'The perfidious king broke his oath.' STRONG NEGATIVE word — implies SERIOUS BREACH OF TRUST. SYNONYMS: treacherous, traitorous, deceitful, untrustworthy, two-faced, double-dealing, false. ANTONYMS: faithful, loyal, trustworthy, dependable. KEY 'PER-' MEANINGS: (1) THROUGH (perimeter, perforate). (2) THOROUGHLY (perfect = thoroughly done). (3) NEGATIVE (perjury = lying, perfidious = breaking trust, perish = thoroughly dead). (4) PERMEATE — go through. (5) PERSPECTIVE — through-look. KEY 'FID-' WORDS revisited: PERFIDIOUS contrasts with FIDUCIARY (trust-based duty). 'Perfidious Albion' — historic French slur on Britain (~17-18th century) for diplomatic betrayals. RELATED WORDS: TREACHERY (act of betrayal), TREASON (legally, betrayal of state — punishable under IPC Section 121-124, Indian Constitution defines treason indirectly through these). UPSC angle: 'sedition' (IPC 124A) is a related but distinct concept — recently struck down/restrained by SC (May 2022 stay; ongoing review). KEY: SC observed 124A may not survive constitutional scrutiny. PYQ FREQUENCY: PERFIDIOUS in CAT, GRE, advanced UPSC English 1× per cycle.

RELATED WORDS: TREACHERY (act of betrayal), TREASON (legally, betrayal of state — punishable under IPC Section 121-124, Indian Constitution defines treason indirectly through these). UPSC angle: 'sedition' (IPC 124A) is a related but distinct concept — recently struck down/restrained by SC (May 2022 stay; ongoing review). KEY: SC observed 124A may not survive constitutional scrutiny. PYQ FREQUENCY: PERFIDIOUS in CAT, GRE, advanced UPSC English 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
BONA FIDE (Latin phrase) means:

(A) In good faith; genuine, sincere
(B) False, fraudulent, illegitimate
(C) Bored or weary, unenthused
(D) Bonus given to officials only
cards.back:
(A) In good faith; genuine, sincere

Word Roots & Word Formation — BONA FIDE — Latin: 'bona' (good) + 'fide' (faith, ablative of 'fides') = 'in good faith'. Means GENUINE, AUTHENTIC, SINCERE; without intent to deceive. PRONUNCIATION: 'BOH-nah FY-dee' (Latin) or 'bo-NAH FYD' (Anglicized). USAGE: (1) 'A bona fide offer' = genuine. (2) 'Bona fide passenger' = legitimate (traveling for genuine reason). (3) Indian Railways: 'BONA FIDE PASSENGER' = legitimate ticket-holder; differs from ticketless travelers. (4) LEGAL: 'Bona fide purchaser' = buyer who purchased in good faith without knowledge of defects. RELATED LATIN LEGAL phrases: (1) MALA FIDE = 'in bad faith' (opposite). (2) DE FACTO = 'in fact' (in practice). (3) DE JURE = 'in law' (in legal theory). (4) HABEAS CORPUS = 'have the body' (writ to produce a person before court — Article 32, 226 in Indian Constitution). (5) SUO MOTU = 'on its own motion' (court taking action without petition). (6) MUTATIS MUTANDIS = 'with necessary changes'. (7) PRO BONO = 'for good' (free legal services). (8) AMICUS CURIAE = 'friend of the court' (advisor to court). UPSC angle: legal terminology in GS-2 polity; SC judgments use these regularly. CIVIL SERVICE law-officer roles (AG, SG) use these phrases professionally. PYQ FREQUENCY: BONA FIDE + Latin phrases in CAT, UPSC, judicial services 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
DIFFIDENT describes someone who:

(A) Lacks confidence; shy, hesitant
(B) Is highly confident and bold
(C) Is contradictory and conflicting
(D) Has different opinions from others
cards.back:
(A) Lacks confidence; shy, hesitant

Word Roots & Word Formation — DIFFIDENT — etymology DIS (apart, away, away from) + FID (trust) = 'lacking trust (in oneself)' = SHY, RESERVED, HESITANT. ANTONYM of CONFIDENT. SAMPLE: 'The diffident new student didn't speak up.' 'She's diffident about asking for help.' SYNONYMS: shy, reserved, timid, hesitant, self-effacing, unassertive, retiring. ANTONYMS: confident, assertive, self-assured, bold, outspoken. EXAM TRAP: students confuse: (1) DIFFIDENT — lacking confidence. (2) DIFFERENT — not the same. — These are DIFFERENT words despite similar appearance. ETYMOLOGICALLY DIFFERENT roots: 'diffident' (DIS + FID); 'different' (DIS + FERRE — to carry, separate). KEY: 'difficult' is also separate (DIS + FACERE). FAMILY of CONFIDENCE-related words: (1) CONFIDENT (assured) ↔ DIFFIDENT (uncertain). (2) CONFIDENCE ↔ DIFFIDENCE. (3) SELF-CONFIDENT ↔ INSECURE. (4) ASSERTIVE ↔ SUBMISSIVE. (5) BOLD ↔ TIMID. (6) DECISIVE ↔ INDECISIVE. PSYCHOLOGY angle: diffidence = trait or state. State diffidence → in unfamiliar situations (mostly normal); trait diffidence → personality (may benefit from social-skills training, CBT, exposure therapy). UPSC INTERVIEW PERSONALITY: candidates are evaluated on confidence (without arrogance) — diffidence often penalized; ASSERTIVENESS WITH HUMILITY is the gold standard. PYQ FREQUENCY: DIFFIDENT in CAT, GRE, advanced UPSC English 1× per 2 cycles. EXAMINER MINDSET (UPSC-level): tests vocabulary precision.

cards.front:
'Predict' literally means to:

(A) Say against
(B) Say beforehand
(C) Say loudly
(D) Say silently
cards.back:
(B) Say beforehand

Word Roots & Word Formation — L. 'pre-' = before + 'dict' = say. Same family: contradict (say against), verdict (true saying), dictate (say/impose), edict (formal proclamation), dictionary (book of sayings).

(B) Say the opposite of what has been said
(C) Say something nervously
(D) Report a conversation
cards.back:
(B) Say the opposite of what has been said

Word Roots & Word Formation — 'contra-' = against + 'dict' = say. To state the opposite; express denial.

Word Roots & Word Formation — L. 'verus' = true + 'dict' = say → 'a true saying' — a court's formal finding. A royal decree is closer to an 'edict' (proclamation).

cards.front:
GEO root means 'earth'. GEOGRAPHY literally means:

(A) Description of the earth (geo + graphy)
(B) Study of rocks (that's geology)
(C) Map of the world (cartography)
(D) Land surveying (a related field)
cards.back:
(A) Description of the earth (geo + graphy)

Word Roots & Word Formation — GEOGRAPHY — etymology GEO (earth, Greek) + GRAPHY (writing, drawing) = 'earth-writing' = description/study of Earth's physical features, climate, populations, resources. KEY GEO-WORDS (memorize): (1) GEOGRAPHY — description of Earth. (2) GEOLOGY — study of Earth's structure (rocks, minerals, plate tectonics). (3) GEOMETRY — 'earth-measure' (originally land surveying; now math of shapes). (4) GEOPHYSICS — physics of Earth. (5) GEOTHERMAL — Earth heat. (6) GEOPOLITICS — politics of geography. (7) GEOCHEMISTRY — chemistry of Earth materials. (8) GEOMORPHOLOGY — study of landforms. (9) GEOCENTRIC — Earth-centered (vs heliocentric, sun-centered). (10) GEODESY — measurement of Earth's shape. RELATED -GRAPHY words: (a) BIOGRAPHY (life-writing). (b) AUTOGRAPHY (self-writing — auto). (c) PHOTOGRAPHY (light-writing). (d) BIBLIOGRAPHY (book-listing). (e) CARTOGRAPHY (map-making, kart from Greek 'chartes' = paper). (f) DEMOGRAPHY (people-writing — demos). (g) ETHNOGRAPHY (culture-writing). (h) CALLIGRAPHY (beautiful writing — kalli = beautiful). (i) STENOGRAPHY (narrow/short writing — shorthand). UPSC: GEOGRAPHY OPTIONAL papers cover physical, human, regional geography, plus environmental geography in PT. PYQ FREQUENCY: GEO root vocab in SSC CGL, CAT, UPSC English 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
TERRESTRIAL means relating to:

(A) Earth or land (terra firma)
(B) Sky and atmosphere only
(C) Water and oceans only here
(D) Outer space (extraterrestrial)
cards.back:
(A) Earth or land (terra firma)

Word Roots & Word Formation — TERRESTRIAL — etymology TERRA (earth, Latin) + -ESTRIAL = 'pertaining to Earth/land'. Used: (1) BIOLOGY — terrestrial animals (live on land vs aquatic, arboreal). Examples: lion, elephant, snake. (2) ASTRONOMY — TERRESTRIAL PLANETS (rocky, like Earth) — Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars (the inner planets). Contrast: GAS GIANTS (Jupiter, Saturn) and ICE GIANTS (Uranus, Neptune). (3) BROADCASTING — terrestrial TV (over-the-air signals from ground antennas, vs satellite TV). EXTRATERRESTRIAL = 'beyond Earth' = space/aliens (movie 'E.T.' = extraterrestrial). TERRA WORD FAMILY: (1) TERRITORY — 'land area' (claimed/owned). (2) TERRAIN — 'physical features of land'. (3) TERRACE — 'flat raised platform'. (4) SUBTERRANEAN — 'below the earth' (underground; e.g., subterranean tunnel, subway). (5) MEDITERRANEAN — 'middle of the lands' (between Europe + Africa + Asia). (6) TERRACOTTA — 'baked earth' (clay pottery, e.g., terracotta army of Qin Shi Huang in China). (7) TERRAFORM — to alter a planet's environment to be Earth-like (sci-fi for Mars colonization). (8) INTERN, INTERMENT — burial in earth. (9) DISINTER — to dig up. PYQ FREQUENCY: TERR-related vocab in SSC CGL, CAT, UPSC English 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
MEDITERRANEAN literally means:

(A) In the middle of the lands (sea between)
(B) By the eastern shores of land (option here)
(C) Land of the medieval era only (option here)
(D) Soft, mediating climate region (option here)
cards.back:
(A) In the middle of the lands (sea between)

Word Roots & Word Formation — MEDITERRANEAN — etymology MEDI (middle, Latin) + TERRA (earth, land) + -ANEAN = 'in the middle of the lands' or 'sea between lands'. The MEDITERRANEAN SEA is enclosed by Europe (north), Africa (south), Asia (east). KEY GEOGRAPHIC FACTS: ~2.5 million sq km; connected to: (1) ATLANTIC OCEAN via STRAIT OF GIBRALTAR (only ~14 km wide, separates Spain + Morocco). (2) BLACK SEA via TURKISH STRAITS (Bosphorus, Dardanelles). (3) RED SEA via SUEZ CANAL (since 1869). MEDITERRANEAN CLIMATE: dry hot summers, mild wet winters; supports olive, grape, citrus, fig — characteristic 'Mediterranean diet'. CIVILIZATIONS born here: Egyptian, Phoenician, Greek, Roman, Byzantine, Ottoman. RECENT EVENTS: refugee crises across Mediterranean from N. Africa to Europe. MED WORD FAMILY (root MEDI = middle, Latin): (1) MEDIATE — be in middle, settle dispute. (2) MEDIAN — middle value. (3) MEDIUM — middle/intermediate. (4) IMMEDIATE — without delay (without anything in middle). (5) INTERMEDIATE — in between. (6) MEDIOCRE — average (medium quality). MEDIEVAL is from a different root (medi + aevum, age) — middle ages. UPSC angle: Mediterranean climate type appears in geography PT — also climate-zone classification (Köppen system). PYQ FREQUENCY: Mediterranean concept in geography MCQ, etymology in CAT.

cards.front:
SUBTERRANEAN refers to something:

(A) Below the earth's surface (underground)
(B) Above the earth in atmosphere (option here)
(C) Across the land surface only (option here)
(D) Beyond Earth in outer space (option here)
cards.back:
(A) Below the earth's surface (underground)

Word Roots & Word Formation — SUBTERRANEAN — etymology SUB (under, Latin) + TERRA (earth) + -EAN = 'under the earth' = UNDERGROUND. EXAMPLES: (1) Subterranean RIVERS — flow underground (Mahanadi tributaries in some regions). (2) Subterranean PASSAGES — tunnels, escape routes (e.g., in ancient forts). (3) SUBWAY systems — subterranean trains (Delhi Metro has many underground sections; New York Subway, London Underground, Paris Metro, Moscow Metro famous worldwide). (4) Subterranean CAVES — Mawsmai (Meghalaya), Belum (Andhra), Borra (Andhra) caves in India. (5) Subterranean ECOSYSTEMS — unique cave-dwelling species (blind fish, salamanders adapted to dark). KEY 'SUB' words (root SUB = under): SUBMARINE (under sea), SUBTERRANEAN (under earth), SUBCONSCIOUS (below conscious thought), SUBSTANDARD (below standard), SUBSCRIBE (sign under), SUBJECT, SUBSIDIZE, SUBORDINATE. RELATED CONCEPTS: TROGLODYTE = cave-dweller; TROGLOBITES = species that live entirely in caves. UPSC angle: SUBTERRANEAN water resources (groundwater) — key for India's water security; aquifer depletion in Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan; managed aquifer recharge as a UPSC GS-3 environment topic. CENTRAL GROUND WATER BOARD (CGWB) monitors. PYQ FREQUENCY: 'sub-' prefix vocab in SSC CGL, CAT 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
GEOTHERMAL energy uses heat from:

(A) Earth's interior (geo + thermal)
(B) Sun directly (solar power)
(C) Wind currents (wind power)
(D) Rivers (hydropower instead)
cards.back:
(A) Earth's interior (geo + thermal)

Word Roots & Word Formation — GEOTHERMAL — etymology GEO (earth) + THERMAL (heat) = 'earth-heat'. Energy harnessed from heat naturally produced inside Earth's mantle/core (radioactive decay + residual heat from Earth's formation 4.5 billion years ago). USES: (1) ELECTRICITY GENERATION — drilling wells to extract steam/hot water that drives turbines. Top countries: USA, Indonesia, Philippines, Turkey, New Zealand, Iceland, Italy. ICELAND gets ~25% of electricity + 90% of home heating from geothermal — sits on Mid-Atlantic Ridge. (2) DIRECT HEATING — homes (Iceland), greenhouses, fish farming, district heating (Boise, Idaho, USA — first geothermal heating system 1892). (3) GEOTHERMAL HEAT PUMPS — household heating/cooling using Earth as thermal reservoir (~10-15°C below surface year-round). INDIA POTENTIAL: 340+ identified hotspots including PUGA VALLEY (Ladakh), MANIKARAN (HP), TATTAPANI (Chhattisgarh), TAPTAPANI (Odisha). PUGA development project initiated 2024. ESTIMATED INDIAN POTENTIAL: ~10 GW (per GSI). VOLCANIC HOTSPOTS — Iceland, Japan, New Zealand have abundant geothermal due to plate tectonics. UPSC angle: geothermal under RENEWABLE ENERGY policy; Ministry of New & Renewable Energy (MNRE); Climate change mitigation (NDC commitments). PYQ FREQUENCY: geothermal in UPSC PT, NEET environment, SSC GA 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
TERRACOTTA literally means:

(A) Baked earth (clay pottery)
(B) Terraced cotton fields here
(C) Ancient temple structure
(D) Sacred earth or ground
cards.back:
(A) Baked earth (clay pottery)

Word Roots & Word Formation — TERRACOTTA — etymology TERRA (earth) + COTTA (cooked, Italian) = 'baked/cooked earth'. CLAY-BASED CERAMIC made by molding clay then firing at relatively low temperatures (~600-1000°C). NATURAL color: orange-brown-red (iron oxide content); after firing, retains color. USES historic + modern: (1) POTTERY — ancient civilizations everywhere; Indus Valley (Harappa, Mohenjo-daro) had extensive terracotta. (2) ROOFING TILES (Mediterranean, Italian style; common in India). (3) ARCHITECTURAL ORNAMENT — facades, friezes. (4) SCULPTURE — TERRACOTTA WARRIORS of CHINA (Qin Shi Huang's tomb, ~210 BCE; ~8,000 life-sized warriors discovered 1974). (5) VESSELS — water pots ('matka' in Hindi) — keep water cool through evaporation. (6) DIYAS (oil lamps for Diwali). INDIA: Bishnupur (West Bengal) — UNESCO terracotta temples. Rajasthan, Tamil Nadu, Bengal — major centers of terracotta craftsmanship. ETYMOLOGY ITALIAN: 'terra' (earth) + 'cotta' (past participle of 'cuocere', to cook). PARALLEL WORDS: BISCOTTI (twice-cooked biscuits), COTTAGE (small heated dwelling — different etymology though). KEY: 'TERRA' appears in many Italian-origin English words about earth/land. UPSC ART & CULTURE: terracotta in CSE Mains has appeared in Indian-art questions. PYQ FREQUENCY: TERR vocab in CGL, IBPS PO, CAT 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
GEODESIC, related to GEO root, means:

(A) Pertaining to Earth's geometry/shape
(B) Pertaining to dictation only here
(C) Relating to medicines for soil
(D) Relating to ancient maps mostly
cards.back:
(A) Pertaining to Earth's geometry/shape

Word Roots & Word Formation — GEODESIC — etymology GEO (earth) + DESIA (division, Greek) — relates to GEODESY (measurement of Earth's shape). KEY USES: (1) GEODESIC DOMES — by Buckminster Fuller (1950s); spherical structures built from triangles, very strong + light. Famous example: EPCOT's Spaceship Earth at Disney World, Florida. (2) GEODESIC PATHS — shortest line between two points on a curved surface (e.g., great circle on Earth's sphere). Airlines fly geodesic routes — appear curved on flat maps but are shortest in 3D space; classic example: Delhi to New York flight crosses near Arctic. (3) GENERAL RELATIVITY — spacetime is curved; objects travel on geodesics (shortest paths). PARALLEL CONCEPTS in MATH: (a) GEODESIC on flat plane = straight line. (b) On a sphere (e.g., Earth) = great circle (e.g., equator, meridians). (c) In Einstein's General Relativity = path through curved spacetime. KEY MEASUREMENTS: GEODESY → defines Earth's shape (oblate spheroid; equatorial radius ~6,378 km, polar ~6,357 km). GPS uses geodesy to compute positions. INDIA's SURVEY OF INDIA (founded 1767) — oldest scientific dept; conducts geodesic surveys for maps + boundaries. RELATED 'DESIA' words: rare; mostly geodesy and derivatives. PYQ FREQUENCY: rare-vocabulary like 'geodesic' in CAT, GRE, UPSC English-comprehension 1× per 2 cycles. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests advanced GEO-root knowledge.

cards.front:
The root 'bio' in words like 'biology' and 'biography' refers to:

(A) Book
(B) Life
(C) Two
(D) Body
cards.back:
(B) Life

Word Roots & Word Formation — Greek 'bios' = life. So biology = study of life, biography = writing about a person's life, biopsy = examining living tissue, antibiotic = against life (microbial). 'Book' would be 'biblio' (bibliography, Bible); 'two' is 'bi-' (bicycle); 'body' is 'soma' (somatic, psychosomatic).

cards.front:
The prefix 'mis-' in words like 'misunderstand' and 'misbehave' means:

(A) Very much
(B) Wrong or bad
(C) Not yet
(D) Before
cards.back:
(B) Wrong or bad

Word Roots & Word Formation — 'Mis-' from Old English/Germanic — carries the sense of 'wrongly, badly, incorrectly'. Examples: mistake (wrong take), misjudge, misfortune, mispronounce, misinform. 'Very much' is not a prefix; 'not yet' is 'pre-' or 'un-'; 'before' is 'pre-' or 'ante-'.

cards.front:
The suffix '-ology' in words like 'biology' and 'geology' means:

(A) Without
(B) Study of
(C) Fear of
(D) Love of
cards.back:
(B) Study of

Word Roots & Word Formation — '-ology' / '-logy' from Greek 'logos' (word, study) — the systematic study of something. Examples: psychology (mind), zoology (animals), theology (god), anthropology (humans), cardiology (heart). 'Fear of' is '-phobia' (claustrophobia, xenophobia); 'love of' is '-phil' (bibliophile, Francophile).

cards.front:
The root 'chrono' as in 'chronology' and 'chronic' means:

(A) Colour
(B) Time
(C) Light
(D) Sound
cards.back:
(B) Time

Word Roots & Word Formation — Greek 'chronos' = time. Chronology = arrangement of events in time; chronic = lasting a long time (as in chronic disease); synchronous = happening at the same time; anachronism = something out of its time period. 'Colour' is 'chrom(o)' (chromatic, monochrome); 'light' is 'photo-' (photograph); 'sound' is 'phono-' (phonetics, telephone).

cards.front:
A word meaning 'fear of enclosed spaces' is:

(A) Agoraphobia
(B) Claustrophobia
(C) Hydrophobia
(D) Xenophobia
cards.back:
(B) Claustrophobia

Word Roots & Word Formation — Claustrophobia — from Latin 'claustrum' (enclosed space) + Greek 'phobia' (fear). Agoraphobia — fear of open / public spaces. Hydrophobia — fear of water (a classic symptom of rabies). Xenophobia — fear / dislike of foreigners. Acrophobia — heights; arachnophobia — spiders; nyctophobia — darkness.

cards.front:
The prefix 'ambi-' as in 'ambiguous' and 'ambidextrous' means:

(A) Against
(B) Both
(C) Without
(D) Across
cards.back:
(B) Both

Word Roots & Word Formation — Latin 'ambi-' = both, on both sides. Ambiguous — having two (or more) possible meanings. Ambidextrous — using both hands equally well. Ambivalent — having both (conflicting) feelings. 'Against' is 'anti-' or 'contra-'; 'without' is 'a-' / 'an-' (atheist, asymmetric); 'across' is 'trans-' (transport, transcontinental).

The root 'cide' in 'homicide', 'pesticide' and 'genocide' means:

(A) Protect
(B) Kill
(C) Wound
(D) Heal
cards.back:

cards.front:
The root LOQU/LOC means 'to speak'. A LOQUACIOUS person is:

(A) Very talkative or chatty person
(B) Quiet and reserved generally
(C) Confused or muddled in speech
(D) Speaking in a foreign language
cards.back:
(A) Very talkative or chatty person

Word Roots & Word Formation — LOQUACIOUS — adjective meaning 'TALKATIVE, given to constant talking, chatty'. Root LOQU = speak. ETYMOLOGY: Latin 'loqui' = to speak. WORD FAMILY: (1) ELOQUENT (out + speak) — fluent and persuasive in speech. (2) SOLILOQUY (alone + speak) — a speech to oneself, famous in drama (Hamlet's 'To be or not to be' is the most famous English soliloquy). (3) COLLOQUIAL (together + speak) — informal, conversational language. (4) VENTRILOQUIST (belly + speak) — entertainer who throws their voice. (5) LOCUTION = a particular phrase or expression. (6) CIRCUMLOCUTION (around + speak) — using too many words to say something simple. (7) GRANDILOQUENT (grand + speak) — pompous, lofty in speech. SAMPLE SENTENCE: 'The loquacious salesman talked us through every product feature for an hour.' SYNONYMS: garrulous, voluble, verbose. ANTONYMS: taciturn, reticent, laconic. PYQ FREQUENCY: vocab roots are top SSC CGL, CAT, IBPS PO English MCQ; ~2 per paper.

cards.front:
What does ELOQUENT mean?

(A) Fluent and persuasive in speech
(B) Speaking in a soft, low voice
(C) Hesitant and awkward in speech
(D) Unable to speak clearly here
cards.back:
(A) Fluent and persuasive in speech

Word Roots & Word Formation — ELOQUENT — fluent, articulate, and persuasive in speech or writing; expressing oneself effectively. ETYMOLOGY: ex (out) + loqui (speak) → 'speaking out powerfully'. NOUN: ELOQUENCE — the quality of being eloquent. SAMPLE: 'Lincoln's Gettysburg Address remains a masterpiece of eloquent oratory'. SYNONYMS: articulate, fluent, persuasive, silver-tongued. ANTONYMS: inarticulate, halting, tongue-tied, fumbling. KEY DISTINCTION: 'eloquent' implies BOTH fluency AND power/persuasiveness; merely talking a lot (loquacious) isn't enough. EXAM-FAVOURITE TRAP: students confuse ELOQUENT (fluent in speech) with ELEGANT (graceful in style) — different roots: elegant is from 'eligere' = to choose. CONTEXT: in literature, an 'eloquent silence' is a non-verbal moment that conveys deep meaning — example of figurative usage. PYQ FREQUENCY: ELOQUENT appears in SSC CGL, CAT, IBPS PO synonym/antonym MCQs 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
A SOLILOQUY in literature is:

(A) A speech delivered alone aloud
(B) A dialogue between two persons
(C) A summary section of a play
(D) An opening scene of any play
cards.back:
(A) A speech delivered alone aloud

Word Roots & Word Formation — SOLILOQUY = a dramatic speech delivered by a character ALONE on stage, expressing inner thoughts to the audience (without other characters hearing). ETYMOLOGY: solus (alone) + loqui (speak) = 'speaking alone'. FAMOUS EXAMPLES: (1) HAMLET — 'To be, or not to be, that is the question...' (Shakespeare, ~1600). (2) MACBETH — 'Tomorrow, and tomorrow, and tomorrow, creeps in this petty pace...' (3) KING LEAR — 'Blow, winds, and crack your cheeks!' DISTINCTION: (a) DIALOGUE = two or more characters speaking. (b) MONOLOGUE = long speech by ONE character to OTHERS on stage. (c) SOLILOQUY = character ALONE, thinking aloud — audience overhears the thoughts. (d) ASIDE = brief comment to the audience while other characters can't hear. ROOT: 'solus' also gives us SOLO (alone), SOLITUDE (state of being alone), SOLITARY, DESOLATE. SHAKESPEARE'S PLAYS contain ~30+ major soliloquies; they remain the gold standard. PYQ FREQUENCY: literary terms in CAT, UPSC, MA Eng entrance MCQs.

cards.front:
The root LECT/LEG means 'read, choose, gather'. INTELLECT literally means:

(A) To choose between options (mind)
(B) Inner ear hearing capacity here
(C) Inside reading capacity always
(D) An intentional action of mind
cards.back:
(A) To choose between options (mind)

Word Roots & Word Formation — INTELLECT — etymology 'inter' (between) + 'lect/leg' (choose, gather) = the FACULTY OF CHOOSING BETWEEN, hence the rational mind, the power of reasoning. WORD FAMILY (root LECT/LEG = read, choose, gather): (1) LECTURE — a reading; an educational talk. (2) LEGEND — what is to be read; a story. (3) LEGIBLE — readable, capable of being read. (4) LEGION — a gathering of soldiers (Roman military unit of ~5,000). (5) ELECT — to choose out, select. (6) ELECTION — the act of choosing (especially political). (7) SELECT — to choose carefully. (8) COLLECT — to gather together. (9) COLLEGE — a gathering of scholars. (10) NEGLECT (neg + lect) = NOT to gather/pick up. (11) ELIGIBLE — fit to be chosen. (12) ECLECTIC — choosing from various sources. EXAM-FAVOURITE: trace word back to root → lock in meaning instantly. SAMPLE SENTENCE: 'Her intellect impressed everyone in the debate.' PYQ FREQUENCY: root-based vocab is the TOP CAT/CGL English-section trick — 2-3 per paper. EXAMINER MINDSET: rewards systematic root-knowledge over rote memorization.

cards.front:
ECLECTIC, from the LECT root, describes a person/style that:

(A) Selects from diverse sources
(B) Refuses to choose at all
(C) Is dull and unoriginal here
(D) Reads one book repeatedly
cards.back:
(A) Selects from diverse sources

Word Roots & Word Formation — ECLECTIC — adjective: choosing from a wide variety of styles, ideas, sources, methods. ETYMOLOGY: Greek 'eklektikos' = ek (out) + legein (choose) — to pick out. SAMPLE USAGES: 'an eclectic music collection' (mix of jazz, classical, rock); 'eclectic taste in art' (open to many genres); 'eclectic philosophy' (drawn from multiple traditions). PHILOSOPHICAL: in philosophy, ECLECTICISM is the practice of drawing from many schools rather than dogmatically following one. SYNONYMS: diverse, varied, wide-ranging, catholic (lowercase, meaning broad-minded). NEAR-SYNONYMS: heterogeneous (mixed in nature), miscellaneous (assorted). ANTONYMS: dogmatic, monolithic, narrow, rigid. POSITIVE CONNOTATION: 'eclectic' is usually praiseful — implies sophistication and openness. EXAM TRAP: students confuse ECLECTIC with ELECTIC (no such word) or EXOTIC (foreign-sourced) or ESOTERIC (hidden, only-for-insiders). PYQ FREQUENCY: ECLECTIC appears in CAT, GRE, UPSC PT high-vocab MCQs 1× per cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests advanced English for elite admissions.

cards.front:
DIALECT, from the LECT root, refers to:

(A) Regional variant of a language
(B) A debate between two parties
(C) Two simultaneous translations
(D) Special vocabulary of a job
cards.back:
(A) Regional variant of a language

Word Roots & Word Formation — DIALECT — etymology 'dia' (across, through) + 'lect' (speak, read) = a regional or social variety of a language with distinct vocabulary, grammar, pronunciation. EXAMPLES: (1) ENGLISH dialects: British English (Cockney, Geordie, Scouse), American English (Southern, New England, AAVE), Indian English (Hinglish, Banglish, etc.). (2) HINDI dialects: Awadhi, Bhojpuri, Maithili, Brij Bhasha, Khariboli, Haryanvi, Marwari. (3) CHINESE: Mandarin, Cantonese, Wu, Hakka — though some linguists treat them as separate languages. (4) ARABIC: Egyptian, Levantine, Gulf, Maghrebi — mutually intelligible to varying degrees. SAMPLE: 'In rural Bengal, the spoken dialect differs significantly from the literary Bengali of Kolkata.' DISTINCTION: (a) LANGUAGE = a system; (b) DIALECT = a regional variety; (c) ACCENT = pronunciation only; (d) IDIOLECT = an individual's unique speech. POLITICAL ANGLE: 'A language is a dialect with an army and navy' (Max Weinreich) — the line between dialect and language is often political, not linguistic. PYQ FREQUENCY: DIALECT in CAT, IBPS English — 1× per cycle.

DISTINCTION: (a) LANGUAGE = a system; (b) DIALECT = a regional variety; (c) ACCENT = pronunciation only; (d) IDIOLECT = an individual's unique speech. POLITICAL ANGLE: 'A language is a dialect with an army and navy' (Max Weinreich) — the line between dialect and language is often political, not linguistic. PYQ FREQUENCY: DIALECT in CAT, IBPS English — 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
The word COLLOQUIAL, from LOQU root, means:

(A) Informal, conversational language
(B) Highly formal academic prose now
(C) Foreign or borrowed word from
(D) Outdated archaic vocabulary type
cards.back:
(A) Informal, conversational language

Word Roots & Word Formation — COLLOQUIAL — adjective describing INFORMAL, EVERYDAY conversational language, as opposed to formal/literary writing. ETYMOLOGY: 'col' (with, together) + 'loqui' (speak) = 'speaking together' (i.e., as in casual conversation). EXAMPLES of COLLOQUIAL English: 'gonna' (going to), 'wanna' (want to), 'kid' (child), 'guy' (person), 'cool' (good), 'ain't' (isn't/aren't). DISTINCTION: (a) FORMAL: 'I would like to inquire about your well-being.' (b) COLLOQUIAL: 'How're you doing?' (c) SLANG: 'How's it hanging?' (very informal, often regional). NOUN: COLLOQUIALISM — an instance of casual expression. EXAM USE: in error-spotting Qs, COLLOQUIAL phrases are often INCORRECT in formal English contexts (academic writing, official letters). KEY DISTINCTION from related words: COLLOQUIAL (everyday) vs COLLOQUY (formal conversation, dialogue) — the noun 'colloquy' is FORMAL, while the adjective 'colloquial' describes INFORMAL speech. PYQ FREQUENCY: COLLOQUIAL appears in SSC CGL, CAT vocabulary 1× per cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: rewards register-awareness in English usage.

cards.front:
PHIL root means 'love'. PHILANTHROPY literally means:

(A) Love of humanity (charity)
(B) Love of money (greed)
(C) Hatred of humanity (misanthropy)
(D) Fear of crowds (agoraphobia)
cards.back:
(A) Love of humanity (charity)

Word Roots & Word Formation — PHILANTHROPY — etymology PHIL (love) + ANTHROPOS (human, Greek) = 'LOVE OF HUMANITY' = practice of donating money/time/effort to benefit other people, esp. through charity. WORD FAMILY (root PHIL = love, friend, fond): (1) PHILOSOPHY — 'love of wisdom' (philo + sophia). (2) PHILANTHROPY — 'love of humanity'. (3) PHILHARMONIC — 'love of harmony' (orchestra name, e.g., New York Philharmonic). (4) BIBLIOPHILE — 'lover of books'. (5) FRANCOPHILE — 'lover of French (culture)'. (6) ANGLOPHILE — 'lover of England'. (7) AUDIOPHILE — 'lover of high-fidelity audio'. (8) CINEPHILE — 'lover of cinema'. (9) PHILATELY — 'love of stamps' (philos + ateleia 'tax-free'); stamp collecting. (10) PHILANDERER — 'lover of (many) men/women' (negative, often a person who has many love affairs). MEDICAL: HEMOPHILIA = 'love of blood' (a misnomer; means tendency to bleed; X-linked recessive disorder; affected Russian Tsar's son Alexei). FAMOUS PHILANTHROPISTS: Andrew Carnegie, Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, Azim Premji (India — Wipro), Ratan Tata (Tata Trusts). INDIAN context: Tata's ~66% wealth in TRUSTS for charity. PYQ FREQUENCY: PHIL root vocab in SSC CGL, CAT, IBPS PO English 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
PHILOSOPHY literally means:

(A) Love of wisdom (philo + sophia)
(B) Knowledge of letters (lit study)
(C) Study of stars (astronomy)
(D) Love of music (philharmonic)
cards.back:
(A) Love of wisdom (philo + sophia)

Word Roots & Word Formation — PHILOSOPHY — etymology PHILOS (love) + SOPHIA (wisdom, knowledge) = 'LOVE OF WISDOM'. Coined by PYTHAGORAS (~570-495 BCE), who described himself as a 'philosopher' (lover of wisdom) — modest compared to claiming to BE wise. BRANCHES: (1) METAPHYSICS — nature of reality, existence. (2) EPISTEMOLOGY — theory of knowledge. (3) ETHICS — moral philosophy. (4) LOGIC — valid reasoning. (5) AESTHETICS — beauty, art. (6) POLITICAL philosophy — state, justice. (7) PHILOSOPHY OF MIND, language, science. KEY GREEK PHILOSOPHERS: Socrates (~470-399 BCE, 'know thyself'), Plato (~427-347 BCE, founded the Academy), Aristotle (~384-322 BCE, founded Lyceum + tutored Alexander). INDIAN PHILOSOPHY: 6 ASTIKA (orthodox) schools — Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Samkhya, Yoga, Mimamsa, Vedanta. NASTIKA (heterodox) — Charvaka, Jainism, Buddhism. KEY THINKERS: Adi Shankaracharya (Advaita), Ramanujacharya (Vishishtadvaita), Madhvacharya (Dvaita). WESTERN MODERN: Descartes ('I think therefore I am'), Kant, Hegel, Nietzsche, Russell, Wittgenstein. SOPHIA root: SOPHISTICATED, SOPHIST, SOPHOMORE (Greek 'sophos'). WORDS WITH SOPHIA: PHILOSOPHY (lover of wisdom), THEOSOPHY (divine wisdom), SOPHIST (wise person, often pejorative), SOPHISTRY (clever but misleading reasoning). PYQ FREQUENCY: philosophy etymology in CAT, GRE, advanced IBPS PO 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
A BIBLIOPHILE is someone who loves:

(A) Books (biblio + phile)
(B) Bicycles (cycling enthusiast)
(C) Insects (entomologist instead)
(D) Stamps (philatelist instead)
cards.back:
(A) Books (biblio + phile)

Word Roots & Word Formation — BIBLIOPHILE — etymology BIBLIO (book, Greek) + PHIL (love) = 'BOOK LOVER'. Often refers to those who collect rare/antique books, but generally means anyone with deep love of books. BIBLIO ROOT WORDS: (1) BIBLIOGRAPHY — list of books cited. (2) BIBLIOTHECA — library (Latin term used in some libraries' names). (3) BIBLE — 'the book' (THE book in Christian context). (4) BIBLIOPHOBIA — fear of books. (5) BIBLIOMANIA — obsessive book collection. WORLD-CLASS BIBLIOPHILES: J.P. Morgan (Pierpont Morgan Library, NY); Sir Thomas Phillipps (collected 60,000+ books, 19th c.); Umberto Eco (~50,000 books). FAMOUS LIBRARIES: (a) Library of Congress (Washington, ~170 million items). (b) British Library (London, ~170 million). (c) Bibliothèque Nationale de France (Paris, ~40 million). (d) Vatican Library. (e) BHANDARKAR ORIENTAL Research Institute (Pune, India — major Sanskrit-manuscript collection). (f) ASIATIC SOCIETY OF BENGAL (Kolkata). RELATED -PHILE WORDS: (1) AUDIOPHILE (sound). (2) OENOPHILE (wine). (3) FOODIE (food, informal). (4) CINEPHILE (cinema). (5) DENDROPHILE (trees). PYQ FREQUENCY: BIBLIOPHILE in SSC CGL, CAT, IBPS PO 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
PHILATELY is the hobby of collecting:

(A) Postage stamps (history + tax-free)
(B) Coins (numismatics is term)
(C) Antiques (general term used)
(D) Autographs (autographology)
cards.back:
(A) Postage stamps (history + tax-free)

Word Roots & Word Formation — PHILATELY — etymology PHIL (love) + ATELEIA (Greek, 'tax-free' or 'exempt from payment') = 'love of (things signifying) tax-free' — referring to PRE-PAID postage. Modern meaning: STAMP COLLECTING + study. ORIGIN: term coined 1864 by Frenchman Georges Herpin. ALTERNATIVE EXPLANATION: stamps mean the recipient doesn't pay (tax-free for them). HOBBY OVERVIEW: most popular collectible globally — 200+ million collectors worldwide; ~30 million in India. KEY ASPECTS: (1) ACCUMULATING stamps. (2) Studying RARITY, history, design. (3) Trading at auctions. INDIA — KEY STAMPS: First Indian stamp = 'Scinde Dawk' (1852, ~₹500 face but rare; original sells for lakhs). Modern stamps: Mahatma Gandhi (1948 series, very valuable in mint condition). VALUABLE WORLD STAMPS: (a) British Guiana 1c Magenta (1856) — sold $9.5M (2014); world's most valuable. (b) Treskilling Yellow (Sweden, 1855). KEY BODIES: (a) PHILATELIC SOCIETY of INDIA. (b) Philatelic Bureaus at India Post. (c) WORLD STAMP exhibitions (e.g., London Stamp Festival). RELATED COLLECTING HOBBIES: NUMISMATICS (coins), DELTIOLOGY (postcards), VEXILLOLOGY (flags). PYQ FREQUENCY: philately definition in SSC CGL, CAT vocabulary 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
HEMOPHILIA is a medical condition involving:

(A) Blood-clotting deficiency (X-linked)
(B) Excessive blood production (rare)
(C) Iron-deficiency anemia condition
(D) Thickened blood (clots easily)
cards.back:
(A) Blood-clotting deficiency (X-linked)

Word Roots & Word Formation — HEMOPHILIA — genetic disorder where blood DOES NOT CLOT properly due to deficiency of clotting factor (Factor VIII for Hemophilia A; Factor IX for Hemophilia B). NAME: HEMO (blood) + PHILIA (love/affinity) = 'love of blood' — historically a misnomer (does NOT mean 'love of blood'; rather 'tendency for blood to leak'). SYMPTOMS: prolonged bleeding from minor cuts, spontaneous internal bleeding (esp. joints — 'haemarthrosis'), easy bruising. INHERITANCE: X-LINKED RECESSIVE — gene on X chromosome. Mostly affects MALES (single X). FEMALES are usually CARRIERS (pass to sons). FAMOUS CASE: ALEXEI ROMANOV (1904-1918), youngest son of Tsar Nicholas II of Russia, had severe hemophilia. His mother Alexandra invited Rasputin to treat him; Rasputin's influence at the court contributed to political destabilization → Russian Revolution 1917 → execution of Romanovs. QUEEN VICTORIA was a CARRIER; passed gene to many European royal families ('royal disease'). TREATMENT: clotting-factor replacement therapy (recombinant or plasma-derived); prophylactic injections; new gene therapies emerging (2024). PYQ FREQUENCY: hemophilia in NEET, AIIMS, SSC GA — 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
An AUDIOPHILE is a person who loves:

(A) High-fidelity audio (music quality)
(B) Reading audiobooks generally
(C) Studying acoustics theoretically
(D) Playing musical instruments
cards.back:
(A) High-fidelity audio (music quality)

Word Roots & Word Formation — AUDIOPHILE — etymology AUDIO (Latin 'audire' = to hear) + PHIL (love) = 'lover of high-quality SOUND/audio'. Hobbyist who pursues audio reproduction at the highest fidelity, often investing in: (1) High-end SPEAKERS (Bose, B&W, KEF, Wilson Audio). (2) High-end AMPLIFIERS (McIntosh, Marantz). (3) TURNTABLES + vinyl records (analog, prized for warmth). (4) HEADPHONES (Sennheiser HD 800, Audeze, Stax — can cost $5,000+). (5) DAC (Digital-to-Analog Converters). MUSIC FORMATS preferred: VINYL records, HIGH-RES DIGITAL (FLAC, DSD), SACD. AVOIDED: low-bitrate MP3, compressed streaming. AUDIOPHILE COMMUNITY: 1000s of forums, Reddit (/r/audiophile), high-end audio shows. CRITICISM: some claims (e.g., gold-plated cables improve sound) are scientifically disputed (PLACEBO effect studies, blind tests often find no difference). VALUE PROPOSITION: 'good enough' vs 'last 5% perfection' — diminishing returns. NAMES: 'budget audiophile' vs 'high-end audiophile'. INDIA: bustling audio-enthusiast scene in Mumbai, Bengaluru, Chennai. RELATED words: VIDEOPHILE (high-quality video), CINEPHILE (cinema lover). PYQ FREQUENCY: audiophile + similar -phile words in CAT, IBPS PO English 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
FRANCOPHILE describes a person with strong affinity for:

(A) France or French culture
(B) Frankenstein-style fiction
(C) Free-flowing creative work
(D) Honest direct conversation
cards.back:
(A) France or French culture

Word Roots & Word Formation — FRANCOPHILE — etymology FRANCO (relating to France) + PHIL (love) = 'lover of France/French culture'. May have love for French language, cuisine, fashion, art, history. OPPOSITES: FRANCOPHOBE — disdain for France. RELATED NATION-WORDS with PHIL/PHOBE: (1) ANGLOPHILE — love of England (Anglophobe = dislike). (2) AMERICOPHILE — love of America. (3) GERMANOPHILE — Germany. (4) RUSSOPHILE — Russia. (5) HISPANOPHILE — Spain. (6) NIPPOPHILE — Japan. (7) SINOPHILE — China (sino = Chinese). (8) INDOPHILE — love of India. NOTABLE Francophiles: Thomas Jefferson (US founding father, served as ambassador to France); Hemingway, James Joyce (lived in Paris); recent celebrities living in France for tax+culture. INDIA — FRANCO-INDIAN connection: French East India Company; PONDICHERRY (Puducherry) was French until 1954; CHANDERNAGORE, KARIKAL etc. were French enclaves. ALLIANCE FRANÇAISE has 16 centers in India promoting French language/culture. ACADEMIC: 'Francophilia' in 18th-19th century Europe — French was prestige language; aristocrats spoke French. PYQ FREQUENCY: -phile/-phobe word pairs in CAT, GRE, advanced IBPS PO English 1× per cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests advanced cultural-vocabulary breadth.

cards.front:
The word PORTABLE means 'able to be carried'. Which other word shares the root 'PORT' meaning 'carry'?

(A) Transport — to carry across
(B) Portrait — a picture only.
(C) Porthole — small ship window.
(D) Sport — game or fun activity.
cards.back:
(A) Transport — to carry across

Word Roots & Word Formation — Latin root PORT- = 'to carry' (from 'portare'). WORD FAMILY: PORTABLE (can be carried), TRANSPORT (carry across), IMPORT (carry IN), EXPORT (carry OUT), DEPORT (carry away — official banishment), SUPPORT (carry from beneath, hold up), REPORT (carry back), PURPORT (claim to carry, profess), COMPORT (carry oneself, behave), DISPORT (entertain, play). RELATED: 'PORT' as harbour/gate is from a different Latin root 'porta' (gate) — PORTAL, PORTICO, PORTER (gatekeeper). PORTHOLE blends 'port' (gate-opening) + 'hole'. PORTRAIT is from Latin 'protrahere' (to draw forth) — same Latin family but different nuance. PYQ-ANGLE: word-root MCQs require students to disambiguate similar-looking words. INSIGHT: knowing 50-100 Latin/Greek roots gives access to 5,000-10,000 English words via context-deduction — examined heavily in SSC CGL Tier 2 vocab. EXAMINER MINDSET: testing METALINGUISTIC awareness — vocabulary by morphological analysis, not rote memorization.

cards.front:
What does the word DEPORT (root: 'port') most likely mean?

(A) To officially expel from a country
(B) To make a sport activity.
(C) To create a supportive environment.
(D) To carry deeply within oneself.
cards.back:
(A) To officially expel from a country

Word Roots & Word Formation — DEPORT = de- (away from) + port (carry) → 'to carry away/expel'. In legal terms, deportation is the formal removal of a non-citizen from a country, usually for visa violations or criminal offenses. INDIA CONTEXT: under the Foreigners Act 1946, India can deport persons present without valid documents — historically, this includes Bangladeshi/Rohingya migrants in some states. SOUL/CHARACTER MEANING: 'deportment' (= behaviour, conduct) — how one CARRIES oneself. TRIPLE-BARREL: 'deportee' = the person deported; 'deportation' = the act; 'deport' = the verb. RELATED — INTERNATIONAL: ASYLUM is the OPPOSITE of deportation — protected status given to refugees. NOTABLE DEPORTATION CASES: Edward Snowden (US whistleblower) sought asylum to AVOID deportation; Julian Assange (WikiLeaks) extradited from UK to US in 2024-25. PYQ FREQUENCY: 'deport/import/export' appear in SSC vocab + economics PYQs as both root-Q and concept-Q.

cards.front:
What is the meaning of the word TRANSMIT (root: 'mit' = send)?

(A) To send across or pass along
(B) To stop sending something always
(C) To receive a message back.
(D) A type of gear in vehicles.
cards.back:
(A) To send across or pass along

Word Roots & Word Formation — TRANSMIT = trans- (across) + mit (send) → 'to send across'. MEANING: pass along (signals, diseases, messages, information). EXAMPLES: 'TV signals are transmitted via satellites.' 'Mosquitoes transmit malaria.' 'Genetic traits are transmitted from parents to offspring.' WORD FAMILY (root 'MIT/MIS' = send): TRANSMIT, EMIT (send out), OMIT (leave out, send-away), ADMIT (send-in, accept), REMIT (send back, pay), SUBMIT (send under, yield), COMMIT (send with, pledge), PERMIT (send through, allow), DISMISS (send away). NOTE: MIT becomes MIS in past forms — TRANSMITTED, OMITTED. APPLICATION IN SCIENCE: a TRANSMITTER (radio/TV) sends signals; a RECEIVER picks them up. In medicine: 'sexually transmitted infections' (STIs); 'vector-transmitted diseases' (mosquito-borne). MISSION = 'a task of being sent' (same root). MISSILE = 'a thing sent forth'. PYQ FREQUENCY: 1-2 'mit/mis' words per SSC CGL Tier 2 vocab section.

cards.front:
What does EMIT mean?

(A) To give off or send out
(B) To receive light from a source.
(C) To absorb from the surroundings.
(D) To bounce light off a surface.
cards.back:
(A) To give off or send out

Word Roots & Word Formation — EMIT = e- (out, from Latin ex-) + mit (send) → 'to send out'. Used for radiations, sounds, smells, light, gases. SCIENCE EXAMPLES: 'The bulb EMITS light.' 'Volcanoes EMIT ash and gases.' 'Bees EMIT pheromones.' RELATED FORMS: EMISSION (act of emitting); EMITTER (device/object that emits); CARBON EMISSIONS (a key climate-change topic). INDIA POLICY ANGLE: India announced NET-ZERO target by 2070 at COP26 (Glasgow, 2021); current per-capita CO₂ emissions ~1.9 tonnes (vs world avg ~4.5, US ~16). PHYSICS: emission spectra (each element emits a unique pattern of light) — basis of spectroscopy. WORD-FAMILY MEMORY-TRICK for 'mit' words: EMIT (out), OMIT (off), TRANSMIT (across), ADMIT (in), REMIT (back), COMMIT (with), PERMIT (through), SUBMIT (under). PYQ ANGLE: SSC, IBPS, RBI Grade B all test 'emit/emit-' frequently — also general-awareness Qs on India's climate commitments.

cards.front:
What does the word REMIT mean (root: 'mit' = send)?

(A) To send back, especially payment
(B) To remember something fondly.
(C) To repeat a task again. (option here)
(D) To remove from a list always.
cards.back:
(A) To send back, especially payment

Word Roots & Word Formation — REMIT = re- (back) + mit (send) → 'to send back'. MOST COMMON USE: send money back (e.g., NRI remittances to India). 'Workers remit ₹50,000 to family every month.' OTHER MEANINGS: (1) FORGIVE — 'remit a debt/sin/punishment' (forgive, cancel). (2) DECREASE — 'symptoms remit' (medical: lessen, abate). (3) REFER — 'remit the case to a lower court' (legal). NOUN — REMITTANCE: money sent back home. INDIA STATS: India is the WORLD'S LARGEST RECIPIENT of remittances — ~$130 billion in 2024-25 (mostly from US, UAE, Saudi Arabia). Kerala receives ~₹1.5 lakh crore annually from Gulf workers. WORLD BANK: remittances to LMICs (Low/Middle Income Countries) reached ~$655 billion in 2023 — exceeding FDI. ECONOMIC IMPACT: India's remittances support ~30 million households, smoothing rural poverty. PYQ FREQUENCY: 'remittances' is a top GK fact for SSC, banking, RBI Grade B. EXAM ANGLE: this Q tests both vocabulary AND general economic awareness.
cards.option2: To repeat a task again. (option here)
cards.option3: To remove from a list always.

cards.front:
Which word means 'A formal expulsion that carries away from a place'?

(A) Deportation — formal expulsion
(B) Importation alone alone alone
(C) Reportation alone alone alone
(D) Comportation alone alone alone
cards.back:
(A) Deportation — formal expulsion

Word Roots & Word Formation — DEPORTATION = the act of deporting; formal removal of a foreign national from a country. RELATED: 'extradition' is a SIMILAR term but specifically refers to handing a person over to ANOTHER country to face legal proceedings — based on bilateral treaties. INDIA'S EXTRADITION TREATIES: India has treaties with ~50 countries; recent high-profile cases — Vijay Mallya, Nirav Modi (extraditions sought from UK), Tahawwur Rana (extradited from US to India in 2025 for Mumbai 26/11 attack involvement). LEGAL FRAMEWORK in India: Foreigners Act 1946, Extradition Act 1962. WORD-CONFUSION: 'reportation' is not a standard English word; 'comportation' is rare/archaic. EXAM-FAVOURITE TRICK: examiners offer plausibly-spelled fakes alongside the correct term. METHOD: think morphology — 'de-port-ation' = 'away-carry-act' = a real English word. PYQ ANGLE: vocabulary + UPSC current-affairs cross-link via extradition.

cards.front:
Which word means 'to give up one's authority and surrender to higher power' (root 'mit' = send)?

(A) Submit (send under, yield)
(B) Permit (allow to pass) alone
(C) Commit (pledge to action) alone
(D) Remit (send back) alone alone
cards.back:
(A) Submit (send under, yield)

Word Roots & Word Formation — SUBMIT = sub- (under) + mit (send) → 'to send under, yield to'. PRIMARY MEANINGS: (1) YIELD — 'submit to authority' / 'submit to fate'. (2) PRESENT — 'submit a report to the boss' (the more common modern usage). (3) PROPOSE — 'I submit that the witness is unreliable' (legal/formal argument). PSYCHOLOGY: 'dominance vs submission' is a key behavioural axis in many species — wolf packs, primates. ETYMOLOGY: 'submission' originally military — surrendering to a stronger force. CHRISTIAN/ISLAMIC USAGE: Islam literally means 'submission [to God]'; 'Muslim' = 'one who submits'. MEMORY TRICK FOR 'MIT' WORDS: VISUALIZE prefixes as DIRECTIONS — sub (under), com (with), per (through), e (out), trans (across), o (off), re (back), a/ad (toward). EXAM-USEFUL: distinguish 'submit' (yield/send under) from other -mit verbs by prefix-meaning. PYQ ANGLE: SSC CGL Tier 2 vocab section reuses this word-family analysis 1-2× per paper.

cards.front:
SCRIBE/SCRIPT root means 'write'. MANUSCRIPT literally means:

(A) Hand-written document (manu+script)
(B) Printed book document only
(C) Typed paper document there
(D) Digital file in computer
cards.back:
(A) Hand-written document (manu+script)

Word Roots & Word Formation — MANUSCRIPT — etymology MANU (hand, Latin) + SCRIPTUS (written, from scribere) = 'WRITTEN BY HAND'. Originally meant any HANDWRITTEN document; modern usage extends to ANY DRAFT/UNPUBLISHED document submitted to a publisher (even typed/computerized). WORD FAMILY (root SCRIBE/SCRIPT = write): (1) MANUSCRIPT — handwritten document. (2) DESCRIBE — write down/express. (3) PRESCRIBE — write before (e.g., doctor's prescription). (4) PRESCRIPTION — what's prescribed (medical, legal). (5) PROSCRIBE — write against (forbid by law). (6) PROSCRIPTION — banishment. (7) ASCRIBE — assign/attribute. (8) SUBSCRIBE — sign under (newspaper subscription). (9) TRANSCRIBE — write across (= copy/transfer text). (10) CONSCRIPT — write together (forced enrollment, military draft). (11) INSCRIBE — write into. (12) CIRCUMSCRIBE — write around (limit). (13) POSTSCRIPT (P.S.) — written after. (14) NONDESCRIPT — not describable; unremarkable. (15) SCRIPT — written text (esp. for film/play). (16) SCRIBBLE — write hurriedly/messily. (17) SCRIPTURE — sacred writing. (18) SCRIBE — professional writer/copyist. (19) SCRIPTORIUM — room for writing (medieval monasteries). (20) MANUSCRIPT culture: pre-printing era, monasteries hand-copied books. INDIA's MANUSCRIPT HERITAGE: ~5 MILLION manuscripts on palm-leaf, birch-bark, paper; mostly Sanskrit, Persian, Pali, Tamil, Telugu, etc. NATIONAL MISSION FOR MANUSCRIPTS (NAMAMI, 2003) — preserves these. UPSC angle: manuscript preservation in cultural heritage. PYQ FREQUENCY: SCRIBE root vocab in SSC CGL, CAT, UPSC English 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
TRANSCRIBE means to:

(A) Convert spoken/written text into another form
(B) Translate to a foreign language
(C) Erase or remove writing fully
(D) Encrypt the message in code
cards.back:
(A) Convert spoken/written text into another form

Word Roots & Word Formation — TRANSCRIBE — etymology TRANS (across, Latin) + SCRIBE (write) = 'write across' = CONVERT one form to another (typically: speech → written; or one written form to another). USES: (1) TRANSCRIPTION of audio interviews → written text (journalism, academia, courts). (2) MEDICAL TRANSCRIPTION — doctor's notes/dictation → patient records. (3) MUSICAL TRANSCRIPTION — converting music to written notation; or piece for one instrument adapted for another. (4) BIOLOGICAL TRANSCRIPTION — DNA → mRNA in genetics (a different but analogous use). (5) PHONETIC TRANSCRIPTION — speech sound → IPA symbols (linguistics). DON'T CONFUSE: (a) TRANSCRIBE — change form (speech → text, etc.). (b) TRANSLATE — change LANGUAGE (e.g., English → Hindi). (c) TRANSLITERATE — change SCRIPT (e.g., Devanagari → Roman). EXAM TRAP: TRANSCRIBE vs TRANSLATE vs TRANSLITERATE — three distinct operations! INDIA AI: TRANSCRIPTION services use AI/ML — Otter.ai, Google Speech-to-Text; major productivity tool. JOBS: medical-transcription industry employs ~50,000 in India. UPSC angle: language preservation — esp. ENDANGERED LANGUAGES; UNESCO Atlas of World Languages in Danger lists ~200 Indian languages as endangered. PYQ FREQUENCY: transcribe vs translate distinction in SSC CGL Tier 2, IBPS PO, CAT 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
PRESCRIBE means to:

(A) Order/recommend (esp. medical or rules)
(B) Forbid by law strictly here
(C) Erase a previous instruction
(D) Sign on bottom of document
cards.back:
(A) Order/recommend (esp. medical or rules)

Word Roots & Word Formation — PRESCRIBE — etymology PRE (before) + SCRIBE (write) = 'WRITE BEFORE' or 'AUTHORITATIVELY ORDER'. KEY USES: (1) MEDICAL: doctor PRESCRIBES medication = formally orders it for a patient. NOUN: PRESCRIPTION = the written order (Rx). India: only registered MD/MBBS doctors can prescribe (under MCI/NMC rules). (2) LEGAL: rule/regulation 'as prescribed' = as defined by law/authority. (3) GENERAL: 'doctor prescribes rest' = recommends. CONTRAST WITH PROSCRIBE (different word!): PRESCRIBE = ORDER (positive); PROSCRIBE = FORBID (negative, ban). 'The govt PROSCRIBED the organization' = banned. PROSCRIPTION (noun) = ban. KEY DISTINCTION (UPSC trap): (1) PRE-scribe — write BEFORE/AHEAD = recommend, order. (2) PRO-scribe — write AGAINST = forbid. RX SYMBOL: 'Rx' on prescription comes from Latin 'recipe' = 'take' (imperative — take this medication). ABUSE of medical PRESCRIPTION authority: 'over-prescription' of antibiotics → ANTIMICROBIAL RESISTANCE — major UPSC GS-3 health concern. INDIA's NATIONAL ACTION PLAN ON ANTIMICROBIAL RESISTANCE (NAP-AMR, 2017). KEY DRUG REGULATION INDIA: Drugs Controller General (DCGI), Ministry of Health, ICMR — oversee prescription rules. UPSC angle: health policy + drug regulation in GS-2/3. PYQ FREQUENCY: PRESCRIBE vs PROSCRIBE distinction in SSC CGL, CAT, UPSC English 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
CONSCRIPTION refers to:

(A) Compulsory military enrollment (draft)
(B) Voluntary signing up for army
(C) Tax collection by government
(D) Public oath of citizenship process
cards.back:
(A) Compulsory military enrollment (draft)

Word Roots & Word Formation — CONSCRIPTION — etymology CON (together) + SCRIPT (write) = 'WRITE/ENROLL TOGETHER' = forced/mandatory enrollment in military service. Also called 'THE DRAFT'. CONTRAST: VOLUNTARY enlistment. COUNTRIES with conscription (current/historical): (1) ISRAEL — Israeli Defense Forces; men + women required to serve (2-3 years). (2) SOUTH KOREA — ~2-year military service for men. (3) NORTH KOREA — 7-10 years!. (4) SWITZERLAND, FINLAND, NORWAY, AUSTRIA, RUSSIA, IRAN — currently maintain. (5) USA — ended 1973 (Vietnam-era end); now all-volunteer. Selective Service registration still required for males 18-25. (6) UK — ended 1960. (7) FRANCE — ended 1996; reintroduced limited service 2019. INDIA: NEVER had conscription. India has all-VOLUNTEER military force (largest volunteer army in world ~1.4 million active personnel). RECENT — 'AGNIPATH SCHEME' (2022) — short-term (4-year) military recruitment scheme. NOT conscription, but reduced-tenure ENLISTMENT. Controversial; ongoing reviews. RELATED CONCEPTS: (a) DESERTION — leaving military without permission. (b) PACIFISM — opposition to all violence/war. (c) CONSCIENTIOUS OBJECTOR — refuses military service on moral/religious grounds. WORLD WARS: massive conscription waves; e.g., USA Civil War 1863, WWI/II — millions drafted. UPSC angle: defence reforms + 'jobs in armed forces' issue. PYQ FREQUENCY: conscription concept in CAT, advanced UPSC English 1× per 2 cycles.

cards.front:
POSTSCRIPT (P.S.) at end of letter literally means:

(A) Written after (added later)
(B) Written before the letter
(C) Written instead of letter
(D) Written over the original here
cards.back:
(A) Written after (added later)

Word Roots & Word Formation — POSTSCRIPT (P.S.) — etymology POST (after, Latin) + SCRIPT (written) = 'WRITTEN AFTER'. ABBREVIATED 'P.S.' Used in LETTERS to add information AFTER the main body + signature. EXAMPLE: 'Dear Mom, ... your loving son, Ravi. P.S. Please send the cake recipe.' KEY USES: (1) AFTERTHOUGHTS — info forgotten in main letter. (2) EMPHASIS — highlight a single key point. (3) Personal/informal touch. P.P.S. (POST-POSTSCRIPT) — added AFTER P.S. (Latin: 'post post scriptum'). ETYMOLOGY of 'POST' prefix: (1) POST = AFTER (postpone, postdate, posthumous). (2) Note: 'post' as 'mail/place' is from Italian 'posta' → station. POST WORD FAMILY: (a) POSTPONE — put after (delay). (b) POSTHUMOUS — after death. (c) POSTERITY — those born after (descendants). (d) POST-MORTEM — after death (medical autopsy). (e) POSTGRADUATE — after graduation. (f) POSTERIOR — back/rear. KEY MODERN USAGE: digital communications (emails) replaced traditional P.S. concept. But still common in informal letters, gift-cards, formal correspondence. PRACTICE — VOCABULARY-style: (a) 'POSTHUMOUS award' = award given after one's death. (b) 'POST-MORTEM' = examination of body to determine cause of death. (c) 'POSTERITY will judge' = future generations. (d) 'POSTNUPTIAL agreement' = signed after marriage. UPSC angle: legal/medical vocabulary; CSAT comprehension. PYQ FREQUENCY: post- prefix vocab in CAT, UPSC English 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
INSCRIPTION refers to writing on:

(A) Stone, metal, or hard surface
(B) Soft paper for daily use
(C) Digital screen for short read
(D) Spoken declaration only here
cards.back:
(A) Stone, metal, or hard surface

Word Roots & Word Formation — INSCRIPTION — etymology IN (into) + SCRIPT (write) = 'WRITTEN INTO/ENGRAVED'. Refers to text engraved/carved on STONE, METAL, MONUMENT, or other hard surface; long-lasting, formal. EPIGRAPHY = study of ancient inscriptions. INDIA's RICH INSCRIPTION TRADITION: (1) ASHOKAN ROCK + PILLAR EDICTS (3rd c. BCE) — earliest deciphered Indian inscriptions; in BRAHMI (most), KHAROSHTHI (NW), GREEK + ARAMAIC (Kandahar). 14 major rock edicts + minor edicts; on EDICTS Ashoka spread DHAMMA (Buddhism). KEY INSCRIPTIONS: (a) GIRNAR (Gujarat) — Ashoka. (b) DELHI-TOPRA, DELHI-MEERUT — pillar edicts. (c) RUMMINDEI (Lumbini, Nepal) — Buddha's birthplace. (2) HATHIGUMPHA INSCRIPTION (Odisha, ~1st c. BCE) — KHARAVELA of Kalinga. (3) JUNAGADH INSCRIPTION of RUDRADAMAN I (~150 CE, Sanskrit). (4) ALLAHABAD PRASHASTI / PILLAR INSCRIPTION (~340 CE, by HARISENA on Samudragupta) — Sanskrit; Sanskrit-Brahmi. (5) AIHOLE PRASHASTI (~634 CE, by RAVIKIRTI on Pulakeshin II of Chalukyas) — earliest Sanskrit poem. (6) NAVARATNA INSCRIPTIONS — at Vikramaditya's court. ASHOKA SCRIPT DECIPHERMENT: by JAMES PRINSEP (1837, British scholar) — major breakthrough. UPSC angle: ANCIENT HISTORY GS-1; epigraphy + archaeology. CAREERS: ASI (Archaeological Survey of India) employs epigraphists. PYQ FREQUENCY: inscriptions in UPSC, MPSC, SSC ancient history 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
ASCRIBE means to:

(A) Attribute or assign (a quality/cause)
(B) Refuse to acknowledge here
(C) Erase from official record
(D) Repeat exactly without change
cards.back:
(A) Attribute or assign (a quality/cause)

Word Roots & Word Formation — ASCRIBE — etymology AD (to, towards) + SCRIBE (write) = 'WRITE TO' = ASSIGN, ATTRIBUTE. SAMPLE: 'She ascribed her success to hard work and luck.' 'The painting was ascribed to da Vinci' (attributed). NOUN: ASCRIPTION. SYNONYMS: attribute, credit, assign, impute, accredit. ANTONYMS: deny, dissociate. CONTRAST: (1) ASCRIBE — generally NEUTRAL or POSITIVE attribution. 'Success ascribed to teamwork.' (2) IMPUTE — often NEGATIVE attribution. 'Imputed bad motives to him.' (3) ATTRIBUTE — neutral, common alternative. (4) CREDIT — positive (credited HIM with the discovery). KEY 'AD-' words (root AD = to, towards, near): (a) ADHERE — stick to. (b) ADJUST — fit to. (c) ADJOIN — join to. (d) ADMINISTER — serve to. (e) ADVOCATE — speak for. (f) ADAPT — fit to. (g) ADJOURN — defer until later. (h) ADJACENT — lying next to. SOCIO-PSYCHOLOGICAL: 'ASCRIPTIVE STATUS' = social status assigned at BIRTH (caste, race, gender) — vs ACHIEVED status (education, occupation). UPSC angle: social stratification + sociology terms in GS-1; CASTE-based ascriptive social structure was a Constitutional concern (Articles 14-17 abolish untouchability). RELATED ATTRIBUTES vocab: (a) ATTRIBUTABLE — capable of being attributed. (b) ATTRIBUTABLE TO — caused by. (c) BY ATTRIBUTION — by assignment. PYQ FREQUENCY: ASCRIBE/IMPUTE/ATTRIBUTE distinctions in CAT, advanced UPSC English 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
The word INSPECT comes from 'in + spect' and literally means:

(A) To stand up
(B) To look into carefully
(C) To think ahead
(D) To hide from view
cards.back:
(B) To look into carefully

Word Roots & Word Formation — L. 'spectare' = to look. 'In-' = into. To inspect = to look into. Same family: respect (look again, regard), suspect (look under, secretly), prospect (look forward), introspect (look within), circumspect (look around, cautious).

cards.front:
'Retrospect' means to:

(A) Look forward
(B) Look backward in time
(C) Look again with approval
(D) Look from afar
cards.back:
(B) Look backward in time

Word Roots & Word Formation — L. 'retro-' = backward + 'spect' = look. Retrospect = looking back on past events. Antonym: prospect (look forward). 'Retrospective' in art = a review of an artist's past work.

(A) Careless and bold
(B) Cautious and prudent
(C) Curious about others

Word Roots & Word Formation — 'circum-' = around + 'spect' = look → one who looks around before acting = careful, prudent. Not to be confused with 'suspect' (to doubt) — both share the spect root but with different prefixes.

cards.front:
TELE root means 'far'. TELESCOPE literally means a device for:

(A) Seeing far (tele + scope=look)
(B) Hearing distant sounds clearly
(C) Communicating across distance
(D) Walking great distances easily
cards.back:
(A) Seeing far (tele + scope=look)

Word Roots & Word Formation — TELESCOPE — etymology TELE (far, Greek) + SKOPEIN (to look, see) = 'instrument for seeing far'. TELE WORD FAMILY (root TELE = far, distant): (1) TELEPHONE — 'far + sound' = sound from far. (2) TELEGRAPH — 'far + write' = writing from far. (3) TELEVISION — 'far + see' = seeing from far. (4) TELEPATHY — 'far + feeling' = communication of feelings from afar (mental). (5) TELESCOPE — 'far + look' = looking far. (6) TELEMETRY — 'far + measure' = measuring at distance. (7) TELECONFERENCE — meeting from far. (8) TELESCOPIC — relating to telescope; collapsible/extendable. SCOPE FAMILY (Greek 'skopein' = to look): MICROSCOPE (small + look), KALEIDOSCOPE (beautiful pattern + look), STETHOSCOPE (chest + look — heart auscultation), HOROSCOPE (hour + look — birth-time horoscope), GYROSCOPE (rotation + look), ENDOSCOPE (within + look — medical procedure), PERISCOPE (around + look — submarine), SPECTROSCOPE (spectrum + look). HISTORY: telescope invented by Hans Lippershey (1608, Netherlands); Galileo improved it (1609) — discovered Jupiter's moons, Saturn's rings, sunspots. Today: HUBBLE (1990), JAMES WEBB (2021) — most powerful space telescopes. PYQ FREQUENCY: TELE root vocab in SSC CGL, CAT, IBPS PO 1-2× per cycle.
