cards.front:
TELEPATHY refers to:

(A) Communication of thoughts across distance (mental)
(B) Visual broadcast across great distances
(C) Loud sound transmission to far areas
(D) Distance measurement using sounds (sonar)
cards.back:
(A) Communication of thoughts across distance (mental)

Word Roots & Word Formation — TELEPATHY — etymology TELE (far) + PATHOS (feeling, suffering, Greek) = 'distant feeling/communication'. Generally refers to alleged direct mental communication between minds without using normal sensory channels. Historically debated as a paranormal phenomenon; rigorous scientific research has not confirmed reliable telepathic abilities. PATHOS WORD FAMILY: (1) PATHOLOGY — study of disease (-pathy = disease). (2) SYMPATHY — 'with + feeling' = sharing another's feelings (especially sorrow). (3) EMPATHY — 'in + feeling' = entering another's emotional state. (4) APATHY — 'without + feeling' = lack of interest or emotion. (5) ANTIPATHY — 'against + feeling' = strong dislike. (6) HOMEOPATHY — 'similar + suffering' = treatment based on 'like cures like'. (7) ALLOPATHY — 'other + suffering' = standard medical practice (using contrary causes). (8) PSYCHOPATHY — 'mind + suffering' = personality disorder. (9) NATUROPATHY — 'natural + therapy'. INDIA HEALTHCARE: AYUSH = AYURVEDA, YOGA, UNANI, SIDDHA, HOMEOPATHY — alternative medicine systems recognized; Ministry of AYUSH established 2014. TELEPATHY in pop-culture: Star Wars 'Force', X-Men's Professor X, etc. — fictional. Real WIRELESS BRAIN-TO-BRAIN communication research underway (Neuralink, BCIs). PYQ FREQUENCY: TELE-PATHY combo vocab in CAT, advanced English MCQs.

cards.front:
DIST root means 'apart, away'. DISTRACT means to:

(A) Pull attention away (dis + tract)
(B) Make something denser packed
(C) Bring closer together quickly
(D) Obtain something in a hurry
cards.back:
(A) Pull attention away (dis + tract)

Word Roots & Word Formation — DISTRACT — etymology DIS (apart, away) + TRACT (pull, draw, from Latin 'trahere') = 'to pull away'. Means to DIVERT someone's ATTENTION. WORD FAMILY (root TRACT/TRAH = pull, draw): (1) ATTRACT (ad + tract) — pull TOWARDS. (2) DISTRACT (dis + tract) — pull APART/AWAY. (3) EXTRACT (ex + tract) — pull OUT. (4) SUBTRACT (sub + tract) — pull FROM UNDER. (5) CONTRACT (con + tract) — pull TOGETHER (also legal binding agreement). (6) DETRACT (de + tract) — pull DOWN, take away. (7) RETRACT (re + tract) — pull BACK. (8) TRACTOR — vehicle that PULLS. (9) TRACTION — pulling action. (10) PROTRACT — pull forward, prolong. (11) ABSTRACT (abs + tract) — pull away from, separate from concrete details. WORD FAMILY (DIS prefix = apart, away, not): DISTANCE, DISTINCT, DISTILL, DISCONTENT, DISTORT, DISTRESS, DISCOURAGE, DISADVANTAGE. KEY DISTINCTION: DIS = away/apart/not (Latin); DI = two (Greek, e.g., DIODE has 2 electrodes; DIOXIDE has 2 oxygens); DYS = bad (Greek, e.g., DYSFUNCTION, DYSLEXIA). PYQ FREQUENCY: TRACT root + DIS prefix vocab in SSC CGL, CAT 2-3 per paper.

cards.front:
DISTINGUISH means to:

(A) Tell apart from others (recognize differences)
(B) Erase something completely from view
(C) Mix things together indistinctly
(D) Hold tightly to a position firmly
cards.back:
(A) Tell apart from others (recognize differences)

Word Roots & Word Formation — DISTINGUISH — etymology DIS (apart) + STINGUERE (Latin, to mark, prick) = 'to mark apart' = to RECOGNIZE DIFFERENCES; tell apart. SAMPLE USAGES: (1) 'Can you distinguish silk from polyester by touch?' (2) 'Twins are sometimes hard to distinguish.' (3) 'He distinguished himself in the field of mathematics' (= excelled, stood out). DOUBLE MEANINGS: 'distinguish' can mean (a) tell apart (most common), (b) become eminent, stand out (figurative). DISTINGUISHED — adjective: EMINENT, IMPORTANT, having achieved fame ('a distinguished scientist'). RELATED: (1) DISTINCT — clearly different, separate ('two distinct species'). (2) DISTINCTION — difference, eminence, honour ('graduated with distinction'). (3) INDISTINCT — vague, blurred. (4) EXTINGUISH (ex + stinguere) — put out, eradicate (a fire, a hope). (5) DISTINGUISHED-LOOKING — looking eminent, impressive. EXAM-FAVORITE distinction: DISTINGUISH (recognize difference) vs EXTINGUISH (put out a fire) — different prefixes, different meanings. SYNONYMS for distinguish: differentiate, discern, discriminate, identify. ANTONYMS: confuse, conflate, blend. PYQ FREQUENCY: DISTINGUISH-EXTINGUISH pair in SSC CGL synonyms-section, CAT, IBPS PO 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
DISTILL (chemistry/cooking) means to:

(A) Purify by evaporation and condensation
(B) Mix substances together evenly
(C) Dissolve a solid in water completely
(D) Filter solid particles from liquid
cards.back:
(A) Purify by evaporation and condensation

Word Roots & Word Formation — DISTILL — etymology DIS (apart) + STILLARE (drop, drip) = 'to drop down' (referring to liquid drops collected after vaporization). Process: liquid is HEATED → vapor rises → CONDENSES on cold surface → DRIPS DOWN as PURIFIED liquid. Used to: (1) PURIFY water (distilled water — extremely pure, used in lab/medical/automotive batteries). (2) Make ALCOHOLIC SPIRITS (whiskey, vodka, brandy — distilling fermented liquid increases alcohol concentration; etymology of 'spirit' = the rising essence). (3) Extract ESSENTIAL OILS from herbs/flowers (rose water, lavender oil, etc.). TYPES: (a) SIMPLE DISTILLATION — single stage; works if boiling points differ by > 25°C. (b) FRACTIONAL DISTILLATION — multiple stages with column; separates closer-boiling liquids (used in petroleum refining: gasoline, kerosene, diesel from crude oil). (c) STEAM DISTILLATION — for heat-sensitive volatiles. (d) VACUUM DISTILLATION — at reduced pressure. KEY EQUIPMENT: still, condenser, fractional column. METAPHORICAL USE: 'distill the essence of an idea' = extract the most important part. RELATED WORDS: DISTILLER, DISTILLATE, DISTILLERY. PYQ FREQUENCY: distillation in NEET, NCERT chemistry, SSC GA 1-2× per cycle.

cards.front:
DISCERN means to:

(A) Perceive or recognize clearly
(B) Refuse to acknowledge openly
(C) Confuse and mix things up
(D) Hide something out of sight
cards.back:
(A) Perceive or recognize clearly

Word Roots & Word Formation — DISCERN — etymology DIS (apart) + CERNERE (to separate, sift, Latin) = 'to separate apart, distinguish'. Means to perceive, distinguish, especially with EFFORT or with a SHARP, KEEN MIND. SAMPLE USAGES: (1) 'I could barely discern the figure in the fog.' (2) 'It's hard to discern truth from rumor on social media.' (3) 'A wise leader discerns hidden patterns in data.' WORD FAMILY (root CERN/CRET = separate, sift): (1) DISCREET — careful, prudent (separate from indiscretion). (2) DISCRETE — separate, distinct (separate countable units). (3) DISCRIMINATE — to differentiate (positive); also unfair distinction (negative). (4) SECRET — set apart (kept hidden). (5) SECRETE — to hide; also to produce/release (biology). (6) CONCERN (con + cern) — to sift through, care about. (7) CRITERION — standard for judgment (sifting). DON'T CONFUSE: DISCREET (careful) vs DISCRETE (separate). 'A discreet person handles sensitive matters without gossip'; 'discrete data points are individually countable'. SYNONYMS for discern: detect, perceive, distinguish, identify, recognize, notice. ANTONYMS: overlook, miss, ignore. EXAM-FAVORITE pair: DISCREET / DISCRETE distinction in SSC CGL Tier 2, CAT, GRE-tier vocab. PYQ FREQUENCY: 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
TELECOMMUTING is a workforce trend where employees:

(A) Work from a distance via technology
(B) Travel to multiple offices daily
(C) Use long phone calls only
(D) Watch television during work hours
cards.back:
(A) Work from a distance via technology

Word Roots & Word Formation — TELECOMMUTING — etymology TELE (far) + COMMUTE (travel to work) = working from FAR/REMOTE location, USING TECHNOLOGY (internet, phone, video conferencing) instead of physically commuting to office. RISE: the COVID-19 pandemic (2020-2022) MASSIVELY accelerated telecommuting / 'WORK FROM HOME' (WFH); ~70% of office workers in tech, finance went remote during peak pandemic. Many companies have continued some form of remote/hybrid work. INDIA — IT SECTOR: TCS, Infosys, Wipro had ~3-5% remote pre-pandemic; ~95% during 2020; now ~30-50% hybrid. ADVANTAGES: (1) No commute time/cost (Indian metro commutes can be 2-4 hours daily). (2) Better work-life balance. (3) Wider talent pool (geographic flexibility). (4) Lower office real-estate costs. CHALLENGES: (1) Isolation, mental health. (2) Work-life boundary blurring. (3) Coordination across time zones. (4) Loss of mentorship for juniors. (5) DIGITAL DIVIDE — not all jobs/people can work remotely. RELATED TERMS: TELEWORK, REMOTE WORK, DIGITAL NOMAD, HYBRID WORK. WORLD HUMAN RESOURCES MGMT: 'work from anywhere' policies emerging. PYQ FREQUENCY: telecommuting / WFH in CAT, IBPS PO essay, current affairs.

cards.front:
The root VID/VIS means 'to see'. EVIDENCE literally means:

(A) What can be seen as proof
(B) What is heard about a case
(C) An emotional argument used
(D) A theoretical assumption made
cards.back:
(A) What can be seen as proof

Word Roots & Word Formation — EVIDENCE — etymology e (out) + vid (see) → 'WHAT IS SEEN OUTWARDLY' → that which is APPARENT, observable, can serve as proof. WORD FAMILY (root VID/VIS = see): (1) VISIBLE — capable of being seen. (2) INVISIBLE — not capable of being seen. (3) VISION — sight, ability to see. (4) VIEW — what is seen. (5) VIDEO — Latin 'I see' (video = first-person singular). (6) SUPERVISE (super + vise) — to oversee. (7) ADVISE (ad + vise) — to give counsel ('look toward'). (8) ENVISION — to see in mind. (9) PROVIDE (pro + vid) — to see ahead, anticipate. (10) PRUDENT — see before, careful (from pro + vidence). (11) REVISE (re + vis) — to look at again. (12) PROVIDENCE — divine foresight. (13) EVIDENT — visible, obvious. (14) PROVIDENT — having foresight. (15) SURVEY (sur + vid) — to look over (from French). EXAMPLES: 'visual', 'vista', 'vis-à-vis' (face-to-face). MEDICAL: 'amblyopia' (lazy eye); 'myopia' (near-sightedness). PYQ FREQUENCY: VID/VIS root vocab in SSC CGL, CAT, IBPS PO English — top common-root MCQ ~2 per paper.

cards.front:
What does PROVIDENT mean (root VID = see + PRO = forward)?

(A) Showing foresight; planning ahead
(B) Spending without future plans
(C) Avoiding all responsibilities here
(D) Demanding all things now today
cards.back:
(A) Showing foresight; planning ahead

Word Roots & Word Formation — PROVIDENT — adjective: showing FORESIGHT, careful PLANNING for the future. ETYMOLOGY: pro (forward) + vid (see) = 'seeing ahead'. EXAMPLES: 'a provident person who saves for retirement'; 'her provident habits ensured the family had savings during the recession'. SYNONYMS: prudent, far-sighted, thrifty, frugal, judicious. ANTONYMS: improvident, reckless, spendthrift, profligate, wasteful. INDIA CONTEXT — EMPLOYEES' PROVIDENT FUND (EPF, 1952): mandatory retirement savings scheme; managed by EPFO (Employees' Provident Fund Organisation) under Ministry of Labour. EPF rate (2024-25): 8.25% on contributions. RELATED: PPF (Public Provident Fund) — 15-year voluntary savings scheme. THE CONCEPT: 'providence' = divine foresight; 'providential' = lucky, as if guided by foresight ('a providential escape'). DON'T CONFUSE: 'PROVIDENT' (forward-looking) vs 'PROVINCIAL' (relating to a province; narrow-minded; from 'province'). EXAM-FAVOURITE: synonym/antonym Qs around 'provident' often use 'prudent' or 'reckless' as test answers. PYQ FREQUENCY: 'provident' in SSC CGL, CAT 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
REVISION, from VIS root, literally means:

(A) Looking again or re-examining
(B) First time seeing something
(C) Memorizing without analysis
(D) Forgetting and starting over
cards.back:
(A) Looking again or re-examining

Word Roots & Word Formation — REVISION — etymology re (again) + vis (see) = 'TO SEE/LOOK AGAIN'. Original meaning: re-examining text/ideas to refine, correct, improve. CONTEXTS: (1) STUDENT REVISION — re-reading material to reinforce learning. (2) MANUSCRIPT REVISION — author edits draft. (3) HISTORIOGRAPHY — 'historical revisionism' = re-examining accepted historical narratives (sometimes pejorative if disputing well-established facts). (4) STATISTICAL REVISION — updating GDP/inflation figures. (5) CONSTITUTIONAL REVISION — formal constitutional amendment. WORD FAMILY: REVISE (verb), REVISION (noun), REVISIONIST (one who revises). DON'T CONFUSE: REVISION (looking again) vs REVISIT (going again to a place); REVIEW (formal evaluation, often by others); RECAP (informal summary). EXAM TIP: students often equate 'revision' with 'memorizing' — but it's literally 'seeing again', which IS a form of mental review. STUDY ADVICE: spaced REVISION (spaced repetition) is the most evidence-backed memory technique — used by Anki app, Duolingo, etc. PYQ FREQUENCY: VIS-root vocab in SSC CGL, CAT 2 per paper. EXAMINER MINDSET: rewards systematic root-knowledge.

cards.front:
What does ENVISAGE mean?

(A) Imagine or picture in mind
(B) Avoid thinking about it now
(C) Forget a past event entirely
(D) Express in writing precisely
cards.back:
(A) Imagine or picture in mind

Word Roots & Word Formation — ENVISAGE — verb meaning 'to IMAGINE, FORESEE, picture in mind'. ETYMOLOGY: en (in) + visage (face — French for face, from VIS/VID 'see'). Literally 'to face up to' or 'to confront in vision'. SAMPLE USAGES: 'I can envisage the project being completed by next year.' 'The architects envisaged a building blending into the natural landscape.' SYNONYMS: envision, imagine, foresee, picture, visualize, anticipate, contemplate. RELATED WORDS: VISAGE = the face, especially as an indicator of mood or character ('a stern visage'). VISTA = a long view through a passage; mental view of future. NUANCE: 'envisage' often implies a CONSIDERED MENTAL PICTURE of something planned for the future — slightly more formal than 'imagine'. CONTEXTS: business plans, architectural designs, political reform discussions. EXAM TRAP: students confuse 'envisage' with 'envy' (jealousy) or 'envious' (jealous) — completely different roots (envy from Latin 'invidere' = to look askance). ALSO: 'face/face' — visage and 'physiognomy' (face-reading) are related concepts. PYQ FREQUENCY: ENVISAGE in CAT, GRE, advanced UPSC essay grading; SSC CGL Tier 2 vocabulary 1× per cycle.

cards.front:
VISIONARY (from VIS root) means a person who:

(A) Has imaginative future-oriented ideas
(B) Sees only the immediate present
(C) Repeats past methods always
(D) Has poor eyesight and vision
cards.back:
(A) Has imaginative future-oriented ideas

Word Roots & Word Formation — VISIONARY — noun/adjective: a person with original, IMAGINATIVE thoughts about the future; or having visions/dreams. Both meanings stem from 'seeing beyond the present'. EXAMPLES: 'Steve Jobs was a visionary entrepreneur.' 'The visionary architect designed a city for 2050.' SYNONYMS (positive): innovator, pioneer, futurist, dreamer (positive sense), prophet (in business/political context). NEGATIVE CONNOTATION possible: a 'visionary' can mean impractical dreamer ('His ideas are visionary but not implementable'). SAMPLE INDIAN VISIONARIES: A.P.J. ABDUL KALAM (Vision 2020), MAHATMA GANDHI (non-violent independence), J.R.D. TATA (industrial India), VIKRAM SARABHAI (space program), VERGHESE KURIEN (White Revolution, Amul founder). RELATED: VISION STATEMENTS (corporate) — describing where an organization aspires to go in 5-10 years. EXAM CONTEXT — UPSC ESSAY: 'visionary leadership' is a frequent essay-prompt theme. PYQ FREQUENCY: VISIONARY appears in SSC CGL synonyms-section, CAT vocab, UPSC essay 1× per cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: rewards depth of vocabulary linked to leadership/strategy concepts.

cards.front:
SUPERVISION literally means:

(A) Looking over (oversight)
(B) Being completely blind always
(C) Refusing to oversee anything
(D) Being totally invisible always
cards.back:
(A) Looking over (oversight)

Word Roots & Word Formation — SUPERVISION — etymology super (above, over) + vis (see) = 'LOOKING OVER'. NOUN: the act of overseeing, monitoring, directing. PARALLEL FORMS: SUPERVISE (verb), SUPERVISOR (noun for the person), SUPERVISORY (adjective). SUPERVISION is core to many domains: (1) WORKPLACE — supervisor manages team. (2) ACADEMIC — PhD supervisor guides research. (3) CHILDCARE — adult supervision required. (4) FINANCIAL — RBI supervises banks; SEBI supervises securities markets. (5) MEDICAL — doctor supervises trainees. ETYMOLOGY DEEP-DIVE: 'super' = above, beyond (also gives super-natural, super-power, super-vise, supersonic). 'vis' = see. So 'supervisor' = 'one who sees from above' — captures the bird's-eye-view metaphor of management. RELATED OVERSIGHT WORDS: AUDIT (ear-related, hear), INSPECT (in + spec, look into), MONITOR (to warn), OVERSIGHT (literal English compound). CIVIL SERVICES: 'supervisory cadre' includes IAS, IPS, IRS officers. PYQ FREQUENCY: SUPERVISION-related vocab in SSC CGL synonyms, CAT 1× per cycle. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests root-meaning under standard English word.

cards.front:
What does INVIDIOUS mean (related to the root VID 'see')?

(A) Likely to cause envy or resentment
(B) Highly visible to all observers
(C) Foreseeing future events here
(D) Having the inability to see well
cards.back:
(A) Likely to cause envy or resentment

Word Roots & Word Formation — INVIDIOUS — adjective: likely to AROUSE RESENTMENT or ANGER in others; UNFAIRLY DISCRIMINATING; tending to give offense. ETYMOLOGY: in (against) + vid (see) → 'looking at WITH ENVY' — old Latin 'invidiosus' = envious, hateful. Same root spawns the word ENVY. SAMPLE USAGES: 'It would be invidious to single out one student over another for praise.' 'The judge faced the invidious task of choosing between two equally talented finalists.' 'invidious comparisons' = unfair, resentment-causing comparisons. SYNONYMS: discriminatory, unjust, unfair, offensive, odious, repugnant, distasteful. ANTONYMS: equitable, fair, impartial. KEY DISTINCTION: INVIDIOUS (causing offense/envy) vs INSIDIOUS (treacherous, gradually harmful) — students often confuse these two. INSIDIOUS = sneaky, gradual, like a hidden disease (e.g., 'insidious effects of smoking'). DON'T CONFUSE: ENVIOUS (jealous of others) is the FEELING; INVIDIOUS describes situations or actions that PROVOKE that feeling. PYQ FREQUENCY: 'invidious' is a top CAT, GRE-tier vocab MCQ; less common in SSC. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests advanced English vocabulary distinctions.
cards.option3: Having the inability to see well

cards.front:
The suffix '-able' (as in readable, achievable, comfortable) typically indicates:

(A) Past tense
(B) Capable of being / fit for / suitable for the action
(C) Without
(D) Performer of action
cards.back:
(B) Capable of being / fit for / suitable for the action

Word Roots & Word Formation — -ABLE / -IBLE — adjective-forming suffix meaning 'capable of being [verb]ed'. Readable = capable of being read. Achievable = able to be achieved. Audible = capable of being heard. Visible = capable of being seen. Convertible = able to be converted. -able usually attaches to verbs of native English origin; -ible attaches to Latin-origin verbs (visible, edible, terrible). The two are interchangeable in some words; spelling must be memorised.

cards.front:
Choose the meaning of 'OBJECT' in: 'I OBJECT to that decision strongly.'

(A) To express disagreement or protest
(B) A physical thing or item.
(C) A goal or purpose alone alone
(D) A grammatical noun-role alone.
cards.back:
(A) To express disagreement or protest

Confusables & Word Usage — OBJECT is a STRESS-SHIFT HOMOGRAPH: noun /ˈɒb-dʒɛkt/ (a thing) vs verb /əb-ˈdʒɛkt/ (to oppose). The stress-pattern flips: NOUN stresses 1st syllable; VERB stresses 2nd. Same spelling, different POS, different meaning. PATTERN: many English nouns/verbs share spelling but flip stress: REcord (n) → reCORD (v); PREsent (n) → preSENT (v); SUSpect (n) → susPECT (v); CONtract (n) → conTRACT (v); INcrease (n) → inCREASE (v); REbel, REfund, EXport, IMport — all follow this rule. MEMORY TRICK: 'NOuns get NOrth-stress' (front), 'VErbs go to the VEry-end' (back). USE: 'I OBJECT to your OBJECTION' — same word, both as verb (to-OBject) and noun (the OBject of contention). EXAMINER MINDSET: tests POS recognition + stress-pattern awareness — a real skill in oral English, dictation, and listening comprehension exams (TOEFL, IELTS, Bank PO interview).

cards.front:
What does 'LEAD' mean in: 'The roof was lined with LEAD to prevent radiation leakage.'

(A) A heavy metallic chemical element
(B) To guide or direct alone alone
(C) A small electrical wire alone alone
(D) The first or main role alone alone
cards.back:
(A) A heavy metallic chemical element

Confusables & Word Usage — LEAD has two pronunciations: /lɛd/ (the metal, atomic number 82) and /liːd/ (to guide). Context — 'roof', 'radiation' — points to the METAL. CHEMISTRY: lead has atomic number 82, density 11.34 g/cm³, melting point 327°C. Used historically for plumbing, paint, gasoline (banned now), bullets, and radiation shielding. SCIENCE LINK: lead's high density makes it excellent for blocking gamma rays and X-rays — used in hospital X-ray room walls and nuclear reactor shielding. HEALTH HAZARD: lead is a neurotoxin; childhood lead exposure causes IQ decline, irreversible. India banned leaded petrol in 2000, leaded paint phased out 2014-2016. PYQ ANGLE: 'lead vs led' (past-tense verb), 'lead' as metal vs verb — high-hit confusion in SSC error-spotting. WRITING TIP: past tense of 'lead' (verb) is 'led' — never spelled 'lead' in past tense.

cards.front:
What does 'TEAR' mean in: 'Don't TEAR that important document.'

(A) To rip or pull apart forcibly
(B) A drop of liquid from eye.
(C) To cry or weep aloud.
(D) A momentary spree of fun.
cards.back:
(A) To rip or pull apart forcibly

Confusables & Word Usage — TEAR has two pronunciations: /tɛər/ (to rip — verb) and /tɪər/ (eye-water — noun). Context 'document' fixes it as the RIP verb. ETYMOLOGY DIVERGENCE: rip-tear from Old English 'teran' (to pluck/pull); eye-tear from OE 'tear'/'tæhher' (drop). Different roots, same modern spelling — coincidental homography. RELATED PAIRS: 'wound' /wuːnd/ (injury) vs 'wound' /waʊnd/ (past of wind); 'minute' /ˈmɪnɪt/ (60 sec) vs 'minute' /maɪˈnjuːt/ (very small). WRITING APPLICATION: legal documents avoid homographs deliberately; contracts use 'rip' or 'destroy' instead of 'tear' to prevent ambiguity. EXAMINER MINDSET: tests whether you can rapidly disambiguate based on surrounding noun/verb cues — a key skim-reading skill.

cards.front:
Choose the meaning of 'BOW' in: 'The orchestra musicians took a BOW after the performance.'

(A) To bend forward in respect
(B) A weapon for shooting arrows.
(C) A decorative knot or ribbon.
(D) The front of a ship alone.
cards.back:
(A) To bend forward in respect

CULTURAL ANGLE: bowing is a universal gesture of respect — Japanese culture has elaborate hierarchy of bow depths (15° casual, 30° respectful, 45° deepest apology); Indian 'pranam' is a bow with folded hands. RELATED HOMOGRAPH: 'sow' /soʊ/ (to plant seeds) vs 'sow' /saʊ/ (female pig). VIOLIN INSIGHT: a violin bow uses horsehair (~150-200 strands per bow); rosin grips the strings. ETYMOLOGY DIVERGENCE: bend-bow from OE 'bugan'; weapon-bow from OE 'boga' — distinct roots collapsed in modern spelling. cards.front:
What does 'WIND' mean in: 'WIND the watch carefully each night.'

(A) To turn a key or coil tightly
(B) Movement of air in atmosphere.
(C) Breath or air in the lungs.
(D) A sense of intuition or hint.
cards.back:
(A) To turn a key or coil tightly

Confusables & Word Usage — WIND has two pronunciations: /wɪnd/ (moving air; noun) and /waɪnd/ (to coil/turn; verb). Context 'the watch' fixes it as the COILING verb /waɪnd/. MECHANICAL WATCHES: traditional pre-quartz watches had a mainspring that you'd 'wind' (coil) using the crown — typically once a day; one full wind storing ~36-48 hours of energy. AUTOMATIC WATCHES (1923 Harwood, popularized by Rolex 1931) self-wind via wrist motion + an internal rotor. SCIENCE: wind-up energy is potential elastic energy stored in a coiled metal spring (Hooke's law). RELATED COIL HOMOGRAPHS: 'wound' (past tense /waʊnd/) vs 'wound' (injury /wuːnd/); 'bind' /baɪnd/. ETYMOLOGY: 'wind' (move air) from Proto-Indo-European 'wē-' (to blow); 'wind' (coil) from PIE 'wendh-' (to turn) — separate roots. EXAM ANGLE: SSC RC passages on traditional crafts (clockmaking, weaving) frequently use 'wind' in coiling sense.
cards.option2: Breath or air in the lungs.
cards.option3: A sense of intuition or hint.

cards.front:
Choose the meaning of 'DESERT' in: 'Soldiers who DESERT during war face severe penalties.'

(A) To abandon a duty or post
(B) A vast dry sandy region alone
(C) A sweet course after meals.
(D) A reward for good deeds.
cards.back:
(A) To abandon a duty or post

Confusables & Word Usage — DESERT has stress-shift homography: NOUN /ˈdɛzərt/ = arid land (Sahara, Thar); VERB /dɪˈzɜːrt/ = to abandon. Context 'soldiers... war' fixes it as the VERB. TRIPLE HOMOPHONE EXTENSION: 'dessert' /dɪˈzɜːrt/ (sweet course) is a HOMOPHONE of the verb 'desert' but spelled differently — distinct from 'desert' the noun (arid land). MEMORY TRICK: 'dessert has TWO Ss because you want SECONDS!' MILITARY HISTORY: desertion is a serious offense globally — under the Indian Army Act, peacetime desertion is punishable up to 7 years' imprisonment; wartime desertion can be capital. (A) ADVISE, the verb 'to give counsel'

cards.front:

(B) EFFECT, the noun 'a result'
(C) AFFECTS, plural form of verb
(D) AFFECTED, past tense of affect

cards.front:
A 'homophone' is a word that:

(A) Has the same spelling but different meanings
(B) Sounds the same as another word but has a different spelling and meaning
(C) Means the opposite of another word
(D) Is borrowed from a foreign language
cards.back:
(B) Sounds the same as another word but has a different spelling and meaning

Confusables & Word Usage — Homophone (Greek: 'same sound') — words with identical pronunciation but different spelling AND meaning, e.g., 'their / there / they're', 'flower / flour'. Don't confuse with: homograph (same spelling, possibly different pronunciation, e.g. 'lead' the metal vs 'lead' to guide); homonym (same spelling AND same pronunciation but different meanings, e.g. 'bank' the river-side vs 'bank' the institution); synonyms (different words, similar meaning); antonyms (opposites).

Domain Vocabulary — MERGER — two (usually equal) companies COMBINE into single entity, often forming new name. Compared with ACQUISITION — one company BUYS another (target retains identity or absorbs). Often grouped as 'M&A'. Reasons: synergy, scale, market share, cost cuts, diversification. HOSTILE TAKEOVER — acquisition against target's wishes. SPLIT / DEMERGER — opposite (one company → two). REVERSE MERGER — small private firm acquires public shell (a backdoor IPO).

Domain Vocabulary — IPO — when a PRIVATE company first OFFERS SHARES to the GENERAL PUBLIC, becoming PUBLICLY-TRADED on stock exchange. Reasons: raise capital, exit for early investors / founders, brand visibility. Process: appoint MERCHANT BANKERS / underwriters; file DRHP (Draft Red Herring Prospectus) with SEBI; price discovery via BOOK-BUILDING; listing on BSE/NSE. RIGHTS issue = to existing shareholders. INDIA's IPO BOOM 2020-24 unprecedented; SEBI = market regulator.

cards.front:
INFLATION as an economic term refers to:

(A) General rise in price level of goods + services
(B) Specific rise in food prices only seasonally
(C) Increase in overall money supply alone
(D) Government raising taxes on the rich here
cards.back:
(A) General rise in price level of goods + services

Domain Vocabulary — INFLATION — sustained INCREASE in GENERAL PRICE LEVEL of goods + services over time → reduces PURCHASING POWER. Measured by: CPI (Consumer Price Index, retail level), WPI (Wholesale Price Index), GDP DEFLATOR. INDIA targets 4% CPI ± 2% (RBI inflation target). CAUSES: (1) DEMAND-PULL (excess demand vs supply — too much money chasing too few goods); (2) COST-PUSH (rising input costs — oil, wages, raw materials); (3) BUILT-IN (wage-price spiral). FIGHTING inflation: RBI raises repo rate (cools demand); govt may control commodity supplies. DEFLATION (opposite, falling prices) is also bad — postpones consumption, hurts growth. Both extremes harm; ~2-4% inflation often viewed as healthy.

cards.front:
GDP (Gross Domestic Product) measures:

(A) Total value of goods + services produced within country
(B) Government's annual tax revenue collection here
(C) Just exports + imports trade combined (option here)
(D) Total wealth of all citizens combined (option here)
cards.back:
(A) Total value of goods + services produced within country

Domain Vocabulary — GDP — TOTAL MONETARY VALUE of all GOODS + SERVICES produced WITHIN A COUNTRY's borders in a year. Three calculation methods: PRODUCTION (sum of value-added), INCOME (sum of incomes — wages + rent + interest + profit), EXPENDITURE (C + I + G + (X−M) — consumption, investment, govt spending, net exports). KEY DISTINCTIONS: GDP = TERRITORIAL (within country); GNP = NATIONAL (by residents anywhere); NDP = GDP − depreciation; NOMINAL vs REAL (real adjusts for inflation). India's GDP (2024-25): ~$3.7 trillion (5th largest after US, China, Germany, Japan; will overtake Japan ~2025-26). PER CAPITA INCOME India: ~$2,500 (lower-middle income). HIGH GDP ≠ high quality of life — distribution matters (cf. Gini coefficient).

cards.front:
In standard accounting, a firm's ASSETS minus its LIABILITIES gives its:

(A) Annual revenue
(B) Owners' equity
(C) Gross profit
(D) Operating cash flow
cards.back:
(B) Owners' equity

Domain Vocabulary — Accounting equation: Assets = Liabilities + Equity → Equity = Assets − Liabilities. Equity (or 'net worth' / 'shareholders' equity') is what owners would retain if all debts were settled. Revenue = total income from sales. Gross profit = revenue − cost of goods sold. Operating cash flow = cash generated by operations, a flow not a stock.

cards.front:
A LIQUIDITY problem in a business primarily means that the firm:

(A) Holds excess physical inventory in its warehouses
(B) Cannot quickly convert its assets into cash to pay bills
(C) Reports continuous quarterly losses on its P&L
(D) Has lost a majority of its retail customers

(B) Cannot quickly convert its assets into cash to pay bills

Domain Vocabulary — Liquidity = ease of converting assets to cash without significant value loss. A liquidity crisis means the firm is technically solvent (assets > liabilities) but cannot meet short-term obligations because cash is locked in real estate, inventory, or long receivables. Distinct from INSOLVENCY (assets < liabilities). Distractor 1 = stocking / inventory issue. Distractor 3 = profitability problem. Distractor 4 = demand / market problem.

cards.front:
The word 'gerrymandering' specifically refers to:

(A) Bribery of officials
(B) Manipulating electoral district boundaries to favour a particular political party
(C) Voting twice in the same election

cards.back:

Domain Vocabulary — Gerrymandering — coined 1812 from US Massachusetts Governor Elbridge GERRY + 'salamander' (the salamander-shaped district map he approved). Means redrawing electoral district lines to benefit one party — by 'packing' opposition voters into few districts (waste their majority votes) or 'cracking' them across many (dilute below-majority everywhere). India's Delimitation Commission (constitutional body, Article 82) draws Lok Sabha + Assembly constituencies to prevent partisan distortion — its decisions cannot be challenged in court. The current delimitation is based on the 2001 Census; next will be after the first census post-2026 (recently constitutionally amended to allow this).

An independent commissioner who investigates complaints of maladministration / corruption against public officials. India's institutions in this lineage: LOKPAL (national, set up 2019 under the Lokpal & Lokayuktas Act 2013; jurisdiction includes the PM, with safeguards); LOKAYUKTA (state-level; first set up in Maharashtra 1971; Karnataka, Kerala, MP have had high-profile cases); RBI Banking Ombudsman (now Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021). cards.front:
A 'theocracy' is a state where:

(A) The military is in power
(B) Religious leaders / religious law govern, with the state ruled in the name of a god / divine authority
(C) Scientists make laws
(D) Industrialists control policy
cards.back:
(B) Religious leaders / religious law govern, with the state ruled in the name of a god / divine authority

Domain Vocabulary — Theocracy — Greek 'theos' (god) + 'kratos' (rule). Modern examples: Iran (Islamic Republic; Ayatollah/Guardian Council have ultimate authority); Vatican City (Pope is head of state). Saudi Arabia is sometimes labelled theocratic but is constitutionally an absolute monarchy (with Sharia as basic law). Israel is a JEWISH STATE but not a theocracy (it's a parliamentary democracy). India — SECULAR (Preamble, post 42nd Amendment 1976); the state has no religion + treats all religions equally. Other governance terms — STRATOCRACY (military rule), MERITOCRACY (rule by the talented), KAKISTOCRACY (rule by the worst), KLEPTOCRACY (rule by thieves), GERONTOCRACY (rule by the old).

cards.front:
In a civil suit, the PLAINTIFF is the person who:

(A) Defends the case in front of the trial judge
(B) Initiates the legal action by filing the suit
(C) Records witness statements in the courtroom
(D) Reads out the final verdict in open court
cards.back:
(B) Initiates the legal action by filing the suit

Domain Vocabulary — PLAINTIFF — the party who FILES a civil suit. The opposing party is the DEFENDANT. In criminal cases, the equivalent of the plaintiff is the PROSECUTION (state). Distractor 1 = the defendant. Distractor 3 = court reporter / stenographer. Distractor 4 = the judge.

cards.front:
PERJURY is the criminal offence of:

(A) Refusing to answer a question put by a magistrate
(B) Wilfully telling a lie under oath in a legal proceeding
(C) Disobeying a lawful court order made by the bench
(D) Bribing a witness to favourably testify in court
cards.back:
(B) Wilfully telling a lie under oath in a legal proceeding

Domain Vocabulary — PERJURY — knowingly false statement under oath. Indian Penal Code Section 191-193 criminalises perjury. Sentence up to 7 years + fine. Distractor 1 = contempt or refusal-to-testify, different offence. Distractor 3 = contempt of court. Distractor 4 = subornation (bribing a witness, distinct offence).

cards.front:
An ACQUITTAL is a court verdict that:

(A) Convicts the accused and imposes a prison sentence
(B) Declares the accused not guilty of the alleged charges
(C) Sends the case to a higher court for fresh review
(D) Postpones the hearing to a later scheduled date
cards.back:
(B) Declares the accused not guilty of the alleged charges

Domain Vocabulary — ACQUITTAL — finding of NOT GUILTY by the court. The accused is then released and cannot be tried again for the same offence (double-jeopardy bar — Article 20(2) of the Constitution + Section 300 CrPC). Distractor 1 = conviction. Distractor 3 = appeal / remand. Distractor 4 = adjournment.

cards.front:
An ALIBI is a defence used by an accused person to show that:

(A) Another known person also committed a similar crime
(B) He was elsewhere when the alleged crime was committed
(C) The crime was committed in self-defence under threat
(D) The witness against him is biased or unreliable
cards.back:
(B) He was elsewhere when the alleged crime was committed

Domain Vocabulary — ALIBI — Latin 'alibi' (elsewhere). The accused proves he was at a DIFFERENT location when the crime occurred → cannot have done it. Burden of proof is on the accused (to a preponderance, not beyond reasonable doubt). Section 11 of Indian Evidence Act allows alibi evidence. Distractor 1 = alternative-suspect theory. Distractor 3 = self-defence plea. Distractor 4 = challenge to witness credibility.

cards.front:
An AFFIDAVIT is most accurately described as:

(A) An informal letter written from one party to another
(B) A written statement of facts sworn before a notary or magistrate
(C) A copy of an original document attested as a true copy
(D) An order issued by a higher court to a lower court
cards.back:
(B) A written statement of facts sworn before a notary or magistrate

Domain Vocabulary — AFFIDAVIT — written sworn statement. Must be sworn before an authorised official (notary public / magistrate / oath commissioner). Used widely in Indian courts and admin to verify facts under penalty of perjury. Distractor 1 = informal letter / private correspondence. Distractor 3 = ATTESTED copy or certified copy. Distractor 4 = writ / order.

cards.front:
An INDICTMENT is a formal:

(A) Apology issued to the court before sentencing
(B) Charge accusing a person of a serious criminal offence
(C) Out-of-court agreement settling a civil dispute
(D) Pardon granted by the executive head of the state
cards.back:
(B) Charge accusing a person of a serious criminal offence

Domain Vocabulary — INDICTMENT — formal accusation, usually presented by a prosecutor (or a grand jury in US). Sets out the criminal charges the accused must answer. In India, the equivalent is the 'chargesheet' (filed by police / investigating agency under Section 173 CrPC) and 'framing of charges' by the trial court. Distractor 1 = apology / mitigation. Distractor 3 = settlement / compromise. Distractor 4 = clemency / pardon (Article 72 / Article 161).

cards.front:
BAIL is the temporary release of an arrested person, typically on:

(A) A pardon from the head of the state in question
(B) A bond or surety guaranteeing the accused's later appearance
(C) Acquittal by the trial judge after first hearing
(D) Settlement of the alleged offence outside the courtroom
cards.back:
(B) A bond or surety guaranteeing the accused's later appearance

Domain Vocabulary — BAIL — temporary release pending trial; the accused signs a bond (and/or sureties stand guarantee) promising to appear when summoned. In India regulated by Cr.P.C. (and now BNSS, 2023). 'Bailable' offences — bail is a right; 'non-bailable' — court's discretion. ANTICIPATORY BAIL (Section 438 Cr.P.C.) — before arrest. Distractor 1 = pardon (clemency, Article 72/161). Distractor 3 = acquittal (final). Distractor 4 = compounding / settlement (separate concept).

cards.front:
Identify the literary device: 'Time is a thief.'

(A) Simile (uses 'like' or 'as')
(B) Metaphor (direct comparison)
(C) Alliteration (repeating sounds)
(D) Onomatopoeia (sound words)
cards.back:
(B) Metaphor (direct comparison)

Domain Vocabulary — METAPHOR = DIRECT comparison (no 'like' or 'as'); says one thing IS another. 'Time IS a thief' implies time silently steals our moments. Compare with SIMILE (uses 'like' or 'as'): 'Time is LIKE a thief' = simile. Other examples of metaphor: 'Life is a journey'; 'Her eyes are stars'; 'Education is the key to success'. INSIGHT — metaphors are POWERFUL because the brain unconsciously equates the two; reshapes thinking. Famous: Shakespeare 'All the world's a stage' (metaphor for life). EXTENDED METAPHOR = a metaphor sustained over many lines (e.g., Robert Frost's 'The Road Not Taken' — life as a forked path).

cards.front:
'She sells seashells by the seashore.' This is an example of:

(A) Hyperbole (deliberate exaggeration)
(B) Alliteration (repeating consonant sounds)
(C) Personification (human traits to things)
(D) Metaphor (direct comparison) here
cards.back:
(B) Alliteration (repeating consonant sounds)

Domain Vocabulary — ALLITERATION = repetition of CONSONANT sounds at start of nearby words. 'Sells seashells seashore' — repeated 'S' sound. Common in TONGUE TWISTERS, poetry, advertising (Coca-Cola, Mickey Mouse, Krispy Kreme). RELATED: ASSONANCE = repeated VOWEL sounds ('hear the mellow wedding bells' — Poe); CONSONANCE = repeated consonants anywhere (not just start) ('pitter-patter'); ONOMATOPOEIA = words that imitate sounds (buzz, hiss, splash, meow). INSIGHT — alliteration creates RHYTHM + makes phrases memorable. Why brand names use it: easier to recall.

cards.front:
'I have told you a million times not to do that!' is an example of:

(A) Irony (saying opposite of meaning)
(B) Hyperbole (deliberate exaggeration)
(C) Simile (using 'like' or 'as')
(D) Metaphor (direct comparison form)
cards.back:
(B) Hyperbole (deliberate exaggeration)

Domain Vocabulary — HYPERBOLE = deliberate EXAGGERATION for effect (not literally meant). 'A million times' = many times. Other examples: 'I'm so hungry I could eat a horse'; 'This bag weighs a tonne'; 'I died laughing'. NOT the same as a LIE — both speaker + listener KNOW it's exaggerated. Used in: poetry, casual speech, marketing, comedy. INSIGHT — opposite of hyperbole is UNDERSTATEMENT / LITOTES (deliberate downplay): 'It's not bad' (= it's good); 'a few problems' (when there are many). Both add EMPHASIS via deviation from literal truth. Hyperbole adds DRAMA; understatement adds IRONY or modesty.

cards.front:
'The wind whispered through the trees' uses which device?

(A) Hyperbole (overstatement device)
(B) Personification (human traits to non-human)
(C) Onomatopoeia (sound-imitating words)
(D) Alliteration (consonant repetition)
cards.back:
(B) Personification (human traits to non-human)

Domain Vocabulary — PERSONIFICATION = giving HUMAN traits / actions to non-human things (objects, animals, ideas). Wind doesn't literally whisper — humans do; attributing whispering to wind = personification. Other examples: 'The flowers danced in the breeze'; 'Time waits for no one'; 'Lady Liberty' (statue personifies liberty as a woman). INSIGHT — personification makes abstract or non-human things RELATABLE + EMOTIONAL. Common in poetry, fables, mythology. ANTHROPOMORPHISM = related — physically attributing human form (Mickey Mouse standing, talking). PATHETIC FALLACY = subset where NATURE reflects human emotion ('the rain wept all day for the lost soul').

cards.front:
'Water, water everywhere, nor any drop to drink' (Coleridge) shows:

(A) Hyperbole (overstatement) only here also
(B) Irony (situational) — surrounded by water yet thirsty
(C) Alliteration (consonant sounds) here also
(D) Onomatopoeia (sound imitation) here also
cards.back:
(B) Irony (situational) — surrounded by water yet thirsty

Domain Vocabulary — IRONY — when there's a contrast between expected + actual / surface + meaning. SITUATIONAL irony = events contrary to expectation. Sailors in OCEAN are surrounded by water yet DYING of thirst (sea water = undrinkable). Coleridge's 'The Rime of the Ancient Mariner' (1798). Three types: SITUATIONAL (gap between expectation + reality); VERBAL (saying opposite of what you mean — close to sarcasm); DRAMATIC (audience knows what character doesn't, e.g., Romeo thinks Juliet is dead — audience knows she's faking). INSIGHT — irony adds depth, often tragic or comic. Common Indian example: rain-shortage in Cherrapunji, once world's wettest place — situational irony.

cards.front:
'My love is like a red, red rose' (Robert Burns) is a:

(A) Metaphor (direct comparison form)
(B) Simile (uses 'like' for comparison)
(C) Personification (human traits given)
(D) Hyperbole (a deliberate exaggeration)
cards.back:
(B) Simile (uses 'like' for comparison)

Domain Vocabulary — SIMILE = comparison using 'LIKE' or 'AS'. 'My love is LIKE a red rose'. Compare to METAPHOR (no 'like/as'): 'My love is a rose' = metaphor. Both compare; simile is EXPLICIT comparison, metaphor is IMPLICIT. Famous similes: 'busy as a bee', 'cold as ice', 'sly as a fox', 'as light as a feather'. INSIGHT — similes are gentler / less assertive than metaphors. 'She is like a queen' (suggests resemblance) vs 'She is a queen' (more declarative). EXAM TIP: search for 'like' or 'as' = simile; absence + still comparison = metaphor.

'The bees buzzed as the kettle whistled' uses which device?

(A) Personification (human qualities)
(B) Onomatopoeia (sound-imitating words)
(C) Hyperbole (overstatement device)
(D) Metaphor (direct comparison form)
cards.back:
(B) Onomatopoeia (sound-imitating words)

Domain Vocabulary — ONOMATOPOEIA = words that IMITATE the sound they describe. 'BUZZ' (bees), 'WHISTLE' (kettle), and others — bang, crash, splash, hiss, meow, oink, tick-tock, gurgle, sizzle. INSIGHT — onomatopoeia bridges sound + meaning; makes writing VIVID + sensory. COMICS use these (POW! BAM! ZAP!). DIFFERENT LANGUAGES have different onomatopoeia for same sound — dog barks: English 'woof', Hindi 'bhau', Japanese 'wan-wan', French 'ouaf'; rooster: English 'cock-a-doodle-doo', Hindi 'kukdu-koo'. Reflects cultural ear-perception. Greek roots: 'onoma' = name; 'poiein' = to make → 'name-making'.

(B) Deliberate exaggeration not meant to be taken literally

cards.back:
(B) Deliberate exaggeration not meant to be taken literally

cards.front:
A CHRONIC illness is one that:

(A) Comes on suddenly and ends in a few days at most
(B) Persists for a long period and recurs over many years
(C) Spreads rapidly between members of a household
(D) Cannot be detected by any standard medical test
cards.back:
(B) Persists for a long period and recurs over many years

Domain Vocabulary — CHRONIC = long-lasting / persistent (months to years; often life-long). Examples: diabetes, hypertension, asthma, chronic kidney disease, rheumatoid arthritis. Opposite term: ACUTE — sudden onset, short duration (e.g., flu, appendicitis). Distractor 1 = acute. Distractor 3 = contagious (infectious). Distractor 4 = idiopathic / occult illness.

cards.front:
A BENIGN tumour is one that:

(A) Spreads rapidly to other organs across the body
(B) Is non-cancerous and does not invade nearby tissue
(C) Is always fatal regardless of treatment given
(D) Forms only in skin cells of older patients
cards.back:
(B) Is non-cancerous and does not invade nearby tissue

Domain Vocabulary — BENIGN — non-cancerous, slow-growing, well-defined boundary, doesn't invade neighbouring tissue or metastasise. Often harmless unless pressing on a vital structure (a benign brain tumour can still need removal due to space limits). Examples: lipoma, fibroma, common moles. MALIGNANT — cancerous, invasive, can metastasise. Distractor 1 = malignant behaviour. Distractor 3 = false generalisation; benign tumours are usually treatable. Distractor 4 = unrelated.

cards.front:
PROGNOSIS in a medical setting refers to:

(A) Identifying the disease from its observable signs and symptoms
(B) Predicting the likely course and outcome of the disease
(C) Selecting the medication best suited to treat the disease
(D) Examining the patient physically to look for any abnormality

(B) Predicting the likely course and outcome of the disease

cards.front:
A CONTAGIOUS disease is one that:

(A) Develops only as a side-effect of medical treatment
(B) Spreads from one person to another by direct or indirect contact
(C) Originates from genetic mutations passed down at birth
(D) Worsens because of an unhealthy lifestyle and poor diet
cards.back:
(B) Spreads from one person to another by direct or indirect contact

Domain Vocabulary — CONTAGIOUS — Latin 'contagio' (contact). Spreads via direct contact, droplets, fomites, etc. Examples: COVID-19, common cold, measles, chickenpox, ringworm. INFECTIOUS — broader term for any disease caused by pathogens (some infectious diseases are not very contagious — e.g., tetanus, rabies require specific exposure). EPIDEMIC — sudden rise in cases above expected baseline in a region. PANDEMIC — epidemic across multiple countries / continents. ENDEMIC — consistently present at a baseline level (e.g., malaria in some regions). Distractor 1 = iatrogenic. Distractor 3 = hereditary / genetic. Distractor 4 = lifestyle disease.

cards.front:
A PLACEBO is best understood as:

(A) A new drug that has just been approved by regulators
(B) An inactive substance given as a control in a drug trial
(C) A targeted antibiotic that fights only one type of bacteria
(D) A herbal supplement sold as a daily wellness product
cards.back:
(B) An inactive substance given as a control in a drug trial

Domain Vocabulary — PLACEBO — Latin 'I shall please'. Sugar pill / saline injection / inert substance with no pharmacological effect. Used as the CONTROL ARM in randomised controlled trials so the active drug's effect can be separated from psychological/observational effects. THE PLACEBO EFFECT — measurable improvement in symptoms even from inert treatment, due to expectation, conditioning, regression to the mean, and clinician attention. Distractor 1 = a new approved drug, not inert. Distractor 3 = narrow-spectrum antibiotic. Distractor 4 = nutraceutical / supplement (active ingredients claimed but unregulated).

cards.front:
An EPIDEMIC differs from a PANDEMIC in that an epidemic is:

(A) Always more severe than any pandemic disease
(B) Confined to a particular region or country, not global
(C) Affects only a single age-group within a country
(D) Caused only by viruses, while pandemics by bacteria
cards.back:
(B) Confined to a particular region or country, not global

Domain Vocabulary — EPIDEMIC — sudden rise in disease cases above the baseline in a particular region / country. PANDEMIC — an epidemic that has spread across multiple countries or continents (a pandemic is a 'large epidemic'). The WHO declares pandemics; COVID-19 was declared a pandemic on 11 March 2020. ENDEMIC — disease that is always present at a baseline rate (e.g., malaria in many tropical regions). OUTBREAK — small, localised cluster of cases. Distractor 1 — severity isn't the defining factor; geographic spread is. Distractor 3 — age isn't the criterion. Distractor 4 — pathogen type isn't the criterion.

cards.front:
An ANTIBIOTIC is a medicine that primarily acts against:

(A) Allergic reactions to common pollen and dust mites
(B) Bacterial infections, by killing or inhibiting bacteria
(C) Viral infections like influenza or the common cold
(D) Inflammatory pain and fever from any general source
cards.back:
(B) Bacterial infections, by killing or inhibiting bacteria

Domain Vocabulary — ANTIBIOTICS — kill bacteria or inhibit their growth. Examples: penicillin (Fleming, 1928), amoxicillin, ciprofloxacin, azithromycin. They DO NOT work against viruses (overprescription drives antibiotic RESISTANCE — a major global-health crisis). Distractor 1 = antihistamines (e.g., cetirizine). Distractor 3 = antivirals (e.g., oseltamivir for flu); cold has no specific antiviral. Distractor 4 = anti-inflammatories (NSAIDs like ibuprofen) and antipyretics (paracetamol). Mis-classifying these is a common medical-vocabulary error.

Quality-control mechanism in modern science. Distractor 1 confuses peer review with conference talks. Distractor 3 — public voting is not standard. A PARADIGM SHIFT (Thomas Kuhn) refers to:

(A) A small refinement to existing scientific knowledge
(B) A fundamental change in basic concepts and practices
(C) Replacement of one government's leader with another
(D) A change of textbook used in a single university
cards.back:
(B) A fundamental change in basic concepts and practices

Domain Vocabulary — Thomas Kuhn — 'The Structure of Scientific Revolutions' (1962). Normal science proceeds within a 'paradigm' (set of shared assumptions). When anomalies accumulate, a 'paradigm shift' occurs — a fundamental rethink. Examples: Ptolemy → Copernicus (geo to helio); Newton → Einstein (absolute to relative); classical → quantum mechanics; geology's continental drift; oncology's gene-targeted therapy. The phrase has become widely used outside science (often loosely). Distractor 1 = 'normal science' (refinement). Distractor 3, 4 = misuses of the term.

cards.option2: Replacement of one government's leader with another
cards.option3: A change of textbook used in a single university

cards.front:
REPLICATION in scientific research is important because:

(A) Repeating a study wastes time and money to no avail
(B) It tests whether the original result is reliable and reproducible
(C) It allows authors to publish the same paper multiple times
(D) It proves that scientific theories never need to be revised
cards.back:
(B) It tests whether the original result is reliable and reproducible

Domain Vocabulary — Replication — independent re-running of an experiment to confirm the original result. Failures of replication, especially in psychology + social sciences (the 'replication crisis' since ~2010s), have prompted reforms: pre-registration of hypotheses, open data, larger sample sizes, paying more attention to effect sizes. A single experiment is rarely conclusive; reliable knowledge requires REPLICATION across labs and decades. Distractor 1 — replication is essential, not wasteful. Distractor 3 = self-plagiarism, unethical. Distractor 4 — replication, when failing, prompts theory revision.

cards.option2: It allows authors to publish the same paper multiple times
cards.option3: It proves that scientific theories never need to be revised

cards.front:
CORRELATION vs CAUSATION — a common scientific reminder is that:

(A) Two correlated events always cause one another
(B) Correlation does not imply causation by itself
(C) Causation always requires a strong correlation first
(D) Correlation is irrelevant to scientific reasoning at all
cards.back:
(B) Correlation does not imply causation by itself

Domain Vocabulary — Correlation = two variables move together statistically. Causation = one variable directly influences the other. Correlation may arise from: (a) genuine causation A→B; (b) reverse causation B→A; (c) common cause / confounder; (d) coincidence; (e) selection bias. The classic example: ice-cream sales correlate with drowning rates → both caused by hot weather (confounder), not by each other. Establishing causation needs randomised controlled trials, instrumental variables, or natural experiments. Distractor 1 — too strong; correlation doesn't always imply causation. Distractor 3 — backwards (causation IMPLIES correlation, not the reverse). Distractor 4 — overstates the criticism.

cards.option2: Causation always requires a strong correlation first
cards.option3: Correlation is irrelevant to scientific reasoning at all

cards.front:
A PLACEBO-CONTROLLED trial is one in which:

(A) All participants receive only the active drug studied
(B) Some participants receive an inactive substance for comparison
(C) All participants receive a different existing drug regimen
(D) Only the lead investigator knows which group is which
cards.back:
(B) Some participants receive an inactive substance for comparison

Domain Vocabulary — Placebo-controlled trial: one group gets the test drug, the other gets a PLACEBO (sugar pill / inert). Differences in outcome attributable to the drug, not to expectation or natural recovery. Often DOUBLE-BLIND (neither participant nor researcher knows assignment) to avoid bias. The gold standard in clinical research. Distractor 1 — without control, can't separate drug effect. Distractor 3 = active-control trial (different design — e.g., compares new drug to current standard). Distractor 4 = single-blind, weaker than double-blind.

cards.option2: All participants receive a different existing drug regimen
cards.option3: Only the lead investigator knows which group is which

cards.front:
An ITINERARY is best described as:

(A) A vehicle used for tourist travel
(B) A planned route or schedule of a journey
(C) A travel diary written after the trip
(D) A passport stamp issued at the border
cards.back:
(B) A planned route or schedule of a journey

Domain Vocabulary — ITINERARY — Latin 'iter' (journey). A planned route + schedule of stops, dates, activities. 'Detailed itinerary for the 7-day trip.' Distractor 1 = vehicle. Distractor 3 = travelogue. Distractor 4 = visa stamp.

cards.front:
A SOJOURN refers to:

(A) A short trip to a nearby destination quickly
(B) A temporary stay at a place during a journey
(C) A permanent residence in a foreign country
(D) A solo backpacking trip across a continent
cards.back:
(B) A temporary stay at a place during a journey

Domain Vocabulary — SOJOURN — French origin; a TEMPORARY stay. Implies the traveller will move on. 'A brief sojourn in Paris before flying to Rome.' Synonyms: stopover, layover, visit. Distractor 1 = excursion. Distractor 3 = settlement / immigration. Distractor 4 = backpacking trip.

cards.front:
An EXPEDITION typically refers to:

(A) A short trip to a local market or shop
(B) An organised journey for exploration or research
(C) A casual weekend visit to relatives' homes
(D) A daily commute to work and back home
cards.back:
(B) An organised journey for exploration or research

Domain Vocabulary — EXPEDITION — Latin 'expedire' (to set free, prepare for action). An ORGANISED journey with a specific purpose: exploration, research, scientific study, military operation. Examples: Antarctic expedition, Mount Everest expedition, Magellan's circumnavigation, Lewis & Clark expedition. Distractors describe routine / casual travel.

cards.front:
A PERIPATETIC person is one who:

(A) Is afraid of any travel beyond home
(B) Travels frequently from place to place
(C) Lives only in one place all life
(D) Refuses to walk and prefers vehicles
cards.back:
(B) Travels frequently from place to place

Domain Vocabulary — PERIPATETIC — Greek 'peripatetikos' (walking around). Wandering, frequent traveller, itinerant. 'Aristotle's peripatetic school' — he taught while walking. Modern usage: 'A peripatetic teacher who works at multiple schools.' Distractor 1 = agoraphobic / hodophobic. Distractor 3 = sedentary. Distractor 4 unrelated.

cards.front:
An EXODUS is most accurately defined as:

(A) A small group's casual short trip
(B) A mass departure of people from a place
(C) A circular movement returning to start
(D) A solo adventurer's brief detour
cards.back:
(B) A mass departure of people from a place

Domain Vocabulary — EXODUS — Greek 'ex-' (out) + 'hodos' (way). MASS DEPARTURE / migration. Famous example: Biblical Exodus (Israelites' departure from Egypt). Modern usage: 'Mass exodus from cities during the COVID-19 lockdown.' Antonym: INFLUX. Synonym: emigration (when crossing borders). Distractors describe other small-scale movements.

cards.option2: A circular movement returning to start

cards.front:
To EMBARK on a journey means to:

(A) End or complete a journey successfully
(B) Begin or start a journey, especially by ship
(C) Cancel a journey midway through it
(D) Pause a journey for a brief rest stop
cards.back:
(B) Begin or start a journey, especially by ship

Domain Vocabulary — EMBARK — Old French 'embarquer' (board a ship). Originally a nautical term: to board a ship. By extension: to BEGIN a journey or undertaking. 'They embarked on a new business venture.' Antonym: DISEMBARK (to get off, especially a ship). Distractor 1 = arrive / disembark. Distractors 3, 4 are unrelated.

cards.option3: Pause a journey for a brief rest stop

cards.front:
A NOMAD is best described as:

(A) A person living permanently in one city
(B) A person who moves from place to place seasonally
(C) A person travelling only for sightseeing tours
(D) A scientist studying ancient migration patterns
cards.back:
(B) A person who moves from place to place seasonally

Domain Vocabulary — NOMAD — Greek 'nomas' (roaming for pasture). Member of a community or culture that MOVES SEASONALLY rather than settles permanently — usually following pasture, water, or herds. Examples: Bedouins (Arabian desert), Mongolian herders, Maasai (East Africa), Banjaras (India), Roma. Modern 'digital nomad' — remote workers travelling continuously. Antonym: SETTLED. Distractors are not nomadic in this sense.
